docs.title: Mediterranean Travels
docs.text: A day-by-day travel guide for a November 2026 journey from Istanbul to Athens, exploring the history of civilization, culture, cuisine, and the people who live along the way.

docs.title: The Journey
docs.text:
Thirteen days through Turkey and Greece, November 11–23, 2026:

  • Nov 11–13: Istanbul on our own. Three days in the city that straddles Europe and Asia.
  • Nov 14–20: the Viking Star cruise. Ancient Mediterranean Treasures, from Istanbul past Troy and Ephesus to Rhodes, Crete, and Athens.
  • Nov 21–23: Athens on our own. Three days in the city where democracy, philosophy, and theater began, with a day trip to the oracle at Delphi on Nov 22.

The Trip Description has the full day-by-day itinerary, and the Viking Cruise Map shows the route port by port, ending with the road to Delphi.

docs.title: How to Use This Guide
docs.text:
There is one chapter for each day of the trip. Read it at breakfast or the night before. Each chapter covers:

  • what we will see that day, and the stories behind it
  • details to notice that most visitors walk past
  • food and drink to try, and the history in the dish
  • the people who live there now, and how to be good guests
  • practical notes on timing, closures, and November weather

The Chapters page lists every day. Use the search bar to find a person, place, or dish.

docs.title: What's Inside
docs.text:
• Chapters: one per day, plus a chapter to read before we leave and one for the trip home.
  • MicroSims: interactive maps and other tools, starting with the cruise route.
  • Learning Graph: the map of ideas behind the guide. It lists the people, places, and events the chapters cover, and shows which ones help explain the others.

docs.title: About
docs.text: A day-by-day travel guide for a November 2026 journey from Istanbul to Athens, exploring the history of civilization, culture, cuisine, and the people who live along the way.

docs.title: Why This Guide Exists
docs.text: It is easy to visit Hagia Sophia, Ephesus, or the Acropolis, take a photograph, and move on. This guide exists to slow down and notice more. It is written for travelers who love the long history of civilization, who want to understand a culture through its food, and who want to meet the people of each place with real empathy, not just walk past them on the way to the next monument.

docs.title: Who It Is For
docs.text: The travelers on this trip: curious adults with no professional background in archaeology or classics. No prior knowledge is assumed beyond having heard of ancient Greece, Rome, Christianity, Islam, and the Ottoman Empire. Every other term is explained when it first appears.

docs.title: How to Use This Guide
docs.text:
• Read one chapter a day. Each chapter matches one day of the trip, from November 11 to November 23, 2026. Breakfast or the night before is the best time.
  • Read the before-you-go chapter first. It sets out the big timeline of the region and a few words of Turkish and Greek.
  • Use the Viking Cruise Map to see where each port is, how the ship gets there, and the road from Athens to Delphi.
  • Search (top right) for any person, place, or dish.
  • Keep a journal. A few lines each evening about what we noticed, ate, and learned from the people we met is worth more than a hundred photographs.

Cruise port times come from cruise-agency listings and can change. Confirm them with Viking, and check opening hours locally, since November is off-season.

docs.title: Color Theme: Terracotta and Olive
docs.text: The site's colors come from the places on the trip: roof tiles, amphorae, and olive groves. Terracotta, the color of fired clay, runs through the header and the links. Olive green, the color of the groves along the Aegean coast and of Glaux the owl's satchel, highlights a link when you point at it. Together they make a warm, earthy palette that belongs to both Turkey and Greece.

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Mediterranean Travels

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This is not a textbook. It is a personal travel guide for a thirteen-day journey through Turkey and Greece, from Wednesday, November 11 to Monday, November 23, 2026. The trip has three parts: three days on our own in Istanbul, the Viking Star's seven-night Ancient Mediterranean Treasures cruise from Istanbul to Athens, and three days on our own in Athens, including a day trip to Delphi.

The guide is meant to be read one chapter per day, ideally at breakfast or the night before. Each chapter prepares us for that day's place: what happened there, who built it and why, what to look for when we are standing in front of it, what to eat, and who lives there now. The goal is not to tick off sights. It is to notice more, understand more, and meet the people of each place with real empathy.

Two chapters break the one-place-per-day pattern on purpose. The first, Paul at Ephesus, is a deep-dive chapter, read before our visit to Ephesus, about the apostle Paul: who he was, what he taught, and how a single traveling teacher with a small team built a movement that reshaped Western philosophy. It places his two to three years in Ephesus inside the whole arc of his life and letters, and it reads his work as a case study in leadership and change. Along the way it draws parallels to a modern change problem: turning schools built around legacy direct instruction into AI-native learning organizations, with notes that link to our companion textbook, AI-Native Schools.

The second, The Oracle and the Algorithm, is a reflective deep dive built around our day at Delphi. For roughly eleven to twelve centuries, people climbed the slopes of Mount Parnassus to ask Apollo's priestess what their choices would bring. Kings, cities, and ordinary farmers all came, and the answers helped decide wars, found colonies, and shape Greek philosophy. Today we ask machine-learning models the same kind of question. The chapter looks at the human need behind both: to see, before we act, what today's actions will do to our future, and what we owe ourselves when we hand that seeing to someone or something else.

A third thread runs through the whole guide: Learning for All. Almost every stop on this route holds a story about who got to learn, who was shut out, and which technologies or institutions widened the circle: an alphabet, a press, a library, a tutor, an endowment. Each daily chapter ends with a short note that connects that day's story to today's effort to use AI to bring a good education to every child on Earth.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: The travelers on this trip: curious adults who love the history of civilization, culture, and food, and who want to understand the people in each place, not just see the monuments. We have no professional background in archaeology, classics, theology, or Middle Eastern or Balkan history. We do have a professional interest in how organizations change, especially schools adapting to AI. One of us works as an evangelist for AI in the democratization of education for all children on Earth. The two deep-dive chapters and the Learning for All notes are written with that work in mind.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: None. The guide assumes only general adult knowledge, such as having heard of ancient Greece, the Roman Empire, Christianity, Islam, and the Ottoman Empire. Every other term is explained when it first appears.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• One chapter per day of the itinerary (thirteen chapters). Istanbul and Athens each get several chapters, so each day can focus on a different layer of the city instead of repeating an overview.
  • A short orientation chapter to read before departure: the big timeline of the region, a few words of Turkish and Greek, and how the trip fits together. It also introduces the Learning for All thread, starting with the word evangelist itself (see below).
  • A deep-dive chapter, Paul at Ephesus, to read the evening of Day 6 (sailing from Çanakkale to Kusadasi), so it is fresh when we walk into Ephesus on Day 7. It is longer than a daily chapter and is described in its own section below.
  • A deep-dive chapter, The Oracle and the Algorithm, about Delphi and prediction. Read the first half (the oracle's story) the night of Day 11, so we know what we are looking at on Day 12. Save the second half (the reflection on prediction and AI) for the 2½-hour drive back to Athens or that evening, when the site is still in our heads. It is described in its own section below.
  • A short closing chapter to read on the way home: connecting what we saw across all the stops, and drawing the Learning for All notes together into a few lessons for spreading education "with" communities rather than "to" them.

Every daily chapter should cover, where it fits:

  1. What we will see, in the order we are likely to see it.
  2. The history behind it, told as stories about people, not lists of dates.
  3. Things to notice that most visitors walk past.
  4. Food and drink to try that day, and the history in the dish.
  5. The people who live there now: daily life, work, faith, and what tourism means to them, especially in the off-season.
  6. Etiquette and a few useful words, so we can be good guests.
  7. Practical notes: timing, distances, closures, and weather.
  8. Learning for All: a short closing note, a few paragraphs at most, that ties one story from the day to the effort to democratize education with AI, with a link to the matching chapter of AI-Native Schools where one fits. The plan for these notes is in the Learning for All section below.

docs.title: Why this chapter exists
docs.text:
Paul of Tarsus may be the most influential teacher in Western history who never held an office, owned a building, or wrote a book. He wrote letters. Around twenty years after Jesus died, Paul was turning a small Jewish renewal movement into a network of mixed Jewish and Gentile (non-Jewish) communities spread across the Roman East, and his letters became the oldest writings in the New Testament. Ideas that later shaped Christian philosophy, from grace and faith to conscience and love as the highest virtue, reach Augustine, Aquinas, Luther, and the modern world largely through him.

Ephesus was the hub of that work. According to the Book of Acts, Paul taught there for two to three years (about 52–55 CE), longer than anywhere else, and "all the residents of Asia" heard the message from that base (Acts 19:10). He wrote at least one letter from Ephesus (1 Corinthians), and possibly more. The chapter uses Ephesus as the place where we can stand inside Paul's story, then widens out to his whole career.

The second purpose is practical. Paul faced a classic change-leadership problem: a respected legacy institution, deeply held rules about who belongs and how learning happens, economic interests tied to the old way, internal factions, and very slow communication. School leaders trying to move from direct instruction (the teacher-at-the-front lecture model) to AI-native learning face a smaller but recognizable version of the same problem. The chapter treats Paul as a case study in leadership, and each lesson ends with a short "For AI-native schools" note that links to the matching chapter of AI-Native Schools.

docs.title: What the chapter should cover
docs.text:
1. Paul's life in brief: born in Tarsus, a Roman citizen and a Pharisee (a strict teacher of Jewish law) trained in Jerusalem; persecutor of the early Jesus movement; his turning point on the road to Damascus; and his travels across Anatolia, Macedonia, and Greece, ending in arrest and death in Rome.
  2. Paul in Ephesus: three months in the synagogue, then two years teaching daily in the rented lecture hall of Tyrannus; his co-workers Priscilla and Aquila; the teacher Apollos; the riot of the silversmiths, led by Demetrius, who made shrines of the goddess Artemis and feared for their trade (Acts 19); his farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus (Acts 20).
  3. Paul's ideas: grace and faith rather than law as the way in; "neither Jew nor Greek" (Galatians 3:28); the community as one body with many parts (1 Corinthians 12); love as the greatest virtue (1 Corinthians 13); and how he borrowed the language of Greek philosophy, especially the Stoics, to reach Greek listeners.
  4. Paul's lasting impact on Christian philosophy: his influence on Augustine, the Reformation, and modern ideas of the individual conscience and human equality; and the harder parts of his legacy, including how his words on Jews, women, and slavery were later used.
  5. Which letters are his: scholars broadly agree that seven letters are Paul's own (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon). Others, including the Letter to the Ephesians, are debated. The Book of Acts was written a generation later and tells Paul's story from its own point of view. The chapter should say which source each claim comes from.
  6. Things to notice at Ephesus: the Great Theater, where the silversmiths' crowd gathered; the street layout Paul would have walked; the single standing column of the Temple of Artemis near Selçuk; the Basilica of St. John; the Church of Mary, where a major church council met in 431; and the Artemis statues in the Ephesus Museum in Selçuk. It should be honest about which sites are traditional rather than historical, such as the tower called "St. Paul's Prison."
  7. A link to Athens: Paul's speech on the Areopagus, the rock below the Acropolis, where he quoted Greek poets to a Greek audience (Acts 17). A bronze plaque with the speech sits at the foot of the rock, so this is something to look for on our Athens days.

docs.title: Lessons in leadership and change
docs.text:
Each lesson pairs a story from Paul's life with a change problem in schools, and points to the AI-Native Schools chapter that treats it in depth.

Lesson from Paul What happened For AI-native schools AI-Native Schools chapter The insider who changes sides Paul was a trained defender of the old system before he led the new one, so he knew its logic from the inside Our strongest change leaders are often veteran teachers who mastered direct instruction and can speak to its real strengths 17. Leading Change: Vision, Culture, and Early-Stage Concerns Deciding what is essential The Jerusalem council (Acts 15, Galatians 2) decided Gentile converts did not have to follow every inherited rule to belong Separate the purpose of school (mastery, character, community) from its inherited "grammar": seat time, bell schedules, the Carnegie unit 3. School Structures, Equity, and the Industrial-Era Legacy and 18. Sustaining Change A compelling, inclusive vision "Neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free" gave people from many backgrounds a reason to join A shared vision of every student learning at their own pace is more persuasive than a technology purchase 17. Leading Change From lecture to dialogue In the hall of Tyrannus Paul "reasoned" daily with listeners, a dialogue more than a sermon The teacher's role shifts from lecturer to coach, mentor, and facilitator 19. Microstrategies for Leading Change and 20. Designing the AI-Native School Day A hub and its spokes From Ephesus, co-workers carried the message to nearby cities such as Colossae, so one base reached a whole region Start with a pilot school or classroom that becomes a hub for others, rather than a district-wide launch 15. Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation Letters as a scalable teaching technology Paul could not be everywhere, so he wrote letters that were read aloud, copied, and passed between communities Intelligent textbooks and open content let good teaching reach students the teacher never meets 6. The Five-Level Model of Intelligent Textbooks and 7. Content Economics and Open Educational Resources Building a team, not a following Priscilla, Aquila, Timothy, Titus, and Phoebe led alongside Paul; Priscilla and Aquila even coached the gifted teacher Apollos Build a guiding coalition and teacher champions who can lead without the founder 17. Leading Change and 19. Microstrategies Meeting people where they are "I have become all things to all people" (1 Corinthians 9:22); in Athens he started from the Athenians' own altar "to an unknown god" Match the strategy to each teacher's stage of concern, and explain the change in the community's own language 15. Technology Adoption and 17. Leading Change Respecting the economics of resistance The silversmiths' riot was about jobs as much as faith Resistance from teachers, unions, and vendors often comes from legitimate fears about livelihoods and should be met with respect, not dismissed 19. Microstrategies Many parts, one body Paul answered factions in Corinth with the image of one body whose parts need each other Treat a school as a system: schedules, assessment, staffing, and culture must change together 18. Sustaining Change: Systems Thinking Expect the messy middle Paul's letters are full of correction, conflict, and discouraged communities Plan for the implementation dip and change fatigue instead of treating early trouble as failure 16. Organizational Change Models Paying his own way Paul worked as a tentmaker so his teaching did not depend on any patron Fund change sustainably and avoid dependence on a single vendor or grant 21. Implementing the AI-Native Model Responsibly Planning for succession At Miletus Paul handed leadership to local elders, knowing he would not return A change that depends on one leader ends when that leader leaves; anchor it in culture and policy 18. Sustaining Change and 21. Implementing Responsibly

docs.title: Where the parallel breaks down
docs.text:
The chapter should close by being honest about the limits of the comparison:

  • Paul was founding a faith, not running a reform program. Treating his mission as a management technique flattens what it meant to him and to the people who believe it today, so the chapter should write with respect for Christian, Jewish, and Muslim readers alike.
  • Much of Paul's success was visible only after his death, and the movement he started later built its own hierarchy and rules. Every new model risks becoming the next legacy system.
  • Paul's sharp break with his own tradition also caused lasting harm, including centuries of Christian hostility toward Jews that drew on later readings of his words. Change leaders should ask who is hurt by the change, not only who benefits.

docs.title: Deep-Dive Chapter: The Oracle and the Algorithm
Why this chapter exists
docs.text:
Every person who ever made a hard decision has wished to see how it would turn out. Should we go to war? Should we marry, move, plant, sail, or invest? The need to see the consequences of today's choices before we live with them is one of the oldest parts of the human condition.

For a very long time, the most trusted answer to that need in the Greek world was a woman sitting on a bronze tripod in the inner room of Apollo's temple at Delphi. The Pythia, Apollo's priestess, gave answers from about the 8th century BCE until Christian emperors shut the old sanctuaries in the late 4th century CE, roughly 1,100 to 1,200 years depending on where we start the count. That is longer than the Roman Empire in the West, and about five times as long as the United States has existed. Greek cities asked Delphi before founding colonies from Sicily to the Black Sea, before going to war, and before changing their laws. The oracle's sayings shaped Socrates, and through him Western philosophy.

Today we ask a different kind of oracle. Machine-learning models predict the weather we will pack for, the route our driver takes to Delphi, the loans and jobs people are offered, and, in the large language models we talk to, simply the next most likely word. This chapter is a slower, more reflective read than the others. It asks what Delphi can teach us about living with machines that predict, and about the questions we bring to them.

docs.title: What the chapter should cover
docs.text:
1. The sanctuary and how a consultation worked: the Sacred Way climbing past the treasuries that city-states built to show off their gifts; the Temple of Apollo; the Pythia and the priests who framed her words; the fees, the sacrifice, and the waiting line; and the omphalos, the stone that marked Delphi as the navel of the world.
  2. How long it lasted, and why: Delphi stayed neutral ground shared by rival Greek states, guarded by a league of neighbors (the Amphictyony), and it adapted over the centuries, for example by answering in plain prose instead of verse. Plutarch, who served as a priest at Delphi around 100 CE, wrote essays on why the oracle had declined, an insider's view of an institution losing relevance.
  3. The famous answers: King Croesus of Lydia told that if he attacked Persia he would destroy a great empire (it was his own); the Athenians told to trust their "wooden walls" before the Persian invasion of 480 BCE, which Themistocles argued meant their ships, leading to the victory at Salamis; and Socrates' friend Chaerephon told that no one was wiser than Socrates, which sent Socrates out questioning everyone to find out what it meant. Most of these stories come from Herodotus and Plato, written after the events, and the chapter should say so.
  4. The oracle's flaws: Herodotus reports that the Pythia was bribed more than once for political ends, and that Delphi gave gloomy, hedging answers as Persia advanced. The chapter should explore the theory that gases rising from a geological fault under the temple affected the Pythia, and why that theory is still debated.
  5. The inscriptions: "Know thyself" and "Nothing in excess," carved at the temple entrance, and what it means that the most famous fortune-teller in history pointed its visitors back at themselves.
  6. Things to notice on site: the Castalian Spring, where visitors purified themselves; the Athenian Treasury; the polygonal wall covered with inscribed records of freed slaves; the theater and the stadium above the temple; the round Tholos at the sanctuary of Athena Pronaia; and in the museum, the bronze Charioteer and the omphalos stone.
  7. Delphi in winter: in myth Apollo left Delphi during the winter months and the oracle fell silent while Dionysus ruled the sanctuary. We arrive in late November, in the oracle's own off-season, and the chapter should use that quiet as a theme.
  8. The people who live there now: the modern village of Delphi, moved off the ancient site so French archaeologists could dig it in the 1890s; the olive groves of Amfissa below; the nearby mountain town of Arachova; and how these communities live with tourism in the off-season.

docs.title: Parallels between the oracle and machine prediction
docs.text:
Each parallel pairs a Delphi story with a question about AI and prediction. Where it fits, it links to the chapters of AI-Native Schools on measuring and forecasting AI itself.

Parallel At Delphi With machine learning and AI The oracle as a data hub Envoys from every Greek city came to Delphi, so its priests heard more news from more places than anyone else in the Greek world. Part of the oracle's wisdom may have been simply knowing more A model is only as good as the data gathered into it; its predictions reflect who was included in that data and who was not Answers that need interpreting The Pythia's words were often ambiguous, and the real decision happened afterward, in debates like the Athenian assembly arguing over "wooden walls" AI predictions come with uncertainty; a forecast is the start of human deliberation, not the end of it. Keep a human in the loop Reading what we want to hear Croesus heard "a great empire will fall" and assumed it meant Persia Confirmation bias: we trust predictions that flatter our plans and question the ones that don't Predictions that change the future In the myth of Oedipus, trying to escape a prophecy is what fulfills it; a city told it would win might fight harder Predictions shape behavior: a model that predicts which students will struggle, or which neighborhoods will see crime, can make it so through the way people respond Who pays the oracle Bribes and political pressure bent some answers Ask who builds, funds, and profits from a model, and whose interests its predictions serve Trust earned over centuries Delphi's authority rested on a long record and a reputation for neutrality, and it faded as that trust eroded Trust in AI should be earned through calibration, a track record of predictions checked against what happened, not through confident language Knowing the limits The oracle went silent for the winter months and answered only on set days Every model has a horizon beyond which its predictions are guesses; forecasts of AI's own growth are a live example (4. Measuring AI Capability, 5. Projecting AI Growth) An answer that starts an inquiry Socrates treated the oracle's answer as a puzzle to investigate, not a verdict to accept Use AI to ask better questions and to think harder, not to stop thinking (12. AI Guardrails) "Know thyself" The temple told every visitor that the real question was about them Prediction can tell us what is likely; it cannot tell us what we value or who we want to be. That part stays with us "Nothing in excess" Greek wisdom warned against overreach, the pride the Greeks called hubris Climate and economic models let us see the long-term cost of today's excess; the hard part, then and now, is acting on what we have been shown

docs.title: The reflection
docs.text:
The chapter should end with a short, personal reflection rather than a summary, built around a few questions to think about on the drive back to Athens:

  • What decision in our own lives would we most like to bring to an oracle, and what would we do if the answer were ambiguous?
  • When have we trusted a prediction because we wanted it to be true?
  • An institution built on foresight lasted about twelve centuries. What would it take for our own prediction machines to deserve that kind of trust, and what would make us stop trusting them?
  • What actions we take today will matter most to people who live a hundred years from now, and how would we know?

docs.title: Where the parallel breaks down
docs.text:
• The oracle was a religious institution, and for the Greeks who consulted it Apollo was real. The chapter should treat that faith with respect, not as an early, failed version of data science.
  • Machine-learning models find patterns in data and can be tested against what actually happens. The oracle could not be tested that way, and its ambiguity often protected it from ever being wrong.
  • The oracle gave one answer to one visitor. Modern models make millions of predictions about people who never asked, which raises questions of consent and fairness that Delphi never faced.

docs.title: Learning for All: A Thread Through the Trip
Why this thread exists
docs.text:
The word evangelist comes from the Greek euangelion, "good news." It took its lasting meaning on this route, in the Greek letters of Paul and the communities he wrote to. For a traveler whose own work is spreading the good news that AI can bring a strong education to every child, this route is full of earlier attempts to do the same thing, and of warnings about how those attempts went wrong.

The pattern repeats from Knossos to Istanbul. Learning starts out locked inside a palace, a temple, a guild, or a royal household. Then a new technology or institution, such as a simpler alphabet, a printing press, a public library, or a charitable endowment, opens it to many more people, usually against resistance from those who benefited from the old way. Each daily chapter's Learning for All note tells one of those stories, briefly, at the place where it happened.

docs.title: The stories, stop by stop
docs.text:
The day assignments are suggestions. The Istanbul and Athens stories can move between those cities' days to fit what we actually visit.

Where The story The parallel for AI and education AI-Native Schools chapter Orientation Euangelion, "good news," and Koine Greek, the everyday Greek that let one set of texts travel from Alexandria to Rome A shared language spreads ideas; AI translation could let every child learn in their mother tongue 7. The reform also cut a generation off from older writing, and it was imposed from the top 3. A caution about AI held by a few companies 18. Sustaining Change Crete (Heraklion museum) Linear B was deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris, an architect rather than a classicist, building on Alice Kober's careful and under-credited groundwork Breakthroughs can come from outside the profession, and the people who lay the groundwork deserve credit 13. Social Learning and Human Skills Crete (Venetian Heraklion) Cretan scholars such as Marcus Musurus edited Greek texts for the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius, whose small, cheap editions put the classics in ordinary readers' hands An early version of open, affordable course materials 7. Content Economics Athens (Lyceum or Academy) Aristotle personally tutored the young Alexander the Great, a one-on-one education only a prince could have Benjamin Bloom's "2 sigma" finding shows how much one-on-one tutoring helps; AI tutoring could make it available to every child 11. Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning Athens (Agora) Socrates questioned anyone in the marketplace for free, while the Sophists sold their teaching to the wealthy Who pays for learning decides who gets it 7. Content Economics Athens (Agora or Acropolis) In Plato's Phaedrus, Socrates warns that writing will make people forgetful and give them the look of wisdom without the substance The first panic about a learning technology, nearly word for word today's worry about AI and over-reliance, and we know it only because Plato wrote it down 12. AI Guardrails Athens (Pnyx) Athenian democracy shut out women, enslaved people, and foreigners "For all" has never meant all the first time; every generation widens the circle 3. School Structures and Equity Athens (National Archaeological Museum) The Antikythera mechanism, a bronze, gear-driven calculator that predicted eclipses; some scholars link it to Rhodes An ancient prediction machine that bridges the Delphi deep dive and modern AI 5. Projecting AI Growth Delphi Covered in the deep-dive chapter, The Oracle and the Algorithm Trust, prediction, and "Know thyself" 12. AI Guardrails

docs.title: How to write the notes
docs.text:
• Keep each note short: one story, one parallel, one link. The day belongs to the place, not to the argument.
  • Tell the history accurately first, and make the parallel second. Where a number or claim is uncertain, such as literacy rates or where the Antikythera mechanism was made, say so.
  • Include the costs alongside the gains: the scribes who lost their trade, the generation cut off from its old script, the people a reform left out.

docs.title: The caution the thread should end on
docs.text: Evangelism has a shadow. Paul adapted his message to each audience and built local leaders. The 1928 alphabet reform and the 1923 population exchange were imposed from above, and both left real losses. The empathy this guide is built around is the correction: democratizing education works best when it is done with communities, in their languages and on their terms, not to them. The closing chapter should make that point using the stories we actually saw.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
1. The long timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean, from the Minoans to modern Turkey and Greece
  2. Minoan Crete: Knossos, palace culture, and Europe's first civilization
  3. Troy, the Bronze Age, and how Homer's Iliad blends myth and history
  4. Classical Athens: democracy, philosophy, theater, and the Acropolis
  5. The Hellenistic and Roman worlds: Ephesus as a great Greco-Roman city
  6. Early Christianity in Anatolia and Greece: Paul at Ephesus, the House of the Virgin Mary, and the Orthodox Church
  7. Paul of Tarsus: his life, his journeys, his letters, and which letters scholars agree he wrote
  8. Paul's ideas and their impact on Christian philosophy: grace, faith, love, community, and his debt to Greek philosophy
  9. Paul as a leader of change: vision, team building, letters as a teaching technology, and handling resistance, with parallels to moving schools from direct instruction to AI-native learning
  10. The Oracle of Delphi: Apollo's sanctuary, the Pythia, famous prophecies, and an institution of foresight that lasted more than a thousand years
  11. Prediction then and now: the human need to foresee the results of our choices, from the oracle to machine learning and AI
  12. Byzantium and Constantinople: Hagia Sophia, the cistern, and a Christian empire that lasted a thousand years
  13. The Crusades and the Knights Hospitaller of Rhodes
  14. Venice in the Eastern Mediterranean: the forts and harbors of Crete
  15. The Ottoman Empire: Topkapi Palace, the mosques, the bazaars, and a multi-faith empire
  16. The end of empires: Gallipoli, the birth of modern Turkey, Greek independence, and the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey
  17. Jewish communities of the region, including Rhodes' Jewish Quarter and the deportation of its community in 1944
  18. Islam in daily life: prayer times, mosque etiquette, and the call to prayer
  19. Turkish cuisine: breakfast, meze, kebab, simit, tea, coffee, and sweets
  20. Greek and Cretan cuisine: olive oil, bread, cheese, fish, wine, and the Cretan diet
  21. Daily life in Turkey and Greece today: families, work, the economy, faith, and attitudes toward visitors
  22. Being a thoughtful traveler: empathy, etiquette, a few words of Turkish and Greek, and seeing past the tourist script
  23. Reading a ruin: how to look at walls, columns, mosaics, and frescoes and understand what they tell us
  24. Learning for all: alphabets, printing, libraries, tutors, and endowments that widened who could learn, and what they teach about bringing AI-powered education to every child

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of the trip, we will be able to:

  • Remember: name the main civilizations of the region in order, and the key site that represents each one on our route.
  • Understand: explain why each place mattered in its own time, and how empires, trade, and faith shaped its people.
  • Apply: use the daily chapter to plan each day around opening hours, port times, prayer times, and weather, and to order and enjoy local food with confidence.
  • Analyze: compare how Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Venetian, and Ottoman builders left their marks on the same places, and spot those layers on our own.
  • Evaluate: weigh competing stories about contested history, such as Troy, Gallipoli, Hagia Sophia, and the population exchange, and understand why Turks and Greeks may remember the same events differently.
  • Create: keep a short daily journal of what we noticed, ate, and learned from the people we met, and turn it into our own story of the journey.

From the Paul at Ephesus chapter in particular, we will be able to:

  • Remember: name Paul's main journeys, the cities he wrote to, and the seven letters scholars agree he wrote.
  • Understand: explain Paul's central ideas, such as grace, faith, love, and one community made of many kinds of people, and how they shaped later Christian philosophy.
  • Apply: use the leadership lessons from Paul's time in Ephesus to plan a next step in moving a school from direct instruction toward AI-native learning.
  • Analyze: match a moment in Paul's story to the change model it illustrates, such as building a guiding coalition, diffusion from a hub, or resistance rooted in economic fear.
  • Evaluate: judge where the parallel between Paul's movement and school change holds and where it breaks down, and weigh the harm as well as the good in his legacy.
  • Create: write a short leadership reflection that connects one Paul story to a change we want to lead, linked to the matching chapter of AI-Native Schools.

From The Oracle and the Algorithm chapter, we will be able to:

  • Remember: describe how a consultation at Delphi worked, and name three famous answers the oracle gave.
  • Understand: explain why the oracle stayed trusted for over a thousand years, and why that trust finally faded.
  • Apply: use questions drawn from Delphi, such as who gathered the data, who pays, and what the horizon is, to judge an AI prediction we meet in daily life.
  • Analyze: compare how the oracle and a machine-learning model each turn information into a prediction, and where human interpretation enters.
  • Evaluate: judge when it is wise to rely on a prediction and when it is better to follow Socrates and treat it as the start of an inquiry.
  • Create: write a short personal reflection on a decision we face today and what we would want to know about its effect on our future.

From the Learning for All thread, we will be able to:

  • Understand: explain how one technology or institution at each of several stops, such as the Greek alphabet, the Library of Celsus, or the 1928 Turkish alphabet reform, widened who could learn.
  • Analyze: identify, for each of those stories, who gained, who lost, and who resisted the change.
  • Evaluate: judge which historical lessons best apply to bringing AI-powered education to every child, and where the comparison fails.
  • Create: write a short "good news" message about AI and education that draws on one story from the trip and respects the community it is meant for.

docs.title: Mediterranean Travels FAQ
docs.text: These questions follow the order a reader meets them: first how the guide works, then the big ideas of the route, the terms behind them, the places where readers often trip up, practical habits, and the harder questions the deep-dive chapters raise. Every answer links to the chapter that treats the topic in full, and the Glossary defines every term in bold.

docs.title: What is Mediterranean Travels about?
docs.text:
Mediterranean Travels is a day-by-day companion for a thirteen-day journey through Turkey and Greece, from November 11 to November 23, 2026. It covers three days on our own in Istanbul, the Viking Star's seven-night Ancient Mediterranean Treasures cruise from Istanbul to Athens, and three days in Athens with a day trip to Delphi.

Each chapter prepares us for one day's place: what happened there, who built it and why, what to look for when we stand in front of it, what to eat, and who lives there now. The goal is not to tick off sights. It is to notice more, understand more, and meet the people of each place with real empathy.

Three threads run through the whole guide: the long history of civilization along the route, two deep dives (Paul at Ephesus, and the Oracle and the Algorithm), and the Learning for All thread about who got to learn at each stop. The full plan is in the Trip Description.

docs.title: Who is this guide written for?
docs.text:
The guide is written for curious adults who love the history of civilization, culture, and food, and who want to understand the people in each place, not just see the monuments. It assumes no professional background in archaeology, classics, theology, or Middle Eastern or Balkan history.

It is also written with a particular interest in mind: how organizations change, especially schools adapting to AI. One of the travelers works as an evangelist for AI in the democratization of education for every child on Earth. That is why the two deep-dive chapters and the Learning for All notes keep connecting ancient stories to modern questions about learning, leadership, and prediction.

Any reader planning a similar trip, a teacher preparing a unit on the Eastern Mediterranean, or a school leader interested in change can use the guide. See About for how it came to be written.

docs.title: Why does a travel guide have a learning graph, a glossary, and MicroSims?
docs.text:
Mediterranean Travels is built as an intelligent textbook, the same way a course textbook would be. A learning graph lists 598 concepts, from Eastern Mediterranean to graffiti, and records which concepts each one depends on. That graph decided the order of the chapters, so that Chapter 1's timeline comes before any site that needs it, and Paul's life comes before his ideas.

The Glossary defines 666 terms, places, people, and dishes. The MicroSims are small interactive programs, such as the Viking Cruise Map and the Antikythera Gears, that let us explore an idea instead of reading about it.

The result is a guide that works like a course without feeling like one. The Learning Graph section shows how the concepts fit together, and the Learning Graph Viewer lets us explore them as a network.

docs.title: What route and dates does the trip cover?
docs.text:
The trip runs thirteen days, Wednesday, November 11 to Monday, November 23, 2026:

  • Days 1–5, Istanbul. Three days on our own, then embarkation on the Viking Star on November 14, with the ship in port until 6:00 PM on November 15.
  • Day 6, Çanakkale, for Troy and Gallipoli.
  • Day 7, Kuşadası, for Ephesus.
  • Day 8, Rhodes, our first day in Greece.
  • Day 9, Heraklion, on Crete.
  • Day 10, Piraeus, the port of Athens, with a final night aboard.
  • Days 11–13, Athens, including the day trip by road to Delphi on November 22.

Greece is one hour behind Turkey in November, so clocks go back an hour when the ship enters Greek waters. The Viking Cruise Map shows every port and the road to Delphi, and Chapter 2 explains the shape of the journey.

docs.title: How should I read this guide?
docs.text:
Read one chapter a day, ideally at breakfast or the night before. Each daily chapter matches one day of the itinerary, so the history is fresh when we walk into the place it describes.

The two "Before We Go" chapters are read before departure, Chapter 1 first. The deep-dive chapters are read on quiet evenings aboard or on the road: Paul's life the evening before Ephesus, Paul's ideas the evening after, the Oracle the night before Delphi, and the Algorithm on the drive back. The closing chapter is for the flight home.

Every daily chapter follows the same pattern where it fits: what we will see, the history behind it, things to notice, food and drink, the people who live there now, etiquette and useful words, practical notes, and a short Learning for All note. Pair the reading with a few lines in a travel journal each evening.

docs.title: Why do the two "Before We Go" chapters come first?
docs.text:
Every later chapter assumes we can place a site on the map and in time. Chapter 1 gives us that map and timeline: the Eastern Mediterranean, Anatolia, the Aegean, and Crete, then the nine periods from the Bronze Age to the Ottoman period, along with Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Without it, Hagia Sophia, Ephesus, and Knossos blur into one long "old."

Chapter 2 covers the practical side: the cruise, November weather and packing, off-season hours, and what it means to be a thoughtful traveler. It also opens the Learning for All thread with writing systems, the alphabet, and literacy, which later chapters build on at Troy, in the Ottoman print shops, and in the 1928 Turkish alphabet reform.

In the learning graph, concepts like Historical Timeline, Bronze Age, and City-State sit near the root, with hundreds of later concepts depending on them. That is why they come first.

docs.title: What are the deep-dive chapters, and when should I read them?
docs.text:
Four chapters break the one-place-per-day pattern on purpose:

  • Paul at Ephesus, Part 1, read the evening of Day 6, sailing from Çanakkale to Kuşadası. It covers Paul's life, his letters, and his two to three years in Ephesus.
  • Paul at Ephesus, Part 2, read the evening of Day 7, after standing in the Great Theater. It covers his ideas, his legacy, and Paul as a case study in leading change.
  • The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1, read the night before Delphi. It explains the Pythia, how a consultation worked, and the famous answers.
  • The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2, read on the 2½-hour drive back or that evening. It pairs each Delphi story with a question about machine learning and AI.

The deep dives are longer and slower than the daily chapters. They are written to be read when there is time to think.

docs.title: What is the Learning for All thread?
docs.text:
Learning for All is a short note at the end of each daily chapter that tells one story about who got to learn at that stop, who was shut out, and which technology or institution widened the circle. It then draws one parallel to today's effort to use AI to bring a good education to every child on Earth.

The stories include the Greek alphabet at Troy, the Ottoman vakıf endowments that paid for free schools, the late arrival of Arabic-script printing in Istanbul, the Library of Celsus at Ephesus, the decipherment of Linear B, Aristotle tutoring Alexander, and the 1928 Turkish alphabet reform.

Chapter 2 sets out the pattern these stories share: learning starts locked up, a new technology opens it, those who benefited from the old way resist, and the circle widens but never all the way. Chapter 21 gathers all the notes into one table and draws lessons for doing education with communities rather than to them.

docs.title: Who is Glaux, and what do the owl boxes mean?
docs.text:
Glaux (pronounced "glowks," the ancient Greek word for owl) is the guide's mascot, a Little Owl (Athene noctua), the owl of Athena and of the ancient Athenian silver coin. Glaux travels with us as a fellow traveler, wearing an Aegean-blue scarf and carrying a satchel with a travel notebook. Glaux's catchphrase is "Look closer."

Glaux appears only in colored boxes, and each pose has one job:

  • Welcome opens a chapter and says why the day matters.
  • Thinking marks an idea worth pausing on.
  • Tip offers a shortcut or practical heuristic.
  • Warning heads off a common mistake and says how to avoid it.
  • Encourage appears at a known hard passage.
  • Celebration closes a chapter by naming what we can now do.

If Glaux is not doing one of those jobs, Glaux is not in the chapter. Chapter 1 has Glaux's self-introduction.

docs.title: What do I need to know before I start?
docs.text:
Nothing beyond general adult knowledge. The guide assumes we have heard of ancient Greece, the Roman Empire, Christianity, Islam, and the Ottoman Empire, and nothing more.

Every other term is explained where it first appears: spolia in Hagia Sophia, stratigraphy at Troy, the classical orders at Ephesus, the Pythia at Delphi, next-word prediction in the Algorithm chapter. Each is also defined in the Glossary.

The one real prerequisite is reading in order. A chapter's "Prerequisites" line lists the earlier chapters it builds on, and the learning graph was built so that no chapter uses an idea before it has been taught. If a later chapter feels thin, the fix is usually to reread the part of Chapter 1 that places that site in its era.

docs.title: What interactive MicroSims, posters, and appendices does the guide include?
docs.text:
The guide includes these MicroSims:

  • Viking Cruise Map: every port on real map tiles, the ship's route, and the road from Athens to Delphi.
  • Eras of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline and Events Timeline: the nine periods and the key events on one scale.
  • Regions of the Eastern Mediterranean Map: Anatolia, the Aegean, Crete, and the Greek mainland.
  • Antikythera Gears: how a train of bronze gears turns a hand crank into a model of the sky.
  • Learning Graph Viewer: all 598 concepts and their dependencies.

The Three Classical Orders poster compares Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian columns. The appendices hold the Pronunciation Guide, a Timeline of Events, Extensions and Excursions, and an essay on Who Created the Antikythera Mechanism. The full list is on the MicroSims page.

docs.title: How do the pronounce buttons work?
docs.text:
Many names on this route are hard to say from their spelling alone: Ephesus, Knossos, Topkapı, Kuşadası, Süleymaniye, Pythia. Where one of these names first appears in the chapters, a 🔊 Pronounce button plays a short recording of it, and an italic respelling shows the stressed syllable in capitals, for example EF-uh-sus or koo-SHAH-dah-suh.

Each term gets exactly one button in the whole book, at its first use in reading order. Later chapters do not repeat it. To hear a name again, open the Pronunciation Guide, which lists every pronounced term in one place, or look it up in the Glossary.

Names with an established English form, such as Ephesus and Byzantine, use the English pronunciation a guide would use. Turkish and modern Greek names with no English form, such as Kuşadası and Arachova, use the local pronunciation.

docs.title: How does this guide connect to AI-Native Schools?
docs.text:
AI-Native Schools is a companion textbook about moving schools from legacy direct instruction to AI-native learning. Mediterranean Travels links to it wherever a story on the route sheds light on a school-change problem.

The links cluster in three places. In Chapter 11, each of Paul's leadership lessons, such as building a team, hub-and-spoke diffusion, and respecting the economics of resistance, points to the matching AI-Native Schools chapter. In Chapter 19, the Delphi parallels point to chapters on measuring and forecasting AI and on AI guardrails. And every Learning for All note ends with a link where one fits, such as the vakıf endowments to the chapter on content economics and open educational resources.

The guide is careful that the history comes first and the parallel second, and each deep dive closes with a section on where its parallel breaks down.

docs.title: Does the guide describe what actually happened on the trip?
docs.text:
Mostly, yes. The chapters were written to prepare for each day, then revised after the trip to reflect what we actually did and photographed. The photos in each chapter are our own, chosen from the trip and published without location data.

Where the day went differently from the plan, the chapter says so. The clearest case is Crete. Chapter 13 still teaches the palace of Knossos in full, because no account of the Minoans can skip it, but on the day we chose Viking's "The Villages of Crete" excursion instead. We spent the morning in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum, where nearly everything movable from Knossos now lives, and the afternoon at the Avli winery and the pottery village of Thrapsano. Chapter 14 follows the day in that order.

Personal touches appear in the first person: the Turkish delight and saffron we bought at the Spice Bazaar, and eggplant as a favorite dish on both sides of the Aegean.

docs.title: What are the main eras of the Eastern Mediterranean, in order?
docs.text:
Chapter 1 uses nine periods, and every site on the route belongs to one or more of them:

  1. Bronze Age (about 3200–1100 BCE): the Minoans at Knossos, the Mycenaeans, and Troy.
  2. Iron Age: the Bronze Age collapse, iron tools, and the Greek alphabet.
  3. Archaic period: city-states, coins, and the first democracy.
  4. Classical period: Athens at its height and the Parthenon.
  5. Hellenistic period: Alexander's successor kingdoms and Koine Greek.
  6. Roman period: the Roman Empire and the Pax Romana, when Ephesus flourished.
  7. Byzantine period: Constantinople and Hagia Sophia.
  8. Ottoman period: Topkapı, the mosques, and the multi-faith empire.
  9. Modern period: the Republic of Turkey and the modern Greek state.

A worked example in Chapter 1 squeezes 5,225 years into one 24-hour day: the Bronze Age fills the morning, the whole Classical period lasts about 43 minutes, and the Byzantine period fills the evening. Period boundaries are local, and a period name tells when, not always who. The Eras Timeline MicroSim lays them out on one scale.

docs.title: What does "civilization" mean in this guide?
docs.text:
The guide uses civilization as a description, not a ranking. A civilization is a way of organizing society that includes cities, a food surplus that frees some people from farming, a government, written or other records, and monumental building. Minoan Crete, with its palaces, storerooms, and Linear A accounts, counts. So do Classical Athens, the Roman Empire, and the Ottoman Empire.

This matters because the word is easily misused to sort peoples into "civilized" and "barbarian," as the Greeks themselves did. Calling the Minoans a civilization says how their society was organized. It does not say they were better than the herders or villagers around them.

In the learning graph, Civilization is one of the most foundational concepts, with hundreds of later concepts depending on it. Chapter 1 introduces it alongside archaeology, the study of the past through the layers people left in the ground.

docs.title: Why was ancient Greece not a country?
docs.text:
Ancient Greece was a shared civilization of more than 1,000 independent city-states, not a single nation. A city-state (polis) was a city and the farmland around it, with its own laws, army, gods, coins, and calendar. Athens, Sparta, Corinth, Rhodes, and Ephesus were all separate states that sometimes allied and often fought each other.

What made them all "Greek" was language, religion, and shared institutions: the Olympian gods, Homer's epics, the Olympic and Pythian Games, and sanctuaries like Delphi that every city respected. A Greek from Ephesus and a Greek from Athens could understand each other, worship the same gods, and compete at the same games, while their cities stood ready to go to war.

This explains a surprise on our route: Byzantium and Ephesus were Greek cities, yet both lie in today's Turkey, because Greek city-states spread across the whole Aegean and beyond. Chapter 1 suggests the phrase "an ancient Greek city in today's Turkey," which is accurate and respects both countries. Chapter 1 introduces the idea, and Chapter 16 shows how one city-state, Athens, governed itself.

docs.title: Why did so many empires fight over the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles?
docs.text:
The two straits are chokepoints on one of the world's great trade routes. The Bosphorus, about 31 km long and 700 m to 3.7 km wide, is the only sea route from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean. The Dardanelles, about 61 km long and narrowest at Çanakkale, carries the same traffic between the Sea of Marmara and the Aegean. Whoever held their shores could tax, protect, or block the grain, timber, metals, and fish moving between the Black Sea and the wider world.

That one fact explains a great deal of the route's history. Troy grew rich guarding the mouth of the Dardanelles. Greeks from Megara founded Byzantium on the Bosphorus around 657 BCE. Constantine made it an imperial capital, Mehmed II built the Rumeli Hisarı fortress to close the strait before his siege of 1453, and in 1915 the Allies attacked Gallipoli to force the Dardanelles open.

Chapter 3 explains the Bosphorus, and Chapter 8 connects Troy and Gallipoli on opposite shores of the same water.

docs.title: How did Byzantium become Constantinople and then Istanbul?
docs.text:
The city has had three main names, each marking a new layer:

  • Byzantium was founded by Greeks from Megara around 657 BCE. Its site was so much better than that of Chalcedon, across the water, that the Chalcedonians were called "the city of the blind."
  • Constantinople was refounded by Constantine the Great, who embraced Christianity, and dedicated on May 11, 330 CE. It was the capital of the Byzantine Empire for 1,123 years. Divan Yolu still follows Constantine's main street, and his column still stands.
  • Istanbul became the Ottoman capital after Mehmed the Conqueror took the city on May 29, 1453. The name comes from the Greek for "to the City."

Turks call 1453 the Conquest; Greeks call it the Capture or the Fall. The city was an imperial capital for almost 1,600 years, from 330 to 1922. Chapter 3 tells the whole story in one sitting, on arrival day.

docs.title: Why did Constantinople's walls hold for a thousand years, and why did they fall in 53 days?
docs.text:
The Theodosian Walls, completed in 413 under Theodosius II, defended the city's land side with five layers in turn: a moat about 20 m wide, an open outer terrace, an outer wall, an inner terrace where the defenders gathered, and the main inner wall, about 12 m high with 96 towers. The sea protected the other sides, and a chain could close the Golden Horn. Add Greek fire, skilled diplomacy, and a gold coin that held its value for about seven centuries, and the Byzantine Empire could outlast attacker after attacker.

Three things changed in 1453. Mehmed II built Rumeli Hisarı on the Bosphorus to cut off help by sea. He brought cannon large enough to batter walls designed for an age of rams and ladders. And he had about seventy ships hauled overland into the Golden Horn, around the chain, so the roughly 7,000 defenders had to stretch along the harbor walls too. After a 53-day siege, the city fell on May 29.

The lesson is about technology and defense. A defense built for one kind of attack can last a thousand years and then fail quickly when the attack changes. Chapter 3 walks the walls and the siege.

docs.title: What happened to Hagia Sophia over its history?
docs.text:
Hagia Sophia has had more lives than almost any building on Earth:

  • 532–537 CE: Justinian built it as a cathedral after the Nika Riots burned the old one. Its dome, about 31 m across on four pendentives, collapsed in 558 and was rebuilt higher in 562.
  • 1054: a papal excommunication laid on its altar became the symbol of the Great Schism between the Eastern and Western churches.
  • 1204: the Fourth Crusade sacked the city and looted the church.
  • 1453: Mehmed II converted it into a mosque, adding minarets, and later sultans added more.
  • 1934: the Republic of Turkey made it a museum, and mosaics were uncovered.
  • 2020: it became a mosque again, with a visitor route through the galleries.

Each change is a layer we can read on the building, from Justinian's dome to Mehmed's minaret to the 19th-century calligraphy roundels. The 2020 decision is also an argument about Atatürk's secular legacy, which is why it is contested history. See Chapter 4 and Chapter 7.

docs.title: What was the Ottoman Empire, and how did it govern so many faiths?
docs.text:
The Ottoman Empire was founded around 1299 by Osman, a Turkish leader in northwest Anatolia. It moved its capital from Söğüt to Bursa to Edirne, took Constantinople in 1453, and at its height under Suleiman the Magnificent (1520–1566) stretched from Hungary to Arabia. It lasted until 1922. Its ruler, the sultan, had to be a member of Osman's family.

The empire ruled Muslims, Christians, and Jews, and it organized them through the millet system. Each recognized religious community, Greek Orthodox, Armenian, and Jewish, ran its own affairs, including religious courts, schools, and charity, under its own leaders. This is why Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 could rebuild their lives in Istanbul, Thessaloniki, and Rhodes.

The millet system offered real protection, but not equality. Non-Muslims paid a special tax and faced limits on dress, building, and office. Chapter 5 covers the palace and the sultans, and Chapter 6 covers the multi-faith empire.

docs.title: What are the Five Pillars of Islam?
docs.text:
The Five Pillars of Islam are the five acts every Muslim is expected to perform:

  1. Profession of faith (shahada): there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God.
  2. Prayer (salat): five daily prayers facing Mecca, 17 obligatory cycles in all, each preceded by ablution, the ritual washing of face, hands, arms, and feet.
  3. Almsgiving (zakat): giving a share of one's wealth to those in need.
  4. Fasting (sawm) from dawn to sunset during the month of Ramadan.
  5. Pilgrimage (hajj) to Mecca once in a lifetime, for those able to make it.

In Istanbul the pillars are visible every day. The call to prayer sounds from each minaret five times, at times that follow the sun. On Friday, the noon prayer is replaced by congregational prayer with a sermon, which is why Day 3 is planned around Friday prayer. Chapter 5 explains the pillars and how to be a good guest in a mosque.

docs.title: Who was Paul of Tarsus?
docs.text:
Paul, also called Saul, was a Jewish teacher born in Tarsus, in southern Anatolia, in the early 1st century CE. Tarsus gave him three worlds at once: he was Jewish, educated in Greek, and, according to Acts, a Roman citizen. He trained as a Pharisee, a member of a respected movement devoted to careful keeping of Jewish law.

Paul first persecuted the early followers of Jesus. Then, around 33–36 CE, on the road to Damascus, he had the experience he described as a call, and he became the movement's most energetic traveling teacher. On his missionary journeys (about 46–57 CE) he founded communities of Jews and Gentiles in cities across Anatolia, Macedonia, and Greece, and wrote letters to guide them. He was arrested in Jerusalem, sent to Rome, and, by tradition, executed there.

His letters, from about 50 CE, are the oldest writings in the New Testament. Chapter 9 tells his life, separating what his own letters say from what Acts and later tradition add.

docs.title: Why was Ephesus so important to Paul?
docs.text:
Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia, a major port, and a pilgrimage center for the goddess Artemis. Roads and sea lanes ran out of it in every direction, which made it an ideal hub. According to Acts, Paul taught there for two to three years, about 52–55 CE, longer than anywhere else, and "all the residents of Asia" heard the message from that base.

He began in the synagogue, then taught daily for two years in the rented hall of Tyrannus. He worked alongside the tentmakers Priscilla and Aquila, who also coached the gifted teacher Apollos. He wrote at least one letter, 1 Corinthians, from Ephesus around 54 CE. His co-workers carried the message to nearby cities such as Colossae.

His stay ended after the riot of the silversmiths, when Demetrius, who made shrines of Artemis, led a crowd into the Great Theater, fearing for his trade. Later Paul said farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus. See Chapter 9 and Chapter 10.

docs.title: Which letters did Paul actually write?
docs.text:
The New Testament contains thirteen letters in Paul's name. Scholars broadly agree that seven are his own, the seven undisputed letters:

  • Romans
  • 1 Corinthians and 2 Corinthians
  • Galatians
  • Philippians
  • 1 Thessalonians
  • Philemon

The other six, including the Letter to the Ephesians, the letters to Timothy, and the Letter to Titus, are disputed. Their vocabulary, style, and concerns differ enough that many scholars think followers wrote them in Paul's name after his death, a common practice in the ancient world.

This matters for reading Paul fairly. Some of the lines most often quoted about women and slavery come from the disputed letters. The Book of Acts, written around 80–90 CE, a generation later, is our only narrative of his life, and it tells his story from its own point of view. Chapter 9 says which source each claim comes from.

docs.title: What were Paul's central ideas?
docs.text:
Chapter 11 focuses on four:

  • Grace and faith. People are put right with God as a gift, received by trust, rather than earned by keeping the law. Lutheran, Catholic, and Orthodox Christians read this differently.
  • "Neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male and female" (Galatians 3:28). The old divisions no longer decide who belongs to the community.
  • One body, many parts (1 Corinthians 12). Paul took a familiar Roman image of society as a body and reversed it: the weakest members are the indispensable ones.
  • Love as the greatest virtue (1 Corinthians 13). Often read at weddings, it was written to a quarreling community.

Paul borrowed the language of Greek philosophy, especially the Stoics, to reach Greek listeners. His ideas passed through Augustine and Luther into Western thought, where they became one root of the ideas of individual conscience and human equality. Some of his harsher lines were also later used to justify Christian hostility toward Jews, which the chapter faces directly.

docs.title: Who were the Minoans, and what was Knossos?
docs.text:
The Minoans were the Bronze Age civilization of Crete, often called Europe's first civilization. The name is modern: Arthur Evans named them after King Minos of Greek myth. We do not know what they called themselves, because their script, Linear A, is still undeciphered.

Knossos was their largest palace, first built around 1900 BCE and rebuilt after an earthquake around 1700 BCE. It was not just a royal home. It was a storehouse, workshop, shrine, and office arranged around a central court, at the heart of a palace economy that collected, recorded, and redistributed goods. Huge storage jars called pithoi held oil, wine, and grain.

The Thera eruption, around 1600 BCE, weakened Minoan Crete but did not end it. Mycenaean Greeks ruled Knossos after about 1450 BCE, and the palace burned around 1375 BCE. The bull-leaping fresco, the throne room, and the myth of the Minotaur all come from this world. Chapter 13 explains the palace and the museum.

docs.title: What were Linear A and Linear B?
docs.text:
Linear A and Linear B are two Bronze Age scripts found on clay tablets in Crete and mainland Greece. Linear A is the older script of the Minoans, and it remains undeciphered; scholars can read a few words from context, such as ku-ro, "total." Linear B is a later adaptation used by the Mycenaeans, and it writes an early form of Greek in about 90 sound-signs, each standing for a syllable. In Linear B, Knossos is spelled ko-no-so.

The tablets were palace accounts, not literature: lists of sheep, oil, chariot wheels, and workers. A few dozen scribes at Knossos kept them on unfired clay, and they survive only because the fires that destroyed the palaces baked them hard.

Linear B was deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952, building on Alice Kober's careful groundwork. When the palaces fell, writing vanished from Greece for about 400 years, because only a few scribes had known it. Chapter 13 tells the decipherment story.

docs.title: How did Athenian democracy work, and who was left out?
docs.text:
Athenian democracy (508–322 BCE) was direct, not representative. Every citizen could attend the Assembly, which met on the Pnyx hill and voted on war, peace, and laws. A Council of 500, chosen by lot each year, prepared its business. Jurors were chosen by lot too, and citizens were paid for public service so that poor men could take part. The democracy's power rested on the poor citizens who rowed the fleet.

The Athenians also invented ostracism: once a year they could vote, by scratching a name on a potsherd, to exile a leading politician for ten years. Ready-made ballots found against Themistocles hint that some voters could not write.

But citizenship belonged only to adult men with two Athenian parents. Women, resident foreigners (metics), and enslaved people had no vote. Chapter 16 estimates that only about one Athenian in six could vote. "For all" has never meant all the first time.

docs.title: What was the Oracle of Delphi, and how did a consultation work?
docs.text:
The Oracle of Delphi was the sanctuary where Apollo's priestess, the Pythia, answered questions from individuals and cities for more than a thousand years. Greek cities asked it before founding colonies, going to war, or changing their laws.

A consultation followed a set sequence. The visitor purified himself in the Castalian Spring, paid a fee, and offered a sacrifice. Priests sprinkled cold water on a goat; if it shivered, the god was willing to answer that day. Visitors waited in a line, with those holding promanteia, the right to consult first, at the front. The Pythia, a woman of Delphi seated on a bronze tripod in the inner room of the Temple of Apollo, gave the god's answer, and the priests announced and perhaps shaped it, in verse in early times and in prose by Plutarch's day.

The scholar Joseph Fontenrose found that most well-recorded answers were plain commands, and that the famous riddles are mostly legend. Chapter 17 walks through all the steps.

docs.title: Why did the Oracle of Delphi last more than a thousand years?
docs.text:
The oracle answered questions for roughly 1,140 years, from about 750 BCE until the Theodosian Decrees of 391–392 CE banned pagan worship. That is longer than the Byzantine Empire. Chapter 17 points to several reasons:

  • Neutral ground. Delphi belonged to no single powerful city. A league of neighbors, the Amphictyonic League, ran the sanctuary, so rival states could all consult it.
  • Information. Envoys from every Greek city came to Delphi, so its priests heard more news from more places than anyone else in the Greek world.
  • Adaptation. The oracle changed over time, for example by answering in plain prose instead of verse.
  • Answers that could not lose. Hedged and ambiguous answers protected its reputation.
  • Faith. For the Greeks who came, Apollo was real, and consulting him was an act of piety.

Its trust also faded slowly. Bribery scandals, gloomy answers as Persia advanced, and later the rise of Christianity eroded it. Plutarch, a priest at Delphi around 100 CE, wrote essays on why the oracle had declined.

docs.title: Was Troy a real place?
docs.text:
Yes, though the war in Homer's Iliad is a poet's memory rather than a history. The real city stood on the Hisarlık mound near the mouth of the Dardanelles, which it guarded. The mound is a tell, built up by about 3,500 years of rebuilding, and archaeologists count nine main cities in its layers, from about 3000 BCE to about 500 CE.

Troy VI and Troy VIIa are the candidates for Homer's city. Troy VI was damaged by an earthquake around 1300 BCE, and Troy VIIa was destroyed by fire around 1180 BCE, during the Bronze Age collapse. Hittite texts name a kingdom called Wilusa, very probably Troy (Homer's Ilios), and a king named Alaksandu.

Homer composed around 700 BCE, about 480 years after Troy VIIa fell, from songs carried across centuries without writing. So the best answer is: a real, rich city, probably destroyed by violence, remembered and transformed in song. Chapter 8 sets out the evidence.

docs.title: What was the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey?
docs.text:
After the Greco-Turkish War of 1919–1922, which ended with the burning of Smyrna, Greece and Turkey agreed in 1923 to a compulsory population exchange. About 1.2 million Orthodox Christians left Turkey for Greece, and about 400,000 Muslims left Greece for Turkey, and none could return.

The rule that sorted people was religion, not language. Turkish-speaking Orthodox Christians from central Anatolia were sent to Greece, and Greek-speaking Muslims from Crete were sent to Turkey. Families who had lived in one place for centuries lost their homes, churches, mosques, and graves.

The Asia Minor refugees reshaped Greece. They built new neighborhoods around Athens and Thessaloniki, and they brought music such as rebetiko and dishes from Smyrna. On the Turkish coast, the end of Greek life is visible in empty churches and renamed villages around Ephesus. Chapter 7 and Chapter 10 tell the story, and both countries remember it differently.

docs.title: Who was Atatürk, and what did his reforms change?
docs.text:
Mustafa Kemal Atatürk (1881–1938), born in Salonica, made his name as an Ottoman commander at Gallipoli in 1915. From 1919 he led the national movement that won the Turkish War of Independence, overturned the Treaty of Sèvres, and secured the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923. He proclaimed the Republic of Turkey on October 29, 1923, and became its first president.

In about fifteen years his reforms changed law, dress, the calendar, surnames, and the alphabet. The caliphate was abolished in 1924, religious courts closed, and the state adopted laiklik, a secularism in which the state manages religion through the Diyanet. In 1928 Turkish switched from Arabic script to a new Latin alphabet of 29 letters, one per sound, and the Nation's Schools taught adults to read it.

On November 10, the anniversary of his death, the whole country stops at 9:05 AM. Chapter 7 covers the reforms, what they gained, and what they cost.

docs.title: Why were the Knights Hospitaller on Rhodes?
docs.text:
The Knights Hospitaller began as a hospital for pilgrims in Jerusalem in the 11th century and grew into a military religious order during the Crusades. After the crusader states fell, they took Rhodes and ruled it as their own island state from 1310 to 1522.

The knights were organized by tongues, groups based on language and region, each with its own inn on the Street of the Knights. They built the Palace of the Grand Master, the Hospital of the Knights (1440–1489), and about 4 km of walls rebuilt for the age of cannon after 1480. From Rhodes they raided Ottoman shipping.

In 1522 Suleiman the Magnificent besieged the city. After six months the knights surrendered on terms and left on January 1, 1523, later settling on Malta. The Rhodes Medieval Town, a UNESCO site since 1988, is their legacy, though much of what we see, including the Palace of the Grand Master, was rebuilt under Italian rule in 1937–1940. Chapter 12 reads each layer.

docs.title: What is the Antikythera mechanism?
docs.text:
The Antikythera mechanism is a geared bronze device from the 2nd century BCE, found in a shipwreck of about 70–60 BCE off the island of Antikythera. Turning a hand crank moved dozens of interlocking gears that modeled the Sun, the Moon and its phases, the calendar, the cycle of the athletic games, and the eclipse cycles. It is often called the world's oldest known analog computer. Its fragments are in Athens's National Archaeological Museum.

The guide calls it an ancient prediction machine. It sits between the oracle and the modern learned model. The oracle gave answers no one could check. The mechanism turned regular, observed cycles into predictions anyone could check against the sky. A machine-learning model, by contrast, learns its patterns from examples.

Who built it is uncertain; some scholars link it to Rhodes. Chapter 20 explains it, the Antikythera Gears MicroSim lets us turn the gears, and the appendix Who Created the Antikythera Mechanism weighs the candidates.

docs.title: How does a predictive model or a large language model actually work?
docs.text:
Machine learning finds patterns in examples instead of following rules a person wrote. A predictive model uses those patterns to turn present facts into a probability about an unknown outcome, such as rain tomorrow or whether a loan will be repaid. It assumes the future will resemble the past, so it is only as good as its training data.

A large language model is a predictive model for text. Its core task is next-word prediction: given the words so far, it assigns a probability to every possible next word, chooses one, adds it, and repeats. Everything a chatbot writes, from a poem to a timetable, is produced this way, one word at a time.

That has a practical consequence. A language model predicts likely answers; it does not look up facts. Likely is not the same as true, which is why its answers need checking. Whether these models "understand" is still an open debate. Chapter 19 explains all three ideas in plain terms, starting from the oracle.

docs.title: What were the Persian Wars, and why do they matter for Athens?
docs.text:
The Persian Wars (499–479 BCE) were the Persian Empire's attempts to conquer Greece. They began with the Ionian Revolt, when Greek cities on today's Turkish coast rose against Persian rule with Athenian help.

In 490 BCE, at the Battle of Marathon, the Athenians and Plataeans defeated a Persian landing. In 480 BCE the Persian king Xerxes invaded with a huge army and burned the Acropolis. Before he came, the Athenians had asked Delphi for advice and were told to trust their "wooden walls." Themistocles argued that this meant ships, and he had already turned the silver of the Laurion mines into a fleet. At the Battle of Salamis, Athens supplied 180 of the 378 Greek ships that won in the narrows. Victories at Plataea and Mycale in 479 BCE ended the invasion.

The wars matter because the burned Acropolis was rebuilt from 447 BCE under Pericles, giving us the Parthenon. Our main source, Herodotus, wrote an inquiry that names its sources and doubts its own numbers. See Chapter 15.

docs.title: Glossary of Terms
docs.text: Terms are in alphabetical order. A 🔊 Pronounce button plays the name aloud; the respelling shows the stressed syllable in capitals. All the hard names are also collected in the Pronunciation Guide.

docs.title: Ablution
docs.text:
The ritual washing of face, hands, arms and feet that Muslims perform before prayer, using fountains or taps found at every mosque.

Example: The rows of taps along the courtyard wall of a mosque are for this washing, not for drinking.

docs.title: Acropolis
docs.text:
The rocky hilltop in the center of Athens, a fortress and sanctuary since the Bronze Age, crowned by the 5th-century BCE temples of Athena built under Pericles.

In Greek the word means "high city," and many towns had one.

Example: The Parthenon, Erechtheion, Propylaea and Temple of Athena Nike all stand on it.

docs.title: Acropolis Museum
docs.text:
The modern museum at the foot of the Acropolis, opened in 2009, which displays sculptures from the hilltop and has glass floors over an excavated ancient neighborhood.

Example: Its top floor is aligned with the Parthenon itself, visible through the glass walls.

See also: Parthenon Marbles Dispute

docs.title: Acting on Foresight
docs.text:
Turning a prediction into a decision and action, which requires judgment, courage and resources, since a warning that no one acts on changes nothing.

Example: Themistocles used the oracle's warning to argue for building ships before the Persians came.

docs.title: Adyton
docs.text:
Say it: AD-ih-ton 🔊 Pronounce

The inner room of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, "the place not to be entered," set lower than the floor, where the Pythia sat on her tripod.

docs.title: Aegean Sea
docs.text:
The arm of the Mediterranean between mainland Greece and Turkey, dotted with islands, across which ships, settlers and ideas have moved for at least five thousand years.

Example: Our ship crosses it from the Dardanelles to Kuşadası, Rhodes, Crete and finally Piraeus.

docs.title: Affordable Course Materials
docs.text:
Textbooks and other learning materials priced low enough that cost does not keep any student from having them, whether in print or in digital form.

Example: Aldus Manutius's small, cheap editions of Virgil were an early version of the idea.

See also: Aldine Editions, Open Educational Resources

docs.title: Agapē
docs.text:
Say it: ah-GAH-pay 🔊 Pronounce

The Greek word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 13 for love, meaning goodwill shown in action, as distinct from erōs, desire, and philia, friendship.

See also: Love as Greatest Virtue

docs.title: Agiorgitiko
docs.text:
Say it: ah-yor-YEE-tee-koh 🔊 Pronounce

A red wine grape native to the Nemea area of the Peloponnese, making soft, fruity red wines and one of the most widely planted native red varieties in Greece.

Example: A glass of it pairs well with lamb souvlaki in a Plaka taverna.

See also: Greek Wine

docs.title: Ahhiyawa
docs.text:
Say it: ah-khee-YAH-wah 🔊 Pronounce
