The habit of asking, at every stop, what the standard story told to visitors leaves out, especially who got to learn there and who did not.

Example: At the Agora, the guide's story of democracy rarely mentions the women, metics and enslaved people who could not vote.

See also: Who Democracy Left Out

docs.title: Selahattin Ülkümen
docs.text:
Say it: seh-lah-hah-TEEN ewl-kew-MEN 🔊 Pronounce

The Turkish consul on Rhodes (1914–2003) who in 1944 insisted to the German commander that Jews with Turkish citizenship and their families were under Turkey's protection, saving several dozen lives.

Example: Israel's Yad Vashem honors him as Righteous Among the Nations.

See also: Rhodes Deportation of 1944

docs.title: Self-Fulfilling Prophecy
docs.text:
A prediction that causes itself to come true, because the people who hear it change their behavior in ways that bring about the predicted result.

Example: Telling a student a model predicts failure can lower expectations until the student does fail.

docs.title: Sephardic Jewish Refugees
docs.text:
Say it: Sephardic seh-FAR-dik 🔊 Pronounce

The Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 and Portugal soon after, many of whom were welcomed into the Ottoman Empire and settled in Istanbul, Thessaloniki, Rhodes and other cities.

See also: Ladino, Hebrew Press of 1493

docs.title: Serpent Column
docs.text:
A bronze column of three twisted snakes, originally set up at Delphi after the Greek victory over Persia at Plataea in 479 BCE and moved to the Hippodrome of Constantinople by Constantine.

Example: Its headless stump stands in a pit in Sultanahmet Square.

docs.title: Seven Undisputed Letters
docs.text: The seven letters that nearly all scholars accept as written by Paul himself: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon.

docs.title: Seven Wonders of the World
docs.text:
A list, drawn up by Greek writers in the Hellenistic period, of seven famous man-made monuments, including the Great Pyramid, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus and the Colossus of Rhodes.

Example: Two of the seven stood on our route, and almost nothing remains of either.

docs.title: Sèvres
docs.text:
Say it: SEV-ruh 🔊 Pronounce

The French town near Paris where a 1920 peace treaty was signed, by which the Allies planned to divide Ottoman lands and give Greece Smyrna and eastern Thrace; Turkey's war of independence overturned it.

docs.title: Shared Greek-Turkish Dishes
docs.text:
Foods common to both Greek and Turkish cooking because of centuries of shared life, such as stuffed vine leaves, yogurt dips, baklava, coffee and eggplant dishes, often under similar names.

Example: Greek papoutsakia and Turkish karnıyarık are both eggplants stuffed with spiced minced meat.

docs.title: Shared Language Spreads Ideas
docs.text:
The pattern in which a new idea can travel as far as a common language reaches, because many peoples who share that language can read and discuss it.

Example: Because Koine Greek was spoken across the eastern empire, Paul's letters could be read from Galatia to Rome.

See also: Koine Greek

docs.title: Shore Excursion
docs.text:
An organized tour sold by the cruise line that takes passengers from the ship to a site or activity on land and returns them before departure.

Example: On Crete, Viking offered both a Knossos tour and "The Villages of Crete," with a winery and a pottery village.

docs.title: Siege of Candia
docs.text:
The siege of Venetian Candia by the Ottomans from 1648 to 1669, one of the longest in history, which ended with the city's surrender and Ottoman rule over all of Crete.

See also: Ottoman Crete

docs.title: Siege of Rhodes 1522
docs.text:
The six-month siege in which the Ottoman army of Suleiman the Magnificent forced the Knights Hospitaller to surrender Rhodes; the knights were allowed to leave with honor at the start of 1523.

See also: Ottoman Rhodes, Suleiman the Magnificent

docs.title: Simit
docs.text:
Say it: see-MEET 🔊 Pronounce

A ring of bread dipped in grape molasses and covered in sesame seeds, sold from street carts across Istanbul and eaten at any time of day.

Example: A simit and a glass of tea on a bench in Sultanahmet Park make an easy breakfast.

docs.title: Simpler Interface to Knowledge
docs.text: Any change that lets more people reach what is known with less specialized skill, such as a script with fewer signs, a printed page, a public library or a clear sign.

docs.title: Şirince
docs.text:
Say it: shih-RIN-jeh 🔊 Pronounce

A hill village about 8 km east of Selçuk, once inhabited by Greek Orthodox families who left in the 1923 population exchange and were replaced by Muslim families from Greece.

Example: Today visitors come for its stone houses and local fruit wines.

See also: Population Exchange of 1923

docs.title: Site Museum
docs.text:
A museum built at or beside an archaeological site to display the objects found there, so visitors can see the finds in the context of the place they came from.

Example: The Troy Museum near Hisarlik displays pottery, weapons and gold from the layers of the mound nearby.

docs.title: Snake Goddess Figurines
docs.text:
Small faience statuettes from Knossos, about 1600 BCE, showing a woman in a flounced skirt with bare breasts holding or wrapped in snakes, probably a goddess or priestess.

Some scholars question how much of their present form was restored after discovery.

Example: The figures are among the most-photographed objects in the Heraklion museum.

docs.title: Socrates
docs.text:
The Athenian thinker (470–399 BCE) who wrote nothing but questioned people in the Agora about justice, courage and virtue, and was executed for impiety and corrupting the young.

Example: Delphi's answer that no one was wiser than he set him on his lifelong questioning.

See also: Socratic Method, Trial of Socrates

docs.title: Socratic Method
docs.text:
A way of teaching and inquiry by asking a series of questions that test a person's beliefs, expose contradictions and lead toward clearer understanding, rather than by giving answers.

Example: A good AI tutor that asks "why do you think that?" instead of supplying the answer follows this pattern.

See also: Lecture to Dialogue, AI as Thinking Partner

docs.title: Sophists
docs.text: Traveling teachers in 5th-century BCE Greece who charged fees to teach rhetoric, argument and skills for public life, criticized by Plato for valuing persuasion over truth.

docs.title: Souvlaki and Gyros
docs.text:
Say it: Gyros YEE-ros 🔊 Pronounce

Two Greek street foods: souvlaki is pieces of meat grilled on a skewer, and gyros is meat sliced from a vertical rotisserie, both often wrapped in pita with tomato, onion and tzatziki.

Example: A gyros wrap from a shop in Monastiraki is a quick lunch between museums.

docs.title: Spice Bazaar
docs.text:
The covered market near the Galata Bridge in Istanbul, built in the 1660s as part of the New Mosque complex, known for spices, dried fruit, nuts, tea and Turkish delight.

Example: We bought Turkish delight and saffron there.

docs.title: Spice Trade
docs.text: The long-distance commerce in pepper, cinnamon, cloves, saffron and other spices between Asia, the Middle East and Europe, which made Mediterranean ports and merchants rich for centuries.

docs.title: Spolia
docs.text:
Say it: SPOH-lee-uh 🔊 Pronounce

Building pieces, such as columns, capitals or carved blocks, taken from older structures and reused in new ones, a practice common in late Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman building.

Example: The two upside-down and sideways Medusa heads in the Basilica Cistern are reused Roman blocks.

See also: Medusa Heads, Reading a Ruin

docs.title: St. Paul's Bay at Lindos
docs.text:
A small, almost enclosed cove below the acropolis of Lindos on Rhodes, where local tradition says Paul's ship landed during a storm.

Example: A small white chapel of St. Paul stands on its shore.

docs.title: St. Paul's Prison Tower
docs.text:
A square stone tower on a hilltop at the western edge of ancient Ephesus that local tradition names as the place where Paul was held. Acts mentions no imprisonment there.

Example: It can be seen from the lower part of the site, near the harbor area.

docs.title: Stadium of Delphi
docs.text: The running track at the highest point of the ancient site, above the sanctuary wall, about 178 meters long, with stone seats, where the athletic events of the Pythian Games were held.

docs.title: Stages of Concern
docs.text: The seven kinds of concern people typically move through when meeting an innovation, from awareness and personal worries to managing it, its effect on students and ways to improve it, part of a model developed at the University of Texas.

docs.title: Stoa
docs.text:
A long covered walkway with a row of columns in front and a wall behind, used in Greek cities for shade, business, teaching and meeting friends.

Example: The reconstructed Stoa of Attalos in the Agora now holds the Agora Museum.

See also: Stoa Poikile, Stoicism

docs.title: Stoa Poikile
docs.text:
Say it: STOH-uh POY-kih-lee 🔊 Pronounce

The "Painted Stoa" on the north side of the Athenian Agora, built in the 460s BCE and hung with famous paintings, where Zeno taught and from which Stoicism took its name.

Example: Its remains, found in 1981, can be seen from Adrianou Street.

docs.title: Stochastic
docs.text:
Say it: stuh-KAS-tik 🔊 Pronounce

A statistician's word for "random" or governed by probability; such a process produces outcomes that vary by chance, even when its rules stay the same.

Example: The phrase "stochastic parrots" was used in 2021 to argue that language models only stitch together word patterns.

See also: Large Language Model

docs.title: Stoicism
docs.text: A philosophy founded in Athens around 300 BCE by Zeno of Citium, teaching that virtue is the only true good and that a wise person accepts what cannot be controlled. It was named after the Painted Stoa.

docs.title: Storage Pithoi
docs.text:
Say it: pithoi PITH-oy 🔊 Pronounce

Very large clay jars, often taller than a person, used by the Minoans to store oil, wine, grain and other goods in palace storerooms.

Example: Rows of these jars still stand in the west storerooms at Knossos, and similar jars are still made in Thrapsano.

See also: Thrapsano

docs.title: Stratigraphy
docs.text:
The study of soil and debris layers at a site, read on the principle that lower layers are generally older, so that the order of layers reveals the order of events.

Example: At Troy, archaeologists separate nine main settlement levels stacked in one mound.

docs.title: Street of the Knights
docs.text:
A straight cobbled street in Rhodes Medieval Town lined with the stone inns where knights from each nation of the Hospitaller order lived and met.

Example: Coats of arms of France, Italy and Spain are carved above the doorways.

docs.title: Student Risk Prediction
docs.text:
The use of a predictive model to estimate which students are likely to fail, fall behind or drop out, so that schools can offer help early.

It can help or harm, depending on how the score is used.

See also: Self-Fulfilling Prophecy, Data Bias

docs.title: Succession Planning
docs.text:
Preparing and trusting other people to take over leadership, well before the founder leaves, so that a change survives its founder's departure or death.

Example: Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus handed leadership to local people.

See also: Farewell at Miletus

docs.title: Suleiman the Magnificent
docs.text:
The Ottoman sultan who ruled from 1520 to 1566, the empire's peak, known in Turkey as "the Lawgiver," who took Rhodes and Belgrade and sponsored great building in Istanbul.

Example: He is buried behind the mosque that bears his name, built by his architect Sinan.

See also: Suleymaniye Mosque, Mimar Sinan

docs.title: Suleymaniye Mosque
docs.text:
Say it: Süleymaniye sue-lay-MAH-nee-yeh 🔊 Pronounce

The mosque built for Suleiman the Magnificent by Mimar Sinan from 1550 to 1557 on Istanbul's third hill, surrounded by schools, a hospital, a soup kitchen and the tombs of Suleiman and Hürrem.

See also: Kulliye Mosque Complex

docs.title: Sultan
docs.text: The title of the ruler of the Ottoman Empire and of other Muslim states, meaning one who holds power. Ottoman rulers also claimed the title of caliph after 1517.

docs.title: Sultanahmet
docs.text:
Say it: sool-TAHN-ah-met 🔊 Pronounce

The historic district at the tip of Istanbul's old peninsula, named after Sultan Ahmed's mosque, which contains Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, the Hippodrome and Topkapı Palace.

Example: Most first-time visitors to Istanbul stay within walking distance of its park.

docs.title: Sustainable Funding
docs.text:
Money that can keep a change going for years, beyond an initial grant or pilot, so that the new practice survives budget shifts.

Example: The Ottoman endowments that paid for schools for centuries are an old model of it.

docs.title: Symposium
docs.text:
In ancient Greece, a drinking party held after dinner in which men reclined on couches, drank wine mixed with water and shared conversation, poetry, music and games.

Example: Plato's dialogue Symposium is set at one, where the guests take turns speaking about love.

docs.title: Systems Thinking
docs.text: A way of understanding a situation as a set of connected parts that affect one another over time, so that a change in one part produces effects elsewhere.

docs.title: Tarsus
docs.text:
An ancient city in Cilicia on the southern coast of modern Turkey, a center of Greek learning under Rome and the birthplace of Paul.

Example: Paul is quoted in Acts calling it "no mean city."

docs.title: Taverna Culture
docs.text:
The Greek custom of long, relaxed meals at a casual neighborhood restaurant, sharing many plates with friends and family over wine and conversation.

See also: Philoxenia

docs.title: Teacher as Coach
docs.text: A role in which the teacher guides, questions and supports students as they work, rather than mainly delivering content, which becomes more important when AI handles some explanation.

docs.title: Teaching Comes to Learner
docs.text: The reversal AI tutoring promises: instead of the student traveling to the teacher, the teacher's attention travels to the student, wherever and whenever the student is ready.

docs.title: Temple of Apollo at Delphi
docs.text:
The main temple of the sanctuary, where the Pythia gave her answers. Its remains date from the 4th century BCE, built after an earlier temple was destroyed by an earthquake.

See also: Adyton, Know Thyself

docs.title: Temple of Artemis
docs.text:
The great Ionic temple near Ephesus dedicated to the goddess Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the World, rebuilt after a fire in 356 BCE and destroyed in late antiquity.

Example: Today a single re-erected column stands in a marshy field, often with a stork's nest on top.

docs.title: Temple of Athena Nike
docs.text:
A small Ionic temple on a bastion beside the entrance to the Acropolis, built in the 420s BCE to Athena as bringer of victory.

Example: It has been taken apart and rebuilt several times, most recently in the 2000s.

docs.title: Temple of Hadrian at Ephesus
docs.text:
Say it: Ephesus EF-uh-sus 🔊 Pronounce

A small, finely carved temple on Curetes Street dedicated in the 2nd century CE to the emperor Hadrian, with an arch decorated with the head of the city's goddess of fortune.

Example: The relief panels inside are copies; the originals are in the Ephesus Museum.

docs.title: Temple of Hephaestus
docs.text:
Say it: Hephaestus heh-FESS-tus 🔊 Pronounce

A Doric temple on a low hill above the Agora, built in the second half of the 5th century BCE to the god of metalworking, the best-preserved Greek temple in Athens.

Example: It survived largely because it served as a church for centuries.

docs.title: Temple of Olympian Zeus
docs.text:
A colossal temple in central Athens begun in the 6th century BCE and completed by the emperor Hadrian around 131 CE, with 104 Corinthian columns of which 15 still stand.

Example: Hadrian's Arch beside it marked the boundary between the old city and his new quarter.

docs.title: Tentmaking
docs.text:
Paul's trade, according to Acts, as a maker of tents or leather goods, which let him support himself rather than depend on the communities he taught.

Example: He worked alongside Priscilla and Aquila, who shared the same craft.

See also: Who Pays for Learning

docs.title: Terrace Houses
docs.text:
A block of richly decorated Roman houses built on the hillside above Curetes Street in Ephesus, now under a protective roof, with wall paintings, mosaics and marble floors.

Example: Walkways let visitors look down into dining rooms and courtyards of wealthy families from the 1st to 7th centuries CE.

docs.title: Testability of Predictions
docs.text:
The quality of a prediction that can be checked against what happens and shown right or wrong; vague or hedged predictions cannot be tested.

See also: Hedging Answers, Model Calibration

docs.title: Theater of Delphi
docs.text:
The stone theater above the Temple of Apollo, seating about 5,000 people, used for the musical and drama contests of the Pythian Games.

Example: From its top rows the view runs down over the temple to the valley of olive trees.

docs.title: Theater of Dionysus
docs.text:
The theater on the south slope of the Acropolis where the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides and Aristophanes were first performed at festivals for the god Dionysus.

Example: Carved marble seats for priests still line its front row.

docs.title: Themistocles
docs.text:
Say it: thuh-MIS-tuh-kleez 🔊 Pronounce

The Athenian leader (about 524–459 BCE) who persuaded the city to build a large fleet of warships and led the Greek victory at Salamis, later ostracized and exiled.

Example: He argued that the oracle's "wooden walls" meant ships, not the old palisade on the Acropolis.

docs.title: Theodosian Decrees
docs.text:
Say it: Theodosian thee-uh-DOH-shun 🔊 Pronounce

The series of laws issued by Theodosius I in the 380s and 390s CE that forbade pagan sacrifices and closed temples, ending official support for the old gods.

Example: They are usually linked to the end of the Oracle of Delphi.

docs.title: Theodosian Walls
docs.text:
Say it: Theodosian thee-uh-DOH-shun 🔊 Pronounce

The land walls of Constantinople, built in the early 5th century CE under Theodosius II, a triple line of moat, outer wall and inner wall about 6.5 km long that protected the city for a thousand years.

Example: Ottoman cannons finally breached them in 1453.

docs.title: Theodosius I
docs.text: The Roman emperor (ruled 379–395 CE) who made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the empire and issued laws banning pagan sacrifice and worship.

docs.title: Theotokopoulos
docs.text:
Say it: theh-oh-toh-KOH-poo-los 🔊 Pronounce

The family name of the painter El Greco, Domenikos Theotokopoulos, born in Candia in 1541, which he kept signing in Greek letters throughout his life in Spain.

See also: El Greco

docs.title: Theotokos
docs.text:
Say it: thee-oh-TOH-kos 🔊 Pronounce

The Greek title for Mary, meaning "God-bearer," confirmed by the Council of Ephesus in 431 CE and central to Orthodox devotion.

docs.title: Thera Eruption
docs.text:
Say it: Thera THEER-uh 🔊 Pronounce

The enormous volcanic eruption of the island of Thera, modern Santorini, around 1600 BCE, which buried the town of Akrotiri and spread ash across the Aegean.

Example: It once was thought to have destroyed Minoan Crete, but the Cretan palaces flourished for more than a century afterward.

docs.title: Thessaloniki
docs.text:
Say it: thess-uh-loh-NEE-kee 🔊 Pronounce

Greece's second-largest city, in Macedonia in the north, a major Roman port where Paul founded a church and to which he wrote his earliest surviving letter.

docs.title: Tholos of Delphi
docs.text:
Say it: Tholos THOH-los 🔊 Pronounce

A circular marble building in the sanctuary of Athena Pronaia, built around 380 BCE, of which three columns have been re-erected; its purpose is unknown.

Example: It is one of the most photographed ruins in Greece.

docs.title: Thoughtful Traveler
docs.text:
A visitor who goes to a place to understand it and its people, not only to see its sights, and who tries to leave the people met better off, or at least no worse off, for the visit.

This is the kind of traveler the book asks its readers to be.

Example: Learning to say "thank you" in Turkish and buying lunch from a family-run shop are small acts of this kind.

docs.title: Thrapsano
docs.text:
Say it: thrap-sah-NOH 🔊 Pronounce

A village in central Crete known for its potters, who make huge clay storage jars by methods similar to those of Minoan times.

Example: Viking's "Villages of Crete" excursion stopped here after a wine tasting.

docs.title: Throne Room at Knossos
docs.text:
Say it: Knossos NOSS-us 🔊 Pronounce

A small room in the palace at Knossos with a stone seat set against the wall, flanked by painted griffins and benches, probably used for ceremonies.

Example: The gypsum chair found there is often called the oldest throne in Europe.

docs.title: Thyiads
docs.text:
Say it: THY-yadz 🔊 Pronounce

Women of Athens and Delphi who, every other winter, climbed Mount Parnassus by night to celebrate Dionysus with dancing and torches.

docs.title: Thyme Honey
docs.text:
A strongly scented honey made by bees from the flowers of wild thyme on Greek hillsides, prized in Greece since antiquity.

Example: Shops in Arachova and Delphi sell local jars of it.

docs.title: Timothy and Titus
docs.text: Two of Paul's closest co-workers: Timothy, from Lystra in Anatolia, whom Paul sent to strengthen communities, and Titus, a Greek Gentile who carried letters and, by tradition, led the church on Crete.

docs.title: Tipping Customs
docs.text:
The local expectations about leaving extra money for service in restaurants, taxis, hotels and tours, which differ between Turkey and Greece and from American practice.

Example: In a Greek taverna, rounding up the bill or leaving about five to ten percent is usual.

docs.title: Titus in Crete
docs.text:
The tradition, based on the New Testament letter to Titus, that Paul left Titus on Crete to organize its churches and that he became the island's first bishop.

Example: His skull is kept as a relic in the Church of St. Titus in Heraklion, returned from Venice in 1966.

docs.title: Topkapi Palace
docs.text:
Say it: Topkapı TOP-kah-puh 🔊 Pronounce

The main residence and seat of government of the Ottoman sultans from the 1460s to 1856, a series of courtyards, pavilions and gardens on the tip of the historic peninsula, now a museum.

See also: Harem of Topkapi, Topkapi Treasury

docs.title: Topkapi Treasury
docs.text:
Say it: Topkapı TOP-kah-puh 🔊 Pronounce

The rooms of Topkapı Palace that display the jewels, weapons, thrones, jeweled objects and diplomatic gifts collected by the Ottoman sultans over four centuries.

Example: Crowds gather around the emerald-studded Topkapı Dagger and the large Spoonmaker's Diamond.

docs.title: Tourism Economy
docs.text:
The part of a region's economy that depends on visitors, including jobs in hotels, restaurants, guiding, transport and shops, and the public income from tickets and taxes.

Example: In Selçuk, many families earn a living from the people who come to see Ephesus.

See also: Off-Season Livelihoods, Overtourism

docs.title: Track Record and Trust
docs.text:
The principle that a source of predictions deserves trust in proportion to its record of predictions written down before the outcomes were known.

Example: Nearly every famous Delphic prophecy was first recorded after the event it seemed to predict.

docs.title: Trade Routes
docs.text:
The regular paths by land and sea along which goods, people and ideas moved between regions, shaped by winds, straits, harbors and the demand for metals, grain, wine and spices.

Example: The Uluburun shipwreck carried copper, tin and luxury goods from several lands, showing how far Bronze Age shipping reached.

See also: Spice Trade

docs.title: Training Data
docs.text:
The set of examples, such as past records, texts or images, from which a machine-learning system learns its patterns. What it contains, and leaves out, shapes what the system can do.

See also: Data Bias

docs.title: Travel Journal
docs.text:
A personal written record kept during a trip, with short daily notes on what we saw, ate and learned and on questions the day raised.

The book adds reflection prompts to it in several chapters.

Example: One entry reads: a simit and a glass of tea on a bench in Sultanahmet Park, the tea too hot to hold.

See also: Leadership Reflection, Delphi Reflection Questions

docs.title: Traveling to the Teacher
docs.text:
The old pattern of education in which the learner goes, often at great cost, to wherever the master teacher is, rather than teaching coming to the learner.

Example: Cicero and Caesar sailed to Rhodes because its best teachers of rhetoric could not be carried home.

See also: Roman Students at Rhodes, Teaching Comes to Learner

docs.title: Treasuries of Delphi
docs.text: Small temple-shaped buildings along the Sacred Way built by Greek cities to hold their offerings to Apollo and display their wealth and victories.

docs.title: Treaty of Lausanne
docs.text: The peace treaty signed in Lausanne, Switzerland, in July 1923 between Turkey and the Allies, which set most of modern Turkey's borders and confirmed the Greek–Turkish population exchange.

docs.title: Trial of Socrates
docs.text:
The prosecution of Socrates in Athens in 399 BCE on charges of not honoring the city's gods and corrupting the young, which ended with a jury of 500 condemning him to drink hemlock.

Example: Plato's Apology gives his version of Socrates' defense speech.

docs.title: Trip Itinerary
docs.text:
The day-by-day plan of the whole journey, including days on our own in Istanbul and Athens before and after the cruise, port calls, excursions and the day trip to Delphi.

Example: The plan pairs each chapter of this book with the day we visit its place.

docs.title: Trojan Horse
docs.text:
The legendary wooden horse in which Greek soldiers hid so that the Trojans would pull it inside their walls, letting the Greeks open the gates at night and take the city.

The story appears in the Odyssey and in Virgil, not in the Iliad.

Example: A large wooden replica stands at the entrance to the site, and another from a 2004 film stands in Çanakkale.

docs.title: Trojan War
docs.text:
The legendary ten-year war in which a Greek army besieged Troy to recover Helen, wife of King Menelaus of Sparta, told in Homer's Iliad and later poems.

Whether a real war lies behind it remains debated.

See also: Iliad, Historicity of Troy

docs.title: Troy
docs.text:
The ancient city in northwest Anatolia near the mouth of the Dardanelles, occupied from about 3000 BCE to Roman times and famous as the setting of Homer's Iliad.

Example: Today the site is a low mound of walls, ramps and trenches where nine main settlements lie one above another.

docs.title: Troy Museum
docs.text:
The museum near the archaeological site of Troy, opened in 2018, that displays finds from all the layers of Hisarlik and nearby sites in a building shaped like a rusted cube.

Example: Visitors begin on the lowest floor with the oldest layers and climb toward Roman Troy.

See also: Site Museum

docs.title: Troy VI and VIIa
docs.text:
The two settlement levels at Troy dated to the late Bronze Age, about 1700 to 1180 BCE, the main candidates for the city of the Trojan War. Troy VI had massive sloping walls; Troy VIIa ended in fire.

Example: The smooth, angled stone walls near the site entrance belong to Troy VI.

docs.title: Tsikoudia
docs.text:
Say it: tsee-koo-DYAH 🔊 Pronounce

The clear Cretan spirit distilled from grape skins and seeds left after winemaking, often offered free at the end of a meal.

Example: A taverna in Heraklion may bring a small carafe of it with fruit after dinner.

docs.title: Turkish Bath
docs.text:
A public steam bath in the Ottoman tradition, with a hot marble platform, warm washing rooms and scrubbing and soaping by attendants, descended from the Roman baths.

See also: Hamam, Roman Bath Culture

docs.title: Turkish Breakfast
docs.text: The traditional morning meal of many small dishes, such as cheeses, olives, tomatoes, cucumbers, eggs, honey and jam, eaten with bread and tea.

docs.title: Turkish Coffee
docs.text:
Very finely ground coffee boiled slowly in a small pot with water and, if wanted, sugar, served unfiltered with the grounds settling in the cup. UNESCO lists its culture as intangible heritage.

See also: Greek Coffee

docs.title: Turkish Cuisine
docs.text:
The cooking of Turkey, drawing on Central Asian, Anatolian, Ottoman, Arab and Mediterranean traditions, with grilled meats, vegetables cooked in olive oil, yogurt, bread, rice and rich sweets.

See also: Ottoman Palace Kitchen, Meze

docs.title: Turkish Delight
docs.text:
A soft, chewy sweet made by cooking sugar and starch, often flavored with rosewater, lemon or fruit and sometimes filled with nuts, cut into cubes and dusted with powdered sugar.

Example: We bought several kinds at the Spice Bazaar.

See also: Lokum

docs.title: Turkish Economy Today
docs.text:
The present state of Turkey's economy, a large manufacturing, agricultural and tourism economy marked in recent years by high inflation and a falling lira that raise the cost of living.

Example: Menu prices in Istanbul may change between one season and the next.

docs.title: Turkish Hospitality
docs.text:
The strong Turkish custom of welcoming guests generously, often with tea, food and conversation, rooted in rural and religious traditions that treat a guest as a gift.

Example: A carpet seller may offer a glass of tea before any talk of buying, and accepting it is polite.

docs.title: Turkish Language
docs.text:
The Turkic language of modern Turkey, brought to Anatolia from Central Asia from the 11th century. It was written in Arabic script until 1928 and in Latin letters since.

Example: Signs in Istanbul use letters such as ç, ş and ğ, added to the Latin alphabet in the 1928 reform.

docs.title: Turkish Tea
docs.text:
Black tea grown mainly on Turkey's Black Sea coast, brewed strong in a two-level pot and served in small tulip-shaped glasses, the country's everyday drink.

Example: Shopkeepers in the Grand Bazaar send out for trays of it for visiting customers.

docs.title: Turkish War of Independence
docs.text:
The struggle from 1919 to 1923 by Turkish nationalists under Mustafa Kemal against occupying Allied and Greek forces and the treaty that would have divided Anatolia.

See also: Sèvres, Treaty of Lausanne

docs.title: Uluburun
docs.text:
Say it: oo-loo-boo-ROON 🔊 Pronounce

A rocky point near Kaş on Turkey's southern coast, where a merchant ship sank around 1300 BCE; its wreck, found in 1982, carried copper, tin, glass and luxury goods from many lands.

Example: Its cargo shows how far Bronze Age trade networks reached.

See also: Trade Routes

docs.title: UNESCO World Heritage Site
docs.text:
A place listed by the United Nations cultural agency as having outstanding value to all humanity, which brings international recognition and commits the host country to protect it.

Example: The historic areas of Istanbul, the Acropolis, Ephesus, Delphi and the Medieval City of Rhodes all hold this status.

docs.title: Üsküdar
docs.text:
Say it: EWS-kew-dar 🔊 Pronounce

A large residential district on the Asian shore of the Bosphorus, facing the historic peninsula, reached by ferry from the European side.

docs.title: Vakif Endowment
docs.text:
Say it: vakıf vah-KUHF 🔊 Pronounce

An Islamic charitable foundation in which property such as shops or farmland is given permanently and its income pays for mosques, schools, soup kitchens, fountains or hospitals.

Example: Rent from shops in the Grand Bazaar paid for the upkeep of nearby religious buildings.

docs.title: Values Beyond Prediction
docs.text: The principle that a prediction can tell us what is likely to happen if we act, but not what we ought to want; choosing what matters is a question of values no model can answer for us.

docs.title: Venetian Crete
docs.text: The period from the early 13th century to 1669 when Crete was a colony of Venice, ruled from the city of Candia, and Greek and Italian cultures mixed in art, building and literature.

docs.title: Venetian Walls of Heraklion
docs.text:
Say it: Heraklion heh-RAH-klee-on 🔊 Pronounce

The massive bastioned walls, about 4.5 km around, that Venice built around Candia in the 16th and 17th centuries, which held off the Ottoman army for more than twenty years.

Example: Nikos Kazantzakis is buried on the Martinengo Bastion at their southern edge.

docs.title: Veteran Teacher Champions
docs.text: Experienced, respected teachers who adopt a change early and help colleagues through it, the school's version of the insider change leader.

docs.title: Viking Star Cruise
docs.text:
The seven-night sailing on Viking's small ocean ship from Istanbul to Piraeus, November 14 to 21, 2026, which carries us between the middle stops of the trip.

The ship holds about 930 adult guests, small by modern cruise standards.

Example: The ship sails from Galataport in Istanbul at 6:00 PM on November 15, just after sunset.

docs.title: Vitruvius
docs.text:
Say it: vih-TROO-vee-us 🔊 Pronounce

A Roman architect and engineer who wrote On Architecture around 25 BCE, the only complete book on architecture to survive from antiquity and the main source for the rules of the column styles.

See also: Classical Orders

docs.title: Weather Forecasting
docs.text:
Predicting future atmospheric conditions using observations and computer models of the atmosphere, usually stated as probabilities, one of the most tested kinds of prediction.

See also: Model Calibration, Prediction Horizon

docs.title: Who Democracy Left Out
docs.text:
The people living under Athenian democracy who had no share in it: all women, metics (resident foreigners), enslaved people and, in practice, many poor citizens far from the city.

See also: Athenian Citizenship, Measuring Who Is Left Out

docs.title: Who Funds the Model
docs.text:
The question of who pays to build and run a prediction system, and how that payment might shape whose interests it serves.

Example: Croesus's gifts bought his Lydians the right to consult Delphi first and without fees.

See also: Bribery of the Oracle, Fees and Sacrifice

docs.title: Who Is Hurt by Change
docs.text:
The question a leader must ask about every change: who loses, how much, and whether the loss was intended, foreseen, shared fairly or could be reduced.

Example: Paul's mission cost the silversmiths income, and his words were later turned against Jews for centuries.

See also: Evangelism's Shadow

docs.title: Who Pays for Learning
docs.text:
The question of where the cost of an education falls: on the learner's family, a patron, the state, or a teacher who gives time for free.

Example: Athens tried every answer: the Sophists charged fees, while Socrates charged nothing.

See also: Sophists, Endowed Free Education

docs.title: Widening the Circle
docs.text:
The process by which access to learning spreads to more people than before, usually because a gatekeeper is bypassed or a gate is opened.

Example: The alphabet, the endowed school and the printing press each widened who could read.

docs.title: Wilusa
docs.text:
Say it: wih-LOO-sah 🔊 Pronounce

A kingdom in western Anatolia named in Hittite records of the 14th and 13th centuries BCE, which most scholars identify with Troy, the Greek Wilios or Ilios.

Example: Hittite letters describe a quarrel over this place with the king of Ahhiyawa, likely the Mycenaean Greeks.

docs.title: Wooden Walls Prophecy
docs.text:
The oracle's answer to Athens before the Persian invasion of 480 BCE that only a "wooden wall" would not fall and that "divine Salamis" would destroy many sons of women.

Example: Themistocles argued it meant the fleet, and the Greeks won at Salamis.

See also: Themistocles, Battle of Salamis

docs.title: World War I
docs.text:
The global war of 1914 to 1918 in which the Ottoman Empire fought alongside Germany against Britain, France and Russia, leading to the empire's defeat and breakup.

See also: Gallipoli Campaign

docs.title: World War II
docs.text: The global war of 1939 to 1945, during which Greece was invaded and occupied by Germany and Italy and the Jews of Greece, including those of Rhodes, were deported to death camps. Turkey stayed neutral until early 1945.

docs.title: Writing Systems
docs.text:
Sets of visible signs used to record language, including picture-based scripts, syllabaries where each sign stands for a syllable, and alphabets where each sign stands for a single sound.

Example: Linear B used about 90 syllable signs, while the Greek alphabet needed only 24 letters.

docs.title: Yerebatan
docs.text:
Say it: yeh-reh-bah-TAHN 🔊 Pronounce

The Turkish name for the Basilica Cistern in Istanbul, Yerebatan Sarayı, "the Sunken Palace," referring to its forest of columns underground.

docs.title: List of Appendices
docs.text:
The following topics do not fit neatly into our travel log, so I have placed them in appendices at the "end" of the book.

  1. Photography Metrics
  2. Pronunciation Guide
  3. Timeline of Events
  4. Extensions and Excursions
  5. Who Created the Antikythera Mechanism

docs.title: Who Created the Antikythera Mechanism
docs.text:
In 1900 a crew of sponge divers sheltering from a storm off the small island of Antikythera, between Kythera and Crete, found a Roman-era shipwreck on the seabed. Over the next year they brought up bronze and marble statues, glass, pottery, and coins. They also brought up a lump of corroded bronze and wood that nobody paid much attention to. In 1902 the archaeologist Valerios Stais noticed a gear wheel in one of its broken pieces. That lump is the Antikythera mechanism, and it now sits in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, which Chapter 20 visits. The link in the title above opens close-up photographs of the fragments.

The ship sank in about 70–60 BCE, dated by the coins from Pergamon and Ephesus found with it. The mechanism itself is older, probably made sometime in the 2nd century BCE. Nobody signed it, and no ancient writer mentions this particular device. This appendix asks what it would have taken to make it, where it was most likely made, and who was living there.

docs.title: What the Mechanism Is
docs.text:
The mechanism was a wooden box about the size of a shoebox, roughly 34 × 18 × 9 cm, with a bronze dial on the front, two on the back, and a hand crank on the side. Turning the crank drove a train of bronze gears inside, and the gears drove pointers on the dials. Turn the crank forward and the dials showed the sky on a future date; turn it back and they showed a past one.

What survives is 82 corroded fragments holding at least 30 gears. The gears were cut from bronze sheet a couple of millimeters thick, with small triangular teeth filed by hand. The largest is about the width of a hand. Every surface of the box was covered with tiny Greek inscriptions, a built-in user's manual of which thousands of characters have now been read. Most of what we know comes from X-ray computed tomography scans made in 2005 by the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project, which let researchers count teeth and read letters hidden inside the corroded lumps.

Where Dial What it showed Front Zodiac ring The positions of the Sun and Moon among the constellations, and, in modern reconstructions, the five planets known to the Greeks Front Calendar ring The 365-day Egyptian civil calendar, with the Egyptian month names inscribed Front Moon ball The phase of the Moon, shown by a small half-silver, half-black ball that turned Back, upper Metonic spiral A 19-year calendar of 235 lunar months, with month names from a real Greek city's calendar Back, upper Games dial Which athletic festivals fell in each year of a four-year cycle, including the Olympic Games Back, lower Saros spiral An eclipse calendar of 223 lunar months, with a symbol on each month that would have a solar or lunar eclipse Back, lower Exeligmos dial A correction telling the user how many hours to add to the eclipse times

The hardest part to build was the Moon. The Moon moves faster across the sky at some points in its orbit than at others. The maker reproduced this with two gears mounted slightly off-center, one driving the other through a pin sliding in a slot, so that the Moon pointer sped up and slowed down once a month. That matches the lunar theory worked out by the astronomer Hipparchus, who did much of his observing on Rhodes.

docs.title: Try a Simplified Gear Model
docs.text: Explore the Antikythera Gears MicroSim to see how tooth counts produce different Sun, Moon, and Mars cycle speeds. The model uses rounded ratios for teaching; it does not reconstruct the ancient mechanism or predict sky positions.

docs.title: One of the Earliest Analog Computers
docs.text:
An analog computer calculates by building a physical model whose quantities behave like the ones you want to know. A slide rule is one: the lengths along its scales stand for logarithms, and sliding one scale along the other adds them. In the Antikythera mechanism, the angle a gear has turned stands for time passed, and each gear ratio stands for a ratio between two cycles in the sky. Turning the crank does the arithmetic.

The historian of science Derek de Solla Price called it "an ancient Greek computer" in Scientific American in 1959, and the label stuck. It is the oldest known geared calculating device, and one of the most significant early analog computers ever made. It is a computer in the old sense of the word, a machine that computes answers, not one that runs programs.

Worked example: why a 235-month spiral? The Greeks needed a calendar that kept lunar months and solar years in step. Here is the arithmetic behind the Metonic dial, with modern values:

Cycle Count Length in days Solar years 19 × 365.2422 6,939.60 Lunar months 235 × 29.5306 6,939.69

Nineteen years and 235 months differ by about two hours, so after 19 years the Moon's phases fall on nearly the same calendar dates again. The maker had to turn that ratio into teeth. Because 235 = 5 × 47, the dial is a spiral of five turns with 47 months on each turn, and a follower pin in the pointer tracks which turn it is on.

The eclipse dial works the same way. Eclipses repeat in a cycle of 223 lunar months, called the Saros, about 18 years and 11 days. Because 223 is a prime number, it cannot be built from smaller gears, so the mechanism has a gear with 223 teeth. A Saros is also about 8 hours longer than a whole number of days, so each repeat of an eclipse happens 8 hours later in the day. The small exeligmos dial, marked for 0, 8, and 16 hours, tells the user how much to add. Three Saros cycles, 54 years, bring the eclipse back to nearly the same hour.

Calling it a computer

A common trap is to picture the mechanism as a general-purpose machine. Its answers were fixed in its gears when it was made, and wrong values in the gears stayed wrong forever. Think of it as a calculator with one job, the motions of the sky, built with great skill.

docs.title: A Machine for Predicting the Future
docs.text:
People have always wanted to know what comes next: whether the harvest will be good, whether a voyage will be safe, whether a war will be won. The Greeks asked gods. Travelers climbed to Delphi to ask the Pythia, as Chapter 17 and Chapter 18 describe, and her answers were famously open to interpretation. Babylonian scribes watched the sky for omens, and over centuries of nightly records they noticed that eclipses and planetary positions repeat in regular cycles.

The mechanism takes those records and turns them into a machine. Its user did not need to ask a god or read an omen. Turning a crank showed when the next eclipse would come, in what month, and at about what hour. The future, at least the part of it written in the sky, became something you could calculate, and the calculation gave the same answer to everyone who turned the crank.

From oracle to model

Notice the shift. The Pythia's answer depended on who she was and how you read her, while the mechanism's answer came from cycles anyone could count, set into a model of the sky. Modern weather models and AI forecasts follow the same idea: find the patterns in past data, build a model, and run it forward.

That is the thread from Delphi to the classroom. Chapter 19 follows it to algorithms, and AI-Native Schools takes it further in Projecting AI Growth, which uses doubling curves to predict how quickly AI tools will spread.

docs.title: The Skills Needed to Build It
docs.text:
No single craft could have produced the mechanism. Its maker, or more likely its workshop, had to combine at least six kinds of expertise.

Skill What it involved Where it came from Observational astronomy Knowing the cycles of the Sun, Moon, and planets, including eclipse periods and planetary periods such as Venus repeating its pattern of appearances every 462 years Centuries of Babylonian records, refined by Greek astronomers Mathematical astronomy A geometric theory of why the Moon speeds up and slows down, and how to model it Hipparchus and his circle, 2nd century BCE Arithmetic and number theory Turning cycle ratios into whole-number gear teeth, factoring numbers such as 235 and 223, and keeping error small Greek mathematics in the tradition of Archimedes Precision metalworking Cutting dozens of bronze gears by hand, with teeth evenly spaced, small enough to fit in a box Bronze workshops that also made statues, weapons, and fittings Mechanical design Mounting gears on shared axles, the pin-and-slot Moon gears, spiral dials with followers, a ball that turned to show phases Greek engineers who built water clocks, automata, and siege machines Calendars and civic life Setting the dials to a particular city's month names and festival calendar, and writing a clear manual A maker who knew the customer's home city

Two more things were needed that are easy to overlook. One was money: a device like this was a luxury object, and someone had to pay months of a skilled workshop's time. The other was a tradition. The mechanism is too refined to be a first attempt, and Cicero mentions two other geared models of the heavens, one built by Archimedes in Syracuse and taken to Rome in 212 BCE, and one built by the philosopher Posidonius on Rhodes in Cicero's own day. The Antikythera mechanism is the only one that survived, probably because it sank. Bronze on land was usually melted down and reused.

docs.title: Why Rhodes Is One of the Most Likely Places
docs.text:
Several cities have been proposed, including Syracuse (because of Archimedes), Pergamon, Corinth's colonies in northwest Greece, and Rhodes. Rhodes has the strongest combined case.

  • Hipparchus observed there. The greatest astronomer of the age recorded observations on Rhodes between about 147 and 127 BCE, and the mechanism's Moon gears follow his lunar theory.
  • Posidonius built a similar machine there. Cicero, who studied with Posidonius on Rhodes (see Chapter 12), wrote that his teacher had made a sphere showing the motions of the Sun, Moon, and five planets.
  • The games dial names a Rhodian festival. The classicist Paul Iversen read one of the damaged names on the games dial as the Halieia, the games Rhodes held for its sun god Helios. A device made for a buyer far away would have little reason to list a minor Rhodian festival.
  • The latitude fits. The star calendar inscribed on the front works best for a latitude between about 33 and 37 degrees north. Rhodes lies at about 36 degrees north; Athens, Corinth, and Pergamon all lie north of that band.
  • The ship's cargo points east. The wreck carried coins from Pergamon and Ephesus and pottery from the eastern Aegean, which suggests a voyage from that region, where Rhodes was the great harbor, toward Italy.

The main evidence pointing elsewhere is the calendar on the Metonic dial, which uses month names from the family of calendars of Corinth and its colonies. Iversen argues that this is probably the calendar of Epirus, in northwest Greece, and proposes that the mechanism was built on Rhodes for a customer from Epirus. A modern watchmaker in Switzerland setting a watch to a buyer's time zone does much the same.

docs.title: Who Lived on Rhodes
docs.text:
In the 2nd and early 1st centuries BCE, Rhodes was one of the richest and most cosmopolitan cities in the Greek world: an independent republic with a famous navy and one of the busiest harbors in the eastern Mediterranean. The people a maker of the mechanism would have met came from many places and classes.

Rhodian citizens and the merchant elite. Power belonged to a citizen class of shipowners, merchants, and naval commanders. Their wealth came from trade, especially grain from Egypt and the Black Sea, and from the harbor dues every passing cargo paid. Rhodian maritime custom was respected enough that Roman law later quoted the "Rhodian law" on dividing losses when a ship had to throw cargo overboard in a storm. That prosperity took a hit in 167 BCE, when Rome made Delos a free port to punish Rhodes; the historian Polybius reports that Rhodes's harbor revenue fell from a million drachmas a year to 150,000.

Sailors, shipwrights, and engineers. The Rhodian navy was the best in the Aegean, and keeping it at sea took carpenters, rope makers, metalworkers, and siege engineers. The skills that built warships and catapults were close cousins of the skills that built gear trains.

Craftsmen and artists. Rhodes had famous bronze casters, the tradition that had produced the Colossus a century earlier, and leading sculptors. The marble base of the Winged Victory of Samothrace, carved as the prow of a warship, is Rhodian marble. Potters in Rhodes stamped the handles of vast numbers of wine jars with the name of the year's priest of Helios and the workshop owner, a kind of official labeling.

Scholars and teachers from abroad. Many of the island's best-known thinkers were not born there. Hipparchus came from Nicaea in Bithynia. Posidonius, a Stoic philosopher, astronomer, and geographer, came from Apamea in Syria and ran a school on Rhodes. The rhetoric teacher Apollonius Molon came from Caria. The Stoic Panaetius was a native Rhodian who worked in Rome and Athens. The astronomer Geminus, who may have been Rhodian, wrote a textbook that explains the same cycles the mechanism displays, including the exeligmos.

Roman students and visitors. Ambitious young Romans sailed to Rhodes to study, as Chapter 12 describes: Cicero, traditionally Julius Caesar, and later Pompey, who came to hear Posidonius. These were exactly the kind of wealthy, educated clients who might want a model of the heavens.

Foreign residents and enslaved people. Inscriptions on Rhodes record large numbers of resident foreigners from Asia Minor, Syria, Egypt, and elsewhere, working as traders, bankers, and craftsmen. Much of the heavy labor, in the harbor, the workshops, and the households, was done by enslaved people, some of whom were themselves skilled workers. The hands that filed the gear teeth may well have belonged to someone whose name no one recorded.

docs.title: So, Who Created It?
docs.text:
We do not know the maker's name, and we may never know it. The evidence points to a skilled workshop, quite possibly on Rhodes, working in a tradition that ran from Archimedes through Hipparchus to Posidonius. Its astronomy drew on Babylonian records, its lunar theory on Hipparchus, its mathematics on Greek number theory, and its craftsmanship on Rhodian bronze work. The dials were set to a customer's calendar, perhaps in northwest Greece.

The dating is still argued over. The eclipse dial appears to start at a new moon in 205 BCE, but a designer could choose a starting date in the past, the way a calendar app lets you scroll back. The style of the lettering suggests the box was made later, perhaps toward the end of the 2nd century BCE. Either way, the mechanism was the work of many minds across several cultures, which is the best answer to the question in this appendix's title.

docs.title: A Technology Lost for 1,500 Years
docs.text:
The strangest fact about the mechanism is what came after it. Simpler geared devices did appear in later centuries, but nothing of comparable complexity survives for well over a thousand years.

Date Device Place c. 205–100 BCE Antikythera mechanism, at least 30 gears Probably Rhodes 6th century CE Portable sundial with a small geared calendar, four surviving gears Byzantine Empire c. 1000 CE A geared lunar calendar described by al-Biruni Central Asia 1088–1092 CE Su Song's water-driven astronomical clock tower Kaifeng, China c. 1327–1336 CE Richard of Wallingford's astronomical clock St Albans, England 1364 CE Giovanni de' Dondi's astrarium, showing the Sun, Moon, and five planets Padua, Italy 1410 CE The Prague astronomical clock, the Orloj Prague, Bohemia

Devices of similar complexity, gear trains that modeled the Sun, the Moon, and the planets, returned only with the great astronomical clocks of Europe in the 1300s and 1400s. Counted from the mechanism's likely date of about 150 BCE to de' Dondi's astrarium, the gap is about 1,500 years; counted from its earliest proposed date of 205 BCE to the Prague clock, it is about 1,600.

Why was the knowledge lost? It lived in a few workshops and in the heads of the people who worked there, not in printed books. Rome's conquest of the Greek east, and wars such as the Roman general Cassius's sack of Rhodes in 43 BCE, broke up the centers where it was practiced. Bronze was valuable, so old machines were melted down. Each time a master died without a student, a little more was gone.

That is why this small box matters to a book about learning. Knowledge held by a few experts can vanish in a generation. Knowledge that is written down, copied, and taught widely survives, which is the story of the printing presses in Chapter 6. AI tutors now offer a chance to spread expert skill to anyone who wants to learn it, so that the next Antikythera mechanism is not the last of its kind for 1,500 years.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:

  • Tony Freeth and colleagues, A Model of the Cosmos in the ancient Greek Antikythera Mechanism, Scientific Reports, 2021: the University College London reconstruction of the planetary display.
  • Paul Iversen, The Calendar on the Antikythera Mechanism and the Corinthian Family of Calendars, Hesperia, 2017: the case for the Epirote calendar and the Halieia of Rhodes.
  • Alexander Jones, Epoch Dates of the Antikythera Mechanism, ISAW Papers 17, 2020: the evidence for the 205 BCE starting date.
  • Jo Marchant, Decoding the Antikythera Mechanism, the First Computer, Smithsonian Magazine: a readable account of how the device was decoded.

docs.title: Extensions and Excursions
docs.text:
Viking sells two kinds of add-ons to the Ancient Mediterranean Treasures cruise. Extensions are hotel stays of two to four nights before the ship leaves Istanbul or after it reaches Athens. Shore excursions are guided outings from the ship in each port. This appendix lists both, as Viking showed them for the 2026 Istanbul-to-Athens sailing, and notes which ones we took.

We booked neither extension. We spent three days on our own in Istanbul before boarding and three days on our own in Athens after leaving the ship, including the drive to Delphi. Comparing our own plan with Viking's packages shows what the packages cover and what we covered by planning ourselves.

Check before you book

These lists come from Viking's itinerary pages in November 2026. Viking changes its excursions, prices, and hotels from year to year, so confirm any option on the Ancient Mediterranean Treasures page or in My Viking Journey before booking.

docs.title: How the Two Kinds of Add-On Work
docs.text:

The included excursion in each port is usually the classic introduction: the Old Town walk in Rhodes, the main street of Ephesus, or the archaeological museum in Heraklion. The optional excursions go farther away, go deeper into one subject, or add food, wine, or a boat.

Istanbul (2 nights) is the short version. One guided day covers the Blue Mosque, the Basilica Cistern, a Bosphorus cruise with a Turkish lunch, and a carpet presentation in the Grand Bazaar. The first and last days are for arriving and moving to the ship.

Cappadocia (3 nights) is the only extension that leaves the coast. After one night in Istanbul, the group flies to central Anatolia and stays in a hotel carved into the soft volcanic rock. The full day there covers the fairy chimneys of the Dervent Valley, a pottery demonstration in Avanos, an underground city, the Göreme Open Air Museum with its rock-cut churches, and Uçhisar Castle. A dawn hot-air balloon ride is an optional extra. Viking notes that the cave hotel is not recommended for guests who have trouble walking.

Best of Istanbul (3 nights) is the fully escorted version of what we did on our own. It has three guided tours: the Sultanahmet monuments, a gourmet lunch and the Grand Bazaar, and a day on the Asian shore with Beylerbeyi Palace and the Spice Bazaar.

docs.title: What We Did Instead
docs.text:
Our three days in Istanbul before boarding covered most of the Best of Istanbul ground at our own pace:

  • Day 1, Istanbul, a City on Two Continents: the Bosphorus, the Golden Horn, and the city's layout.
  • Day 2, Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia: Hagia Sophia, the Basilica Cistern, and the Hippodrome.
  • Day 3, Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer: Topkapı Palace and the Süleymaniye and Blue Mosques.

The one thing none of our days covered is Cappadocia, which is a flight away. It is the strongest case for an extension on this route, because it cannot be done as a day trip from the ship.

docs.title: Our Excursion: The Villages of Crete
docs.text:
Crete was the one port where we chose a village day over the famous ruins. The excursion drove inland from Heraklion to two stops. The first was a vineyard and winery at Avli, with a tasting of Cretan wines. The second was Thrapsano, a village known across Greece for its potters, who throw the tall storage jars called pithoi.

Those jars connect the village day back to Knossos. The storerooms of the Minoan palace held rows of pithoi almost as tall as a person, used for olive oil, wine, and grain about 3,500 years ago. Thrapsano's potters still make jars in the same shape for the same purposes, and for gardens. A village workshop shows how the craft moved from palace to farm to the present day, something a museum case cannot show.

The village day also fits the book's habit of asking who lives in a place now. Heraklion's Old Town shows Crete's history. Thrapsano and the vineyards show how many Cretans make a living today: in farming, wine, and crafts, most of it far from the cruise port.

docs.title: Post-Cruise Extensions in Athens
docs.text:
The ship arrives in Piraeus on Day 10, and guests leave it on Day 11. Viking offered three ways to stay on in Greece.

Extension Nights From Style Highlights Athens 2 $899 Hotel and transfers, sightseeing on your own Athens Marriott, optional Cape Sounion, Agora, and Plaka outings Classic Greece 4 $1,599 Fully guided Acropolis and Acropolis Museum, Mycenae and Epidaurus, Delphi Greek Traditions 3 $1,799 Fully guided Nafplio, ancient Nemea, olive oil, honey, wine, and a cooking class

Athens (2 nights) is mostly a hotel stay with a Viking host, two breakfasts, and transfers. Sightseeing is on your own, with optional guided outings to Cape Sounion, the Agora, and the Plaka.

Classic Greece (4 nights) is the guided tour of the mainland's great sites: a day for the Acropolis and its museum, a day for Mycenae and Epidaurus in the Peloponnese, and a day for Delphi, with lunch in the mountain village of Arachova.

Greek Traditions (3 nights) moves to Nafplio, the first capital of modern Greece, and centers on food and farming: an olive oil mill, an apiary, a winery, a cooking class, and the ruins of the Temple of Zeus at Nemea.

docs.title: What We Did Instead
docs.text:
Our three days in Athens after the ship follow the Classic Greece route, except for Mycenae and Epidaurus:

  • Day 11, The Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus.
  • Day 12, Delphi, a drive of about 2½ hours each way.
  • Day 13, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today.

Mycenae and Epidaurus are the main sites on this route that we did not reach. They would fill one more day from Athens, as a day trip from the ship or as part of the Classic Greece extension.

docs.title: Choosing Well in November
docs.text:
• Short days. Daylight ends before 5:30 PM in Athens in late November, and many sites close earlier in winter. The longest excursions (Delphi from Piraeus, Gallipoli, Lindos, Phaistos) leave little slack.
  • Weather. Open-air sites like Troy, Ephesus, Lindos, and Delphi have little shelter. Bring a rain layer and shoes with grip for wet marble.
  • Walking. Lindos (195 steps), the Acropolis, and Assos involve steep or uneven climbs. The museum excursions are the gentle choice in each port.
  • One deep day beats two shallow ones. In a port with two famous sites, such as Troy and Gallipoli, or Knossos and Heraklion's museum, choose the one you most want to understand and read that chapter the night before.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This guide is organized into 21 chapters covering 598 concepts. There is one chapter for each day of the trip, November 11–23, 2026, plus two chapters to read before we leave, two deep dives on Paul at Ephesus, two deep dives on the Oracle and the Algorithm, and one chapter for the trip home. Day 9 on Crete has two chapters, one for Knossos and one for Venetian Heraklion.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean - The geography of the route and the long run of eras from the Bronze Age to the Ottomans, so every later chapter has a place on the timeline.
  2. Before We Go, Part 2: Traveling Well and the Learning for All Thread - How the trip fits together and how to travel well in the off-season, plus the start of the Learning for All thread on literacy, alphabets, and AI in education.
  3. Day 1: Istanbul, a City on Two Continents - Arrival day in Istanbul: how a Greek colony on the Bosphorus became Constantine's capital and then Mehmed's, plus a first Turkish breakfast and first Turkish words.
  4. Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia - Justinian's city: the Hippodrome, Hagia Sophia, and the Basilica Cistern, with the skills of reading a ruin and the long story of the Orthodox Church, the schism, and the Fourth Crusade.
  5. Day 3: Ottoman Istanbul, Topkapı, and Friday Prayer - Topkapı Palace, Suleiman and Sinan, and the Süleymaniye complex on a Friday, with Islam in daily life and the charitable endowments that paid for free schools.
  6. Day 4: Bazaars, Scripts, and Presses - The Grand Bazaar and Spice Bazaar before we board the Viking Star, the multi-faith Ottoman city, and the long, contested arrival of printing in Istanbul.
  7. Day 5: The End of Empire and the Birth of Modern Turkey - Ottoman decline, Greek independence, Gallipoli, and Atatürk's republic, ending at Gülhane Park where the 1928 alphabet reform began.
  8. Day 6: Troy and Gallipoli - Two battlefields three thousand years apart: the mound of Hisarlik and Homer's Iliad, then the Gallipoli peninsula and how Turks and Anzacs remember 1915.
  9. Paul at Ephesus, Part 1: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Ephesian Years - A deep dive on Paul of Tarsus: the Greek and Roman world he inherited, his life and journeys, which letters are really his, and his two to three years in Ephesus.
  10. Day 7: Ephesus, a Greco-Roman City - Walking Ephesus from Curetes Street to the Library of Celsus and the Great Theater, the Temple of Artemis and the silversmiths' riot, and the Christian sites around Selçuk.
  11. Paul at Ephesus, Part 2: Ideas, Legacy, and Lessons in Leading Change - Paul's central ideas and their long legacy, good and harmful, and what his movement teaches about leading schools from direct instruction to AI-native learning.
  12. Day 8: Rhodes, From the Colossus to the Knights - Hellenistic Rhodes and its school of rhetoric, the medieval town of the Knights Hospitaller, Lindos, and the Jewish Quarter whose community was deported in 1944.
  13. Day 9, Part 1: Knossos, the Minoans, and Linear B - Morning at Knossos and the Heraklion Archaeological Museum: Minoan palace culture, Evans' reconstructions, and how Linear B was deciphered.
  14. Day 9, Part 2: Venetian Heraklion and Crete Today - Afternoon in Venetian Heraklion: the Koules fortress and city walls, the Cretan Renaissance and El Greco, Cretan scholars and the Aldine press, and the Cretan diet and village life today.
  15. Day 10: Athens, the Acropolis, and the Persian Wars - Arrival at Piraeus and the Acropolis: the Parthenon and its sculptures, the Persian Wars that paid for them, and the Greek theater and its tragedies.
  16. Day 11: Athens, the Agora, Democracy, and Paul on the Areopagus - The Ancient Agora and the Pnyx, how Athenian democracy worked and whom it left out, Socrates on trial, the Stoics, and Paul's speech on the Areopagus.
  17. The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 1: The Oracle - How the Oracle of Delphi worked, its famous answers and its flaws, the inscriptions 'Know thyself' and 'Nothing in excess,' and why it lasted twelve centuries and then fell silent.
  18. Day 12: Delphi - The day trip to Delphi in the oracle's own off-season: the Sacred Way and treasuries, the theater and stadium, the Charioteer, Athena Pronaia, and the villages that live beside the site.
  19. The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm - What Delphi teaches about living with machines that predict: data, ambiguity, bias, self-fulfilling predictions, calibration, horizons, and consent, ending in a personal reflection.
  20. Day 13: Athens, Museums, Tutors, and the City Today - The National Archaeological Museum and the Antikythera mechanism, Aristotle's Lyceum and the case for one-on-one tutoring, and the everyday life of modern Athens.
  21. Going Home: Learning With Communities, Not To Them - A closing chapter for the trip home that ties the Learning for All stories together into lessons for spreading education with communities rather than to them.

docs.title: How to Use This Guide
docs.text:
Read each day's chapter at breakfast or the night before. The deep-dive chapters have their own reading times: Paul Part 1 the evening of Day 6 and Part 2 the evening of Day 7; the Oracle the night of Day 11 and the Algorithm on the drive back from Delphi. Chapters follow the order of the trip, and every concept is introduced before any later chapter relies on it, so reading in order means nothing is used before it has been explained.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of the concepts it covers. If a chapter refers back to an idea you skipped, its Prerequisites section shows which earlier chapter explains it.

docs.title: Before We Go, Part 1: The Long Timeline of the Eastern Mediterranean
Summary
docs.text: This chapter lays out the map and the timeline for the whole trip. It places the Eastern Mediterranean, Anatolia, the Aegean, and Crete on the map, then walks the eras in order from the Bronze Age through the Archaic, Classical, Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman periods. It introduces the civilizations and faiths every later chapter builds on: the Minoans and Mycenaeans, the Greek city-states, the Roman Empire and the Pax Romana, and Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Read it before departure; afterward we should be able to place any site on the route in its era.

docs.title: Why Start With a Map and a Timeline
docs.text:
In thirteen days we will stand inside a Byzantine 🔊 Pronounce BIZ-un-teen cathedral that became a mosque, walk a Roman marble street where a Greek goddess was worshipped, climb a Bronze Age palace on Crete, and look up at a temple built by the first democracy. The trouble is that the route runs backward and forward through time. Istanbul, our first stop, is mostly Byzantine and Ottoman. Troy and Knossos 🔊 Pronounce NOSS-us, in the middle of the cruise, are far older than anything in Istanbul. Classical Athens comes at the end. Without a map and a timeline in our heads, the stops blur into one long afternoon of "very old stones."

This chapter is that map and timeline. It is the longest chapter in the guide because almost every later chapter leans on it, so it is worth reading slowly, perhaps in two sittings before we fly. Everything here gets a fuller story later, at the place where it happened. The goal now is only to know where each place sits on the map and where each site sits in time.

Hello, I'm Glaux

🔊 Pronounce GLOWKS, with the "ow" of "owl"

I'm Glaux, a little owl, the same small owl that sat on Athena's shoulder and on every silver coin of ancient Athens. I've been watching people build on top of each other's ruins here for a very long time, and I'm still curious about who lived in each layer. On this trip I'll turn up for six jobs:

  1. Welcome you to each day and say why the place is worth our attention.
  2. Think with you when an idea changes how we see everything around it.
  3. Tip you off to a shortcut or a question that saves time on site.
  4. Warn you about a common mix-up before it trips us.
  5. Encourage you when a stretch of history gets tangled.
  6. Celebrate what you can do at the end of each chapter.

If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter. Look closer.

docs.title: The Eastern Mediterranean
docs.text:
The Mediterranean is the sea almost enclosed by Europe, Asia, and Africa; its name comes from the Latin for "in the middle of the land." The Eastern Mediterranean is the half of that sea east of Italy and Libya, together with the lands around it: Greece and its islands, Turkey, Cyprus, the coast of Syria, Lebanon, Israel, and Palestine (often called the Levant), and Egypt. It is the one place on Earth where three continents come within sight, or a short sail, of one another. Istanbul itself sits on two of them.

That geography explains most of the history in this book. The Eastern Mediterranean is a crossroads. Grain, metal, wine, olive oil, ideas, alphabets, armies, and faiths all moved across it, and they moved most easily by sea. Overland travel in antiquity was slow and expensive: a cart of grain could double in price after about a hundred miles of road. A ship could carry the same grain the length of the Aegean for a fraction of that. So the cities that mattered most were the ones with good harbors at the right places on the sea lanes.

The Turks and the Greeks give the sea different names, and the names are a small lesson in point of view. In Turkish the Mediterranean is Akdeniz, the "White Sea," and the Black Sea is Karadeniz, the "Black Sea." One explanation is an old Turkic habit of naming directions by color, with white for the west and black for the north. In Greek the Mediterranean is simply Mesógeios, the "middle of the earth." Each name puts its speakers at the center.

Worked example: three continents in one trip. Let's place our stops by continent. Istanbul is split by the Bosphorus 🔊 Pronounce BOS-fer-us strait: our hotel and the old city are in Europe, and the ferry to Kadıköy lands in Asia. Çanakkale 🔊 Pronounce chah-NAHK-kah-leh, Kuşadası 🔊 Pronounce koo-SHAH-dah-suh, and Ephesus 🔊 Pronounce EF-uh-sus are in Asia, on the western edge of Turkey. Rhodes lies in Europe politically, as part of Greece, but it is only about 18 km from the Turkish coast. Crete is in Europe, yet its south coast is only about 300 km from Libya, in Africa. Athens and Delphi are in mainland Europe. The point is not the labels. The point is that the "continents" here are a few hours apart by boat, which is why this one sea held so many different peoples together.

The map below follows our cruise from Istanbul to Athens and the day trip to Delphi. Click each port to see its date, its key sights, and a tip for the day.
