Chapter Anchors: Plataea, 479 BCE; 31 communities named; moved by 330 CE; the Third Sacred War, 356–346 BCE; Pausanias the travel writer, 2nd century CE; the upper jaw of one head in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums; ten claims, three bins.

docs.title: The Omphalos
docs.text:
The omphalos (Greek for "navel") is the sacred stone that marked Delphi as the center of the world. Chapter 17 told the best-known story behind it: Zeus released two eagles from the ends of the earth, and they met above Delphi. The poet Hesiod, around 700 BCE, told another. When Rhea saved the infant Zeus from his father Cronus, who swallowed his children, she gave Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes instead, and Zeus later set that stone up at Pytho, under Parnassus, as a sign for mortals. Pausanias saw a small stone near the temple that the Delphians anointed with oil every day and wrapped in raw wool at festivals, and said it was believed to be the stone of Cronus.

Several stones have carried the name. The one most visitors photograph is in the museum: a marble cone carved with a net of woolen bands, made in Hellenistic or Roman times, which may copy the stone that stood in the temple. Beside the Sacred Way, a plainer stone of the same beehive shape also waits for photographs; it too is a copy. The original, if a single original ever existed, is lost. What survives is the idea: a place that called itself the center of the world, and convinced the Greeks.

docs.title: The Pythian Games
docs.text:
The Pythian Games were the athletic and musical festival held at Delphi every four years in honor of Apollo, one of the four great Panhellenic games that were open to Greeks from every city. They began as a contest in singing a hymn to Apollo with the kithara, the concert lyre. After the First Sacred War, which Chapter 17 described, the Amphictyonic League reorganized them in 582 BCE as a festival held every four years, adding athletics and horse races. The music came first in the program, then the athletic events in the stadium, then the chariot and horse races on the plain below Delphi, where the racecourse has never been found. The prize was a crown of laurel, Apollo's tree; tradition says the branches were brought from the Vale of Tempe in Thessaly, where Apollo had been purified after killing the serpent.

The four Panhellenic games formed a circuit, spaced so that there were great games somewhere in Greece every year. Having described the Pythian program, we can compare the four.

Games Place God Crown Held from How often Olympic Olympia Zeus Wild olive 776 BCE (traditional date) Every 4 years Pythian Delphi Apollo Laurel 582 BCE Every 4 years Isthmian Isthmus of Corinth Poseidon Pine, at times wild celery c. 582 BCE Every 2 years Nemean Nemea Zeus Wild celery c. 573 BCE Every 2 years

Winners were celebrated in poetry. The poet Pindar wrote twelve odes for Pythian victors, among them men from the Greek cities of Sicily, whose rulers spent fortunes on chariot teams. One of those rulers' brothers paid for the bronze in the museum that Part Five visits.

docs.title: The Theater of Delphi
docs.text:
The Theater of Delphi is the stone theater above the Temple of Apollo, at the top of the walled sanctuary, where the musical contests of the Pythian Games were held. Its first form dates from the 4th century BCE; it was rebuilt in stone in the 2nd century BCE, with help from King Eumenes II of Pergamon, and remodeled again under the Romans. Its 35 rows of seats held about 5,000 people, a fifth of the Great Theater of Ephesus in Chapter 10, but no theater on our route has a finer view. From the top rows we look down over the temple's columns into the Pleistos gorge.

The theater of Delphi above the Temple of Apollo. Photo by Dan McCreary

The theater had a modern second life. In 1927 and again in 1930, the Greek poet Angelos Sikelianos and his American wife, Eva Palmer-Sikelianos, staged Delphic Festivals here, with Aeschylus' Prometheus Bound performed in the ancient way, with masks, a chorus, and costumes woven by hand. They dreamed of making Delphi a center for peace between nations. The festivals were too expensive to continue, but they helped inspire the modern revival of ancient drama in ancient theaters, which still fills the theater at Epidaurus every summer.

docs.title: The Stadium of Delphi
docs.text:
The Stadium of Delphi is the running track and its stone seating at the highest point of the ancient site, above the theater and outside the sanctuary wall, where the athletic contests of the Pythian Games were held. It is one of the best-preserved stadiums in Greece. The track is about 178 m long. The stone starting and finishing lines survive, with grooves cut for the runners' toes, and a Roman entrance of four pillars stands at its east end. Pausanias credits the rich Athenian Herodes Atticus with giving it stone seats in the 2nd century CE; they held about 6,500 spectators.

The climb from the theater is steep, and in winter the path is not always open. The view from the top, of the whole sanctuary falling away below, is the reward for those who make it.

Polished Stones and Closed Paths

Watch out: the paving of the Sacred Way has been polished by millions of feet and turns slippery in rain or frost, and the upper paths, including the one to the stadium, are sometimes closed for rockfalls or ice. Wear shoes with grip, come down the steps slowly, and ask at the ticket gate which paths are open before planning the climb.

docs.title: Part Four: Athena Before the Temple
The Athena Pronaia Sanctuary
docs.text:
The Athena Pronaia sanctuary is the lower sanctuary at Delphi, a short walk east of Apollo's, below the modern road, dedicated to Athena Pronaia, "before the temple," because it was the first shrine a pilgrim reached on the road from the east. Villagers later took its marble for building, and so it is still called the Marmaria, "the marbles." On a long, narrow terrace above the Pleistos gorge it holds the foundations of two temples of Athena, two small treasuries, one of them built by Massalia, the Greek colony that became Marseille, altars, and in the middle the round Tholos. Between it and the Castalian Spring lie the gymnasium and palaestra, where athletes trained for the games.

The Pleistos valley below Delphi. Photo by Dan McCreary

Worked example: the rocks that saved Delphi. Let's test a story Herodotus tells about this shrine. In 480 BCE, he says, a Persian detachment marched on Delphi to plunder it. As it reached the shrine of Athena Pronaia, thunderbolts fell from the sky and two great crags broke off Parnassus and crashed down on the Persians, who fled. Herodotus adds that the rocks still lay in Athena's precinct in his own day. What do we make of it? The rockfalls are believable: the cliffs above the Marmaria really do drop boulders, and rockfall damaged the old temple of Athena in the early 20th century. A Persian force may well have turned back here. That the god sent the rocks at exactly the right moment is the part no source could check. As with the Serpent Column, the place supplies what is possible, and the writer supplies the meaning.

docs.title: The Tholos of Delphi
docs.text:
The Tholos of Delphi is the circular marble building of the early 4th century BCE in the sanctuary of Athena Pronaia, the most photographed ruin at Delphi. A tholos is any round building. This one had an outer ring of 20 Doric columns and, inside the round wall, 10 Corinthian columns; three of the outer columns were set up again by archaeologists in the 20th century, which is why it photographs so well. The Roman architect Vitruvius says that its architect, Theodorus of Phocaea, wrote a book about it.

And there the certainty ends. No ancient writer says what the Tholos was for. Scholars have proposed a shrine to an earth goddess, a hero's memorial, a hall for some rite we no longer know, or a treasury. The building is one of the most admired in Greece, and nobody knows why it was built. That is worth remembering when a guide speaks with confidence: the best-preserved building can still be the least explained.

docs.title: The Delphi Archaeological Museum
docs.text:
The Delphi Archaeological Museum is the site museum, beside the road between the sanctuary and the modern village, that holds the finds of the excavations at Delphi. Chapter 8 explained the advantage of a site museum, and Delphi shows it at its best: nearly everything here was found a few hundred meters away. The first museum opened in 1903, during the great excavation, and the building has been enlarged and rebuilt several times since. Its rooms follow the centuries, from the earliest offerings to the Roman emperors, and a walk through them in order of date passes these highlights.

  • Kleobis and Biton, two marble youths of about 580 BCE from Argos. Herodotus says Solon named these brothers, who pulled their mother's cart to Hera's festival and then died in their sleep, the second-happiest of men, in the conversation with Croesus that Chapter 17 retold. Some scholars think the statues show the twin gods Castor and Pollux instead.
  • The Sphinx of the Naxians, of about 560 BCE, a winged lion with a woman's head that once sat on a tall Ionic column near the polygonal wall.
  • The Siphnian Treasury frieze, of about 525 BCE, with the gods fighting the giants and the gods debating the Trojan War.
  • The silver bull and the gold and ivory heads, 6th-century BCE offerings found in 1939 in pits under the Sacred Way, where damaged treasures had been buried.
  • The Athenian Treasury metopes, with Heracles and Theseus.
  • The Delphic Hymns, the inscribed music from the treasury's wall.
  • The Dancers' Column and the omphalos, a column of acanthus leaves with three dancing women at the top, and the carved marble navel stone.
  • The Charioteer, in a room of its own.
  • Antinous, a marble statue of the young favorite of the emperor Hadrian, from the 2nd century CE.

docs.title: The Charioteer of Delphi
docs.text:
The Charioteer of Delphi is the life-size bronze statue of a young chariot driver, about 1.8 m tall, made around 478 to 470 BCE, that survives from a group set up to celebrate a victory in the chariot race of the Pythian Games. The inscription on its base names Polyzalos, ruler of the Greek city of Gela in Sicily and brother of Hieron of Syracuse; the inscription was altered in antiquity, and scholars still debate whose name was carved first. The group once included the chariot, four horses, and probably a groom, and fragments of horses' legs and tail and a child's arm survive with it. French excavators found the driver in 1896, buried near the temple, probably by the earthquake of 373 BCE.

Worked example: looking closer at the Charioteer. Let's stand in front of it and read the details in order, from the head down. The eyes are inlaid with white and colored materials, so they seem to look back at us; few Greek bronzes keep their eyes. The eyelashes are fine strips of metal. The lips were once inlaid with copper, a slightly redder metal, to give them color. The headband, the victor's ribbon, was inlaid with a silver pattern. The robe, the long garment charioteers wore, falls in straight folds like the fluting of a column, and the right hand still holds part of the reins. The face is calm. This is not the race but the moment after it, the victory lap, and the sculptor has shown control instead of effort. Greek art was moving from the stiff, smiling statues of the Archaic period toward the Classical style of the Parthenon, and the Charioteer stands at that turning point.

Saved by Being Lost

Think about why the Charioteer is here at all. Thousands of bronzes once stood in this sanctuary; Nero alone took about 500, and most of the rest were melted down for their metal. This one survived because it was buried and forgotten, so what we can see today is not a fair sample of what Delphi once held, only what happened to escape.

docs.title: Part Six: Delphi After the Oracle
The French Excavation of Delphi
docs.text:
After the oracle closed at the end of the 4th century CE, Delphi did not simply empty. A Christian town grew on the site, then shrank, and by the time western travelers came looking, the ruins lay under a mountain village called Kastri 🔊 Pronounce kah-STREE, "the little castle." Its houses stood on the sanctuary's terraces, and its people reused the ancient stones in their walls. Travelers who knew their Greek authors came looking for Delphi: the Italian merchant Cyriac of Ancona copied inscriptions here in 1436, and in 1676 the French doctor Jacob Spon and the English traveler George Wheler identified the village as the site of the oracle.

The French excavation of Delphi is the archaeological excavation of the Sanctuary of Apollo by the French School at Athens, led by Théophile Homolle, which began in 1892, after the village of Kastri was moved off the site, and uncovered most of what we see today. After years of negotiation, in which American archaeologists also bid for the site, the Greek government gave the excavation rights to France. Kastri's houses were bought and demolished, and its people were moved to a new village built a short distance to the west, which took the name Delphi. The excavators then cleared tons of earth and rubble from the slope. Within a few years they had found the treasuries, the polygonal wall with its inscriptions, the Delphic Hymns, and, in 1896, the Charioteer.

For the people of Kastri, the excavation meant losing their homes, their fields, and the graves of their families, so that the world could see what lay beneath them. Archaeology often makes such trades, and they are worth naming. The sanctuary we walk today exists because a village was taken away.

Delphi's story after the oracle falls into four stages, and naming them makes the dates easier to hold. First the site was silenced: the oracle closed and the sanctuary was built over. Then it was found: travelers identified it from their reading. Then it was dug up: the excavation revealed and recovered it. Finally it was shown: museums, rebuilding, festivals, and world recognition presented it to visitors. The timeline below places the key dates in those stages.

docs.title: Diagram: Delphi After the Oracle
docs.text:
Delphi After the Oracle

Type: timeline sim-id: delphi-after-the-oracle-timeline Library: vis-timeline Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify nine events in Delphi's history after the oracle into the four stages silenced, found, dug up, and shown, with at least 8 of 9 correct, predicting each event's stage before its description is revealed.

Prerequisites: the closing of the oracle and the Theodosian Decrees (Chapters 3 and 17), the village of Kastri, the French excavation of Delphi, the Athenian Treasury, the Charioteer of Delphi, the Delphi Archaeological Museum, the Delphic Festivals in the Theater of Delphi, and the four stages silenced, found, dug up, and shown (all defined in this chapter above the block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the nine events, the learner commits a stage before the event's description and stage are revealed. A prediction is correct when it matches the Correct stage column in Content. Mastery is at least 8 of 9 correct. Scrolling and zooming the timeline are exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The ruins of Delphi were always visible and visited, when they lay under a village for centuries. (2) Archaeologists found Delphi by digging, when travelers identified it first from ancient texts. (3) The excavation was the end of the story, when rebuilding, museums, and festivals shaped what visitors see today. (4) What we see at Delphi is exactly as the excavators found it, when the Athenian Treasury was rebuilt.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying each event into a named stage is an Understand task: the learner must explain to themselves what the event did to the site. Predicting before the reveal makes the learner commit, and the four stages give the dates a structure that is easier to remember than a list.

Content:

Stages, with the definitions shown in a legend: Silenced (the oracle closes and the sanctuary is abandoned or built over); Found (travelers identify the site from ancient texts and inscriptions); Dug up (excavation reveals and recovers the sanctuary and its finds); Shown (the site and its finds are rebuilt, displayed, performed in, or recognized for visitors).

Events, in date order:

# Date Event label Description revealed after prediction Correct stage Why (shown as feedback) 1 391–392 CE Theodosian Decrees Imperial decrees ban sacrifice and close the temples; with no sacrifice, the oracle falls silent. Silenced The decrees ended consultations and began the sanctuary's long burial. 2 1436 Cyriac of Ancona The Italian merchant and antiquarian visits and copies inscriptions. Found He came looking for Delphi because of what he had read. 3 1676 Spon and Wheler The French doctor Jacob Spon and the English traveler George Wheler identify the village of Kastri as Delphi. Found They matched the place to the ancient descriptions. 4 1892 The great excavation begins The French School at Athens, led by Théophile Homolle, begins excavating after Kastri is moved west. Dug up Moving the village opened the sanctuary to excavation. 5 1896 The Charioteer found Excavators find the bronze Charioteer buried near the temple. Dug up It was recovered from the earth that had protected it. 6 1903 The first museum opens A museum near the site opens to display the finds. Shown It presented the finds to visitors. 7 1903–1906 The Athenian Treasury rebuilt French archaeologists rebuild the Athenian Treasury from its original blocks, paid for by the city of Athens. Shown Rebuilding turned scattered blocks into a building visitors can see. 8 1927 The first Delphic Festival Angelos and Eva Palmer-Sikelianos stage Aeschylus' Prometheus Bound in the ancient theater. Shown The theater was used again for drama. 9 1987 World Heritage Site Delphi is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Shown The listing recognized the site for the whole world.

Provenance: Events 1 to 9 and their dates come from this chapter's sections "The French Excavation of Delphi", "The Theater of Delphi", "The Athenian Treasury", "The Charioteer of Delphi", and "The Delphi Archaeological Museum", and from Chapter 17 (the closing of the oracle, the UNESCO listing in 1987).

Rules:

  • The timeline spans 300 CE to 2000 CE. No events fall between 400 CE and 1400 CE; that stretch may be compressed, provided the sim states that it is compressed and still shows the length of the gap in years.
  • Events are revealed one at a time in date order. Each starts as a dated card showing only its label.
  • For each card, the learner chooses one of the four stages; the description and the correct stage are then revealed and the card is marked correct or incorrect.
  • A revealed prediction cannot be changed.
  • Score = number of correct predictions, from 0 to 9. Mastery is score >= 8.
  • The correct totals are 1 Silenced, 2 Found, 2 Dug up, and 4 Shown.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the four stage definitions in the legend.
  2. The first event card appears on the timeline with its date and label only.
  3. The learner predicts its stage. The description, the correct stage, and the Why text appear, and the card takes the mark of its correct stage.
  4. The learner repeats step 3 for all nine events.
  5. After the ninth event, the timeline shows all events grouped by stage, with the long gap between event 1 and event 2.
  6. The learner should notice that more than a thousand years separate the silence from the rediscovery, and that four of the nine events concern how Delphi is shown, not how it was found.

Feedback: Nine predictions, fixed date order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [stage]. [why text]" Incorrect: "This one is [correct stage]. [why text]" The score "Predictions correct: n of 9" is shown throughout. A Restart option clears all predictions.

Starting State: An empty timeline from 300 CE to 2000 CE, the legend of four stages, and the question "The oracle fell silent in 391 CE. How did Delphi come back?"

Chapter Anchors: Theodosian Decrees 391–392 CE; Cyriac of Ancona 1436; Spon and Wheler 1676; excavation begins 1892; Charioteer found 1896; first museum 1903; Athenian Treasury rebuilt 1903–1906; Delphic Festivals 1927 and 1930 (the timeline shows 1927); UNESCO 1987; four stages; nine events.

docs.title: Modern Delphi Village
docs.text: Modern Delphi village is the small town just west of the archaeological site, built from 1892 for the people moved from Kastri, which lives today mainly from the visitors to the ruins. Its hotels, shops, and tavernas line two long streets that run along the slope, and from their back terraces the view falls away over the olive plain to the town of Itea and the blue line of the Gulf of Corinth. In summer the village is full of tour groups; on a Sunday in late November, many places keep shorter hours, and some close for the winter, the off-season pattern Chapter 8 described at Troy. The house of Angelos and Eva Palmer-Sikelianos is now a small museum of the Delphic Festivals. Most visitors see Delphi village only through a coach window. A walk along its main street, with a coffee on a terrace above the olives, shows what became of the people who were moved so that the sanctuary could be uncovered.

docs.title: Arachova
docs.text:
Arachova is the mountain town on the road between Livadeia and Delphi, at about 950 m on the slopes of Parnassus, known for its stone houses and steep lanes, its handwoven textiles and formaela, a hard local cheese that is fried or grilled, and its winter visitors. In 1826, during the Greek War of Independence, Greek forces under Georgios Karaiskakis defeated an Ottoman army here, and a monument in the town remembers the battle.

A roadside sign spelling out Arachova, the mountain village above Delphi. Photo by Dan McCreary

Arachova's year runs the opposite way from the coast's. Chapter 8 described the off-season livelihoods of places like Çanakkale, busy in summer and quiet in November. Arachova's busiest time is winter, when the ski slopes higher up the mountain open and Athenians drive up for the weekend; its quiet season is the summer. On November 22 we pass through between the two, as shopkeepers get ready for the ski season, which depends each year on the snow.

docs.title: The Amfissa Olive Groves
docs.text:
The Amfissa olive groves 🔊 Pronounce AHM-fee-sah are the great plain of olive trees, often called the "sea of olives," that runs from below Delphi past the town of Amfissa down to Itea and the Gulf of Corinth, often described as one of the largest continuous olive groves in Greece. Seen from the terraces of Delphi, it fills the valley floor with gray-green. Its best-known product is a table olive, Konservolia Amfissis, with protected designation of origin in the European Union. In late November the harvest is under way, so the nets spread under the trees that Chapter 12 described may be out on the plain below us.

The sea of olive trees below Delphi. Photo by Dan McCreary

This plain was once the god's. After the First Sacred War, Chapter 17 explained, the land below Delphi was dedicated to Apollo and left unfarmed. When the people of Amphissa farmed it in the 4th century BCE, the league declared the Fourth Sacred War against them and called in Philip of Macedon. Today the land is planted from edge to edge, and nobody thinks it sacrilege. A plain that was once forbidden ground now feeds a region.

docs.title: Thyme Honey
docs.text:
Thyme honey is honey made by bees from the flowers of wild thyme, which covers the dry, rocky hillsides of Greece; it is pale amber, strongly scented, and one of the most prized Greek honeys. Greek beekeepers move their hives up and down the mountains with the seasons, and on Parnassus they also make honey from the fir forests. Chapter 14 found thyme honey with yogurt on a Cretan menu; here we can buy it from the people who keep the bees.

Bees belong to Delphi's oldest stories. Chapter 17 recalled the legendary second temple, built by bees of wax and feathers. The poet Pindar called the Pythia "the Delphic bee," and the Homeric Hymn to Hermes tells of three winged sisters living under a ridge of Parnassus who prophesy truthfully when they have eaten honey. Whatever the stories mean, they show that honey and prophecy were neighbors on this mountain long before honey was sold in jars along the road.

Honey Counts as a Liquid

A common trap: at airport security, honey counts as a liquid, so a jar larger than 100 ml in a carry-on bag will be taken away. Pack honey in checked luggage, sealed in a plastic bag and wrapped in clothes, or buy it in small jars.

docs.title: Loukoumades
docs.text:
Loukoumades are small puffs of yeasted dough, fried until golden and then soaked in honey or syrup and sprinkled with cinnamon, walnuts, or sesame. They are eaten hot, from a plate shared at the table, and sold all over Greece. The Turkish version, lokma, is the same sweet, and the Greek name comes from the Turkish one; in Turkey, especially around İzmir, families give lokma away to neighbors and passersby in memory of someone who has died, a small cousin of the charity Chapter 5 found in the imaret. Despite the similar sound, loukoumades are not related to loukoumi, the Turkish delight Chapter 6 bought, whose name comes from a different Arabic phrase.

Food writers often claim that loukoumades were the first recorded dessert, given as "honey tokens" to winners at the ancient Olympic Games. The claim is repeated widely, usually without naming the ancient passage it depends on. Until someone shows us that passage, Chapter 4's test puts it on the shelf with the legends: a good story, best enjoyed with a hot plate of loukoumades and a spoonful of Parnassus honey.

docs.title: Practical Notes for Day 12
docs.text:
• Order of the day. Leave Athens early; the drive is about two and a half hours each way. Our photos show the olive plain at about 11:00 AM, the sanctuary from about 12:40 to 1:45 PM, and Arachova at about 4:15 PM on the way home. Decide in advance between climbing to the stadium and having more time in the museum.
  • Hours. Greek sites and museums keep shorter winter hours, and Delphi's site and museum close in the afternoon. Last entry is earlier than closing, the upper paths may close in bad weather, and some ticket arrangements change from year to year, so check on the day.
  • Weather and light. Delphi is several degrees colder than Athens, as Chapter 17 predicted, and the wind on the terraces is sharp. The sun sets at Delphi at about 5:15 PM, so most of the drive back is in the dark.
  • Winter roads. The road through Arachova can see snow and ice from late autumn, and on winter weekends ski traffic fills it once the season opens. The coach company decides whether to go; carry an extra layer and something to eat in case of delays.
  • Footing. The ancient paving is uneven and slippery when wet. Shoes with grip matter more than anything else we pack today.
  • Food. Lunch in Delphi village or Arachova: formaela cheese, grilled lamb or goat, horta, and, for us, a plate of melitzanosalata, the smoky eggplant dip of Chapter 15. Finish with loukoumades, and buy thyme honey to take home in the checked bag.
  • Tonight. Read Chapter 19 on the drive back or this evening, while the Pythia's tripod is still in mind. Tomorrow, Day 13, is our last day in Athens, with its museums and its streets; read Chapter 20 before breakfast.

docs.title: Learning for All: Freedom Carved Where Everyone Could Read It
docs.text:
Chapter 2's route table gives Delphi a story about trust, prediction, and "Know thyself." Chapter 17 told the oracle's side of it, and Chapter 19 will set it beside the prediction machines of our own time. Today's note is about a different kind of trust, the trust we put in a record, and it comes from the polygonal wall.

Run Chapter 2's four-step pattern on the freedom records. Locked up: an enslaved person's status was whatever the owner, the owner's heirs, or a stranger with a claim said it was; a private promise of freedom could be denied, and a freed person had no papers anyone was bound to respect. Opened: at Delphi the freedom was written in stone, in the busiest place in the sanctuary, dated, witnessed, and backed by a guarantor and by the god himself. Anyone could read it, or have it read to them, and no one could quietly erase it. A woman whose freedom was questioned could point to the wall. Resisted: the owners wrote their own interests into the same records. The paramone clause kept many freed people serving for years, and the price came from savings that took a working life to gather. Never all the way: only those who could save the price were freed, many could not read their own record, and the system freed individuals without ever questioning slavery itself.

The lesson for AI and education is about who keeps the record of what a person has achieved, and who can show it. Today a student's learning leaves records everywhere: grades in one school's system, scores in an app, progress in an online course. Too often the record belongs to the system, not to the learner, and it disappears or stays locked when the student moves on. The companion textbook AI-Native Schools describes how an intelligent textbook can record what a student has mastered in a standard format and keep that record portable and under the student's and family's control, in Tracking Mastery: xAPI, Learning Record Stores, and MicroSims. The Delphic wall got two things right: the record was trusted because a neutral keeper stood behind it, and the person it described could always point to it. It got one thing very wrong for our purposes: it was public to everyone. A learner's record should be just as trustworthy and just as much the learner's own, and private unless the learner chooses to show it.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The day trip to Delphi is about 180 km and two and a half hours each way; on a winter day, choose the three or four things that matter most.
  • The Castalian Spring, between the Phaedriades, is where every visit began, with purification in cold water.
  • The Sacred Way of Delphi zigzags from the gate to the altar, lined with rival cities' monuments. The treasuries of Delphi, more than twenty, held offerings and advertised their cities.
  • The Athenian Treasury, about 500–490 BCE and rebuilt in 1903–1906, may or may not have been paid for by Marathon; it carries the Delphic Hymns.
  • The polygonal wall holds up the temple terrace and has stood about 2,500 years. Its manumission records, more than a thousand at Delphi, record people buying their freedom through a sale to Apollo, often with a paramone condition.
  • The Serpent Column stood by the altar from 479 BCE until Constantine moved it by 330 CE. Delphi keeps its place and a bronze copy, Istanbul keeps the bronze, and the written sources keep its story.
  • The omphalos marked Delphi as the navel of the world; the carved stone in the museum is a Hellenistic or Roman piece.
  • The Pythian Games, reorganized in 582 BCE, put music first and crowned winners with laurel. The Theater of Delphi held about 5,000; the Stadium of Delphi at the top of the site keeps its starting lines.
  • The Athena Pronaia sanctuary, the Marmaria, was the first shrine on the road from the east; its round Tholos of Delphi, of the early 4th century BCE, is famous and unexplained.
  • The Delphi Archaeological Museum keeps the finds beside their site. The Charioteer of Delphi, about 478–470 BCE, survived because it was buried.
  • The French excavation of Delphi began in 1892 after the village of Kastri was moved; modern Delphi village is the town built for its people.
  • Arachova, at about 950 m, lives from winter visitors. The Amfissa olive groves fill the once-sacred plain. Thyme honey and loukoumades are the sweet end of the day.

From the Spring to the Stadium

You can now walk Delphi from the Castalian Spring to the stadium and tell what each terrace was built to say, read the parts of a freedom record on the polygonal wall, and trace the Serpent Column from Apollo's altar to the Hippodrome and back. You also know why a village moved so that we could see all this. Next stop: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm, where the oracle's questions meet the prediction machines of our own day.

docs.title: The Oracle and the Algorithm, Part 2: The Algorithm
Summary
docs.text: Read this deep-dive chapter on the drive back from Delphi or that evening. It explains machine learning, predictive models, training data, and large language models in plain terms, then pairs each Delphi story with a question about AI: the oracle as a data hub, ambiguous answers and keeping a human in the loop, confirmation bias, self-fulfilling prophecy, who funds the model, calibration and trust, and the prediction horizon. It asks what 'Know thyself' and 'Nothing in excess' mean for values and climate models. It closes honestly with where the parallel breaks down and with reflection questions for our own decisions.

docs.title: The Drive Back from Delphi
docs.text:
Day 12, Sunday, November 22, ends on the road. The sun sets over Delphi at about 5:15 PM, so by the time the coach has wound down through Arachova and out onto the plain of Boeotia, the windows are dark and the temple terraces are a memory a few hours old. It is a good time for this chapter. Last night, Chapter 17 explained the oracle as an institution and left us seven questions. This morning, Chapter 18 walked us up the Sacred Way past the stones where those questions were asked. Tonight we put the same questions to the prediction machines of our own time.

Chapter 2 started this conversation. It explained that most of today's artificial intelligence is built by machine learning, that the chatbots we use are large language models that predict the next word, and that a chatbot asked when Hagia Sophia would close for Friday prayer could only predict a typical answer. It promised that the Delphi chapters would come back to this, because asking a source about the future is a very old human habit in a new form. This chapter keeps that promise. It explains, in plain terms and with worked examples, how machines learn to predict, and then it sets each Delphi story beside a question we should ask of any AI: where its knowledge comes from, who interprets its answers, who pays for it, how we would know whether to trust it, and what no prediction can decide for us.

The Tripod and the Phone

This morning we stood where kings waited for a god's answer; tonight half the coach is asking a phone what time the traffic will clear. The questions have barely changed in 2,500 years, and Croesus, Themistocles, and Socrates still have a lot to teach us about how to ask them. By the time we reach Athens, an AI's answer will look less like a verdict and more like the start of a conversation. Look closer.

The chapter has eight parts. Part One explains how machines learn from examples, and how the examples can mislead them. Part Two looks at three prediction machines we already use: the weather forecast, the language model, and the honest range around every prediction. Part Three asks the oracle's questions about data, interpretation, and bias. Part Four follows predictions that change the world they predict. Part Five asks what earns trust: who pays, how well calibrated a source is, its track record, whether its claims can be tested, and how far ahead it can see. Part Six turns an answer into the start of an inquiry. Part Seven asks what "Know thyself" and "Nothing in excess" mean for values, climate, and long-term choices. Part Eight asks who consented to being predicted, admits where the parallel between the oracle and the algorithm breaks down, and ends with questions for our own decisions.

docs.title: Machine Learning
docs.text:
Chapter 2 defined machine learning briefly: instead of being given step-by-step rules, a computer program is shown a large number of examples and adjusts itself until it can find the patterns in them. Because most of this chapter rests on that idea, it is worth taking slowly. Machine learning is the branch of artificial intelligence in which a program improves at a task by learning from data rather than by following rules a person has written for it. The result of the learning is called a model: a set of numbers, often millions or billions of them, that turns an input (a photo, a sentence, a list of facts about a loan applicant) into an output (a label, a next word, a probability).

There are two ways to get a computer to do something. The traditional way is to write the rules: "if the email contains these words, mark it as spam." That works when people can state the rules. But many things we do easily, such as recognizing a face or understanding a spoken sentence, follow rules that no one can write down. Machine learning turns the problem around. We supply examples with the right answers, and the program finds its own rules.

Worked example: teaching a program to tell Doric from Ionic. Let's teach a computer the difference between two of the column styles we have seen all week: the plain cushion-shaped top of a Doric capital, as on the Parthenon and the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, and the paired scrolls of an Ionic capital, as on the Erechtheion. A rule-writer would have to describe a scroll in terms of pixels, which is nearly impossible. A machine-learning approach goes like this.

  1. Collect labeled examples. We gather 10,000 photos of capitals, and a person labels each one "Doric" or "Ionic." These labeled examples are the training data, the subject of the next sections.
  2. Hold some back. We set 2,000 photos aside, unseen, for testing. The program learns from the other 8,000.
  3. Start with a guess and adjust. The model begins with random internal numbers, called parameters, and guesses a label for each training photo. Every wrong guess nudges the parameters slightly in the direction that would have made the guess less wrong. After many passes through the 8,000 photos, the guesses are mostly right.
  4. Test on the photos it never saw. If the model labels 1,900 of the 2,000 held-back photos correctly, its test accuracy is \( 1{,}900 \div 2{,}000 = 0.95 \), or 95 percent. That number, not its score on the training photos, tells us how well it generalizes, that is, how well it handles examples it was not trained on.
  5. Use it, and keep checking. Now we can point a phone at a capital in a museum and get "Ionic, 97 percent." But if we show it a broken Corinthian capital in fog, a style it was never taught, it will still answer "Doric" or "Ionic," because those are the only two answers it knows.

Notice what the model learned and what it did not. It found patterns of light and shape that separate the two labels in the photos it was given. It does not know what a column is, who carved it, or why. Everything it can do comes from the examples, and everything the examples leave out, it cannot do. The table below sets the two approaches side by side.

Rules written by people Machine learning Where the rules come from A person states them The program finds them in examples Works best when The rules can be stated: tax tables, ship schedules The rules are too complex to state: faces, speech, language Can explain its answer Yes: point to the rule Often only partly; the "rules" are millions of numbers Fails when A case arises that the rule-writer did not foresee A case arises that the examples did not contain What it needs An expert Many good examples with correct answers

A Model Is a Summary of the Past

Think of a trained model as a very detailed summary of the examples it was shown, compressed into numbers. When it predicts, it is really asking, "what usually came next in cases like this one?" Every strength and every weakness in the rest of this chapter follows from that one fact.

docs.title: Predictive Model
docs.text:
A predictive model is a model that estimates an unknown outcome, usually a future one, from information available now. Its inputs are the facts we know (the date, the weather, a person's payment history); its output is a prediction, often a probability ("a 30 percent chance"). Not every model predicts the future: the column classifier labels something present. But the method is the same, and most of the models that shape our lives, from weather forecasts to credit scores, are predictive.

Worked example: will the coach be late tonight? Let's build a tiny predictive model of our own drive home, using invented numbers to show the idea. Suppose a coach company had kept records of 500 past Sunday trips from Delphi to Athens in November, and noted three facts about each: whether there was snow on the road near Arachova, whether the ski season was open (which fills the road on winter weekends), and whether the coach arrived more than 30 minutes late. The "model" is simply the fraction of late trips in each kind of day.

Snow near Arachova? Ski season open? Past trips Late trips Predicted chance of being late No No 300 30 10 percent No Yes 100 25 25 percent Yes No 60 24 40 percent Yes Yes 40 24 60 percent

Tonight there is no snow and the ski season has not opened, so the model predicts a 10 percent chance of a late arrival. Three things about this toy are true of every predictive model. First, it does not know why coaches are late; it only knows how often lateness went with snow and skiers in the past. Second, it assumes that the future resembles the past: a new road, a new tunnel, or a strike would make every number in the table wrong. Third, its prediction is about a kind of day, not about this particular coach: "10 percent" means that on about 1 night in 10 like this one, the coach is late, and it cannot say whether tonight is that night. Real predictive models use many more inputs and far more complicated arithmetic than counting, but they rest on the same three assumptions.

docs.title: Training Data
docs.text:
Training data is the set of examples from which a machine-learning model learns: the labeled column photos, the 500 past coach trips, or, for a language model, a vast collection of written text. A model can only be as good as its training data, because the data is the only experience it has. Three questions decide whether the data is good enough: Is there enough of it? Is it correctly labeled? And does it look like the cases the model will meet in use?

Worked example: the model that learned the weather. Let's go back to the column classifier and suppose something went wrong that we did not notice. Most of our Doric photos came from tourists at outdoor sites such as the Parthenon and Delphi, so they show blue sky behind the stone. Most of our Ionic photos came from museum catalogs, so they show capitals indoors against a gray wall. The model scores 95 percent on the test set, because the test set was drawn from the same collection. Then we show it an Ionic capital photographed outdoors at the Erechtheion against a bright sky, and it answers "Doric." It had learned a shortcut: blue sky means Doric. Nothing in its training told it that the sky was not part of the answer. This kind of failure has been reported many times in real systems, and it is hard to catch, because the shortcut works on every example that resembles the training data. The fix is to make the training data look like the world the model will be used in, here by adding outdoor Ionic and indoor Doric photos, and to test the model on examples gathered in a different way from the training set.

docs.title: Data Bias
docs.text:
Data bias is a systematic difference between the training data and the world it is supposed to represent, which makes a model's predictions worse, or unfair, for some cases or some groups of people. The weather shortcut above came from data bias, but a harmless kind. The serious kinds involve people. Three kinds come up again and again, and naming them makes them easier to spot.

Kind of bias What goes wrong A travel-sized example Sampling bias Some cases or groups are missing or rare in the data A restaurant app trained on reviews written in English by tourists recommends places near the hotels and misses the taverna the village uses Historical bias The data accurately records a past that was itself unfair A model trained on which guides a tour company hired over 30 years learns the company's old preference for men Measurement bias What is recorded is only a stand-in for what we care about "Number of five-star reviews" stands in for "good food," but rewards places that ask every customer for a review

Worked example: who is missing from the reviews? Let's follow the first row. Suppose a recommendation model learns from 50,000 restaurant reviews in Athens, and 90 percent of them were written by visitors who stayed within a mile of their hotels. The model will learn, correctly, that those visitors liked certain places near the Plaka. It will then predict that we will like them too, and it will rarely recommend a neighborhood taverna, not because the food is worse but because few reviewers went there. The model is accurate about its data and biased about the city. Chapter 2's advice, "ask someone who lives here," is the human correction for exactly this bias: it adds a voice that the data left out.

The Data Cannot Show Who Is Missing

A common trap is to trust a model because it was trained on "millions of examples." Millions of examples from the same kind of person still leave everyone else out, and nothing in the numbers will warn you. The fix is to ask one question of any prediction: whose experience was in the data, and is mine like theirs?

docs.title: Loan and Hiring Algorithms
docs.text:
Loan and hiring algorithms are predictive models that help banks decide who gets credit and employers decide whom to interview or hire, by estimating from an applicant's data how likely they are to repay a loan or succeed in a job. They are attractive for real reasons: they are fast, consistent, and do not have bad moods. But they learn from past decisions and past outcomes, so they can carry historical and measurement bias straight into the future, at a scale no single biased manager could reach.

Worked example: removing the column does not remove the bias. Let's follow the best-known case. In 2018 the news agency Reuters reported that Amazon had abandoned an experimental program that rated job applicants' résumés. It had been trained on about ten years of résumés submitted to the company, most of them from men, and it learned to mark down résumés that included the word "women's," as in "women's chess club captain," and those from graduates of two women's colleges. The engineers edited the program to ignore those particular terms, but could not be sure it would not find other ways to sort candidates, so the project was dropped. The lesson is general. Taking "gender" or "race" out of the data does not stop a model from learning them, because other details, such as a club, a college, a first name, or a home address, can act as proxies, stand-ins that carry the same information. In lending, a home address can be such a proxy: in the United States, neighborhoods were long segregated, and in the 1930s government maps marked many Black neighborhoods as poor risks, the practice called redlining, so where a family lives can still carry the history of who was refused credit.

Most countries now have laws that forbid lenders and employers to discriminate, and many require them to explain a refusal. A well-run system is tested for unequal results across groups before and after it is used. AI-Native Schools shows how such an audit works, using the "four-fifths rule" from employment law, in Student Privacy and Data Governance, because the same kind of model now makes judgments about students.

docs.title: Part Two: Three Prediction Machines We Already Use
Weather Forecasting
docs.text: Weather forecasting is predicting the state of the atmosphere for a place and time, and it is the oldest and most successful prediction machine we use every day. Modern forecasts start from millions of measurements, from weather stations, balloons, ships, aircraft, and satellites, and feed them into computer models that apply the laws of physics to the atmosphere, divided into a grid of boxes, to calculate how it will change. Because the starting measurements are never perfect, forecasting centers run the model many times with slightly different starting conditions. This set of runs is called an ensemble. If 6 of 10 runs bring rain to Delphi tomorrow afternoon, the forecast says "60 percent chance of rain." So a percentage in a forecast is a statement about many possible tomorrows: on days like this one, rain falls about 6 times in 10. Machine learning is now being used alongside the physics as well, both to correct the models' known errors and, increasingly, to forecast directly from past weather data. Forecasters also check themselves: national weather services compare their forecasts with what actually happened and publish the results. That habit, as Part Five shows, is what makes their percentages worth trusting.

docs.title: Prediction Uncertainty
docs.text:
Prediction uncertainty is the range of outcomes that remain possible after a prediction is made, together with how likely each one is. Every honest prediction has some, and the question is never whether a prediction is uncertain but how uncertain it is and whether it says so. Uncertainty comes from several sources, and they call for different responses.

Source What it means Example from today Imperfect measurement We do not know the present exactly No station measures the wind on every bend of the Arachova road Chaos Tiny differences grow into large ones A small error in today's temperature becomes a wrong forecast in ten days Missing factors Something that matters is not in the model Our coach model knows snow and skiers but not a breakdown or a strike A changed world The future stops resembling the past A new road would make every past travel time out of date Model error The model's own rules are wrong or too simple A model that treats every November Sunday as the same

Worked example: three ways to say the same forecast. Let's state tomorrow morning's weather in Athens three ways and notice what each one tells us. A single number: "13 °C at 9 AM." It is clear and easy to plan with, but it hides how sure the forecaster is. A range: "between 10 and 15 °C at 9 AM." Now we know to bring a layer, because the low end is cool. A probability: "a 20 percent chance of a shower before noon." Now we can weigh the cost of carrying an umbrella against the cost of getting wet, as Part Seven does. The weather is the same in all three; what changes is how much of the forecaster's uncertainty reaches us. A good source shows its uncertainty. A source that always speaks in single confident numbers is not more certain; it is only hiding the range.

This matters for language models in particular, because their fluent sentences carry no visible error bars. A chatbot can state a museum's closing time in exactly the same confident tone whether it is reporting a well-documented fact or guessing. We can ask it how sure it is, and what would change its answer, and sometimes the reply is useful. But a model's description of its own confidence is itself a prediction, and it is not always a well-calibrated one.

docs.title: Large Language Model
docs.text:
A large language model (LLM) is a machine-learning model trained on an enormous collection of text to predict what comes next in a piece of writing, and then refined so that its predictions take the form of helpful answers. Chapter 2 introduced it. Here are three more details. First, the model reads and writes in tokens, pieces of words; a common word may be one token, a rare one several. Second, it is built in stages: first it learns to predict text from a vast body of writing; then it is trained further on examples of good answers and on people's ratings of its replies, which teaches it to answer questions politely and to decline some requests. Third, unless it is connected to a search tool or a document, it does not look anything up; it produces what its training makes likely.

Whether such a model "understands" what it says is an open debate. Some researchers argue that it only stitches together patterns of words, a view captured in a much-discussed 2021 paper that called such models "stochastic parrots," using stochastic 🔊 Pronounce stuh-KAS-tik, a statistician's word for "random." Others point to evidence that these models build internal representations of the things they write about, and that predicting text well requires something like understanding. Both sides agree on the practical point: a language model can be useful, and it can be fluently, confidently wrong, and the two can appear in the same paragraph.

docs.title: Next-Word Prediction
docs.text:
Next-word prediction is the core task of a language model: given the words so far, assign a probability to every possible next word (strictly, next token), choose one, add it to the text, and repeat. Everything a chatbot writes, from a poem to a timetable, is produced one word at a time this way. How the next word is chosen from the probabilities is controlled by a setting called temperature. At temperature 0, the model always takes the single most likely word. At temperature 1, it picks at random in proportion to the probabilities, so a word with a 20 percent probability is chosen about 1 time in 5. Above 1, the probabilities are flattened, so unlikely words are chosen more often; below 1, they are sharpened toward the favorite.

Worked example: completing the god's advice. Let's give an imaginary small model the words carved on the temple porch, "Know ___," and suppose it assigns these illustrative probabilities to the next word: thyself 60 percent, yourself 20, the 10, your 6, nothing 4. The table shows how temperature changes them. The rule is to raise each probability to the power \( 1/T \), where \( T \) is the temperature, and then rescale so the five add up to 100 percent.

Next word Temperature 0.5 Temperature 1.0 Temperature 2.0 thyself 86.7 60.0 39.1 yourself 9.6 20.0 22.6 the 2.4 10.0 15.9 your 0.9 6.0 12.4 nothing 0.4 4.0 10.1

At temperature 0.5, the model says "thyself" almost 9 times in 10; at 2.0, fewer than 4 times in 10, and "nothing" turns up about once in 10. Low temperature makes a model predictable and repetitive; high temperature makes it varied and more likely to wander. Now suppose the words are "On Sundays the Grand Bazaar is ___," and the model gives closed 45 percent and open 30 percent. At temperature 1, about 3 answers in 10 will say "open," which Chapter 2 told us is usually false. The model has not changed its mind about the facts. It is sampling from what is likely to be written, and likely is not the same as true. That is why the same question can get different answers on different days.

The MicroSim below lets us set the temperature and watch the choices change, predicting each effect before we see it.

docs.title: Diagram: Next-Word Prediction and Temperature
docs.text:
Next-Word Prediction and Temperature

Type: microsim sim-id: next-word-temperature-toy Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: infer Learning Objective: The learner will infer how changing the temperature changes which next word a language model chooses and how often, answering at least 4 of 5 prediction questions correctly before the sampled results are revealed.

Prerequisites: large language model, token, next-word prediction, temperature, probability (defined in "Large Language Model" and "Next-Word Prediction" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of five challenge questions, the learner commits to one answer before pressing Reveal. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct answer in Content. Mastery is at least 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt. Moving the temperature and drawing samples in free exploration is not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A language model always gives the same answer to the same words (challenge 1 and free exploration). (2) A higher temperature makes the model more accurate or more "creative" without cost (challenges 2 and 5). (3) If the most likely word is correct, the model will never say the wrong one (challenge 3). (4) Temperature changes what the model knows, rather than how it chooses (challenge 4).

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level inference needs the learner to predict an effect from the rule and then see whether the prediction holds. Committing to an answer before the sampled results appear forces that inference, and drawing 20 samples turns a probability into a visible count.

Content:

Four prompts, each with five candidate next words and their probabilities at temperature 1.0 (illustrative):

Prompt Word 1 Word 2 Word 3 Word 4 Word 5 1. "Know ___" thyself 60% yourself 20% the 10% your 6% nothing 4% 2. "Nothing in ___" excess 55% the 15% particular 12% life 10% common 8% 3. "On Sundays the Grand Bazaar is ___" closed 45% open 30% busy 15% quiet 6% crowded 4% 4. "The oracle at Delphi was ___" consulted 30% famous 25% a 20% closed 15% silent 10%

Probabilities after applying the temperature rule, in percent, rounded to one decimal (for checking the sim):

Prompt Temperature 0.5 Temperature 2.0 1 86.7 / 9.6 / 2.4 / 0.9 / 0.4 39.1 / 22.6 / 15.9 / 12.4 / 10.1 2 85.0 / 6.3 / 4.0 / 2.8 / 1.8 35.8 / 18.7 / 16.7 / 15.2 / 13.6 3 63.2 / 28.1 / 7.0 / 1.1 / 0.5 32.7 / 26.7 / 18.9 / 11.9 / 9.8 4 40.0 / 27.8 / 17.8 / 10.0 / 4.4 24.9 / 22.7 / 20.3 / 17.6 / 14.4

A fact note shown with prompt 3: "The Grand Bazaar is usually closed on Sundays (Chapter 2). The model's probabilities describe what is often written, not what is true."

Five challenge questions, in this order:

# Prompt and setting Question Choices Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Prompt 1, temperature 0 In 20 tries, which word will the model choose? thyself every time; mostly thyself, sometimes yourself; a different word each time thyself every time At temperature 0 the model always takes the most likely word, so the same words always get the same answer. 2 Prompt 1, temperature raised from 1.0 to 2.0 What happens to the probability of "nothing"? It goes up; it goes down; it stays at 4% It goes up A higher temperature flattens the probabilities, so the least likely word rises from 4.0% to 10.1%. 3 Prompt 3, temperature 1.0 About how many of 20 sampled answers will say "open"? about 0; about 6; about 15 about 6 At temperature 1 each word is chosen in proportion to its probability: 30% of 20 is 6, even though "open" is usually false. 4 Prompt 1, temperature lowered from 1.0 to 0.5 What is the probability of "thyself" now? about 30%; about 60%; about 87% about 87% A lower temperature sharpens the probabilities toward the favorite: 60% becomes 86.7%. The model's knowledge is unchanged; only its way of choosing changed. 5 Prompt 4 At which temperature are the five words closest to equally likely? 0; 0.5; 2.0 2.0 The highest temperature flattens the most: at 2.0 the five range only from 24.9% to 14.4%.

Provenance: All probabilities are illustrative, invented to show the rule; the sim labels them "Illustrative probabilities, not from a real model." The temperature rule is the standard softmax-temperature rescaling described in the chapter section "Next-Word Prediction." The Grand Bazaar fact is from Chapter 2, "Artificial Intelligence."

Rules:

  • Temperature T: minimum 0.0, maximum 2.0, step 0.1, default 1.0, no unit.
  • For T > 0: adjusted probability of word i = p_i^(1/T) divided by the sum over all five words of p_j^(1/T). Display to one decimal place.
  • For T = 0: the most likely word has probability 100% and the others 0%. (No prompt has a tie for first place.)
  • Draw 20: draws 20 independent samples from the adjusted probabilities and shows how many times each word was chosen. Counts always total 20. Samples are random each time; a new draw replaces the previous counts.
  • Changing the prompt or the temperature clears the previous counts.
  • Challenge mode: the prompt and temperature are set by the challenge and locked until the learner has committed an answer and pressed Reveal; Reveal then shows the adjusted probabilities and a fresh draw of 20.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads challenge 1 and chooses an answer.
  2. The learner presses Reveal. The adjusted probabilities and a draw of 20 appear, followed by the feedback.
  3. The learner continues through challenges 2 to 5.
  4. After challenge 5, free exploration unlocks: the learner chooses any prompt, moves the temperature, and draws samples as often as they like.
  5. In free exploration, the learner should notice that at temperature 1.0, prompt 3 produces "open" in some draws, and that at temperature 0 it never does.

Feedback: Five challenges, fixed order, one scored attempt each. Correct: "Correct:" followed by the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite. The answer is [correct answer]:" followed by the Why text. A running count "Correct on first attempt: n of 5" is shown. After challenge 5: if the score is at least 4, "You can predict what temperature does: it changes how the model chooses, not what it knows."; otherwise, "Try challenges 2 and 4 again in free exploration: watch the bars as you move the temperature."

Starting State: Challenge 1 is shown: prompt 1, temperature locked at 0, the five candidate words with no bars yet, and the question "In 20 tries, which word will the model choose?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example uses prompt 1 with thyself 60, yourself 20, the 10, your 6, nothing 4 percent, and gives 86.7 / 60.0 / 39.1 percent for "thyself" and 0.4 / 4.0 / 10.1 percent for "nothing" at temperatures 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0. It states that about 3 answers in 10 to prompt 3 will say "open" at temperature 1, with closed 45 and open 30 percent. Temperature 0 always takes the most likely word.

docs.title: Part Three: The Oracle's Questions, Asked of Machines
Oracle as Data Hub
docs.text:
The first of last night's questions was whether Delphi, by hearing questions from cities all over the Greek world for centuries, became better informed. The idea of the oracle as a data hub is that the sanctuary worked, among other things, as a meeting point for information: envoys arrived from colonies in Sicily and on the Black Sea, from Sparta and Athens and Lydia, and each brought news along with a question. The priests heard which cities were planning colonies, which were at war, and which were struck by plague. Some historians have suggested that this flow of information helps explain why many of the oracle's practical answers, about where to settle or which god to honor, were sensible. It is a reasonable suggestion, not a proven one: we have no archive of the questions Delphi heard, and no ancient writer says the priests kept one.

The comparison with a language model is close, and so is the warning. A model trained on text from all over the world is a kind of data hub too, a place where an enormous number of voices have been gathered and compressed. And like Delphi's, its sources are uneven. The envoys who reached the oracle were mostly from cities that could afford the journey, and Croesus' Lydians, Chapter 17 showed, went to the front of the line. The text that reaches a language model comes mostly from people and languages that write a great deal online. A hub knows a great deal about the people who come to it, and much less about the people who never make the trip.

docs.title: Interpreting Ambiguous Answers
docs.text:
Interpreting ambiguous answers is the work of deciding what an answer that can be read in more than one way actually means for our decision. The wooden wall is the great example. Chapter 17 told how the Athenian Assembly argued over the god's words: some said the wooden wall was the old thorn hedge around the Acropolis, others said it was the fleet; the professional interpreters read "divine Salamis" as a warning, and Themistocles read it as a promise. The answer itself decided nothing. The interpreting did.

AI answers are often ambiguous in the same way, not because a god is being cryptic but because a model produces the kind of answer that usually fits a question, and usual answers are hedged. "Many visitors drive to Delphi in winter without difficulty, but conditions on mountain roads can change quickly" is true, fluent, and nearly useless for deciding about tomorrow.

Worked example: reading an AI answer the way the Assembly read the oracle. Let's suppose that last night we had asked a chatbot, "Should we take the coach to Delphi tomorrow if snow is forecast above Arachova?" and received the answer above. Let's apply the Assembly's method in four steps.

  1. List the readings. It could mean "go, it is usually fine," or "be careful, it might not be," or simply "I do not know tomorrow's road conditions."
  2. Ask what each reading predicts. "Usually fine" predicts the road will be open. "I do not know" predicts nothing at all; it is Chapter 17's hedge, an answer that cannot lose.
  3. Bring other evidence. The real forecast for the Arachova road, the coach company's own decision (it decides whether to go), and the hotel clerk who has driven that road every winter.
  4. Decide, and own the decision. The Athenians voted, and the choice was theirs. Ours is too: if we go and the road closes, it was not the chatbot that chose.

The method turns an answer from a verdict into one piece of evidence among several, which is all an answer ever was.

Ask the Source How It Could Be Wrong

Here's a quick diagnostic for any vague AI answer: reply, "What would have to be true for that to be wrong, and how would I check it?" A useful answer names something concrete, such as an official site, a date, or a condition. If the reply only repeats the hedge, treat the first answer as saying "I don't know."

docs.title: Human in the Loop
docs.text: Human in the loop means designing a system so that a person reviews, and is responsible for, the decisions that an automated system recommends, rather than letting the system act on its own. The Athenian Assembly was a human in the loop of the oracle: the god's answer came in, but citizens argued over it and voted, and Themistocles, Chapter 17 noted, was valued for his own forecasting judgment, not only for his reading of the god. A human in the loop is only a safeguard if the human can actually disagree. People tend to accept a machine's recommendation even when they have reason to doubt it, a tendency researchers call automation bias. A loan officer who approves whatever the score says, or a teacher who never questions an at-risk flag, is in the loop on paper only. A meaningful loop needs three things: the person has time to think, has information the machine lacks, and is free to overrule it without penalty.

docs.title: Confirmation Bias
docs.text:
Confirmation bias is the habit of noticing, seeking, and believing the evidence that supports what we already think, and of overlooking the evidence against it. Croesus is its patron saint. Told that if he made war on Persia he would destroy a great empire, he heard only the reading he wanted, and never asked the obvious follow-up the Pythia later threw back at him: which empire? Xenophon, in Chapter 17, showed the same habit one step earlier, in the question itself: having already decided to go, he asked only how to succeed.

We do both with machines. We phrase questions so that they carry our answer ("Why is Delphi better than the beach for our last Sunday?"), and language models make the trap deeper, because they tend to follow the framing of a question and are trained partly on people's approval of their replies, which can teach them to agree with us. A model asked a leading question will often supply the reasons we wanted.

The Leading Question Gets the Agreeable Answer

A common slip is to ask an AI "Isn't it true that...?" and take its agreement as independent support. It happens because the model follows our framing, as Apollo answered Xenophon's question rather than the one he should have asked. The fix is to ask the question both ways, or to ask directly for the strongest case against our plan, and compare the two answers.

docs.title: Part Four: Predictions That Change the World
Self-Fulfilling Prophecy
docs.text:
A self-fulfilling prophecy is a prediction that comes true partly because it was made: people who hear it change their behavior in ways that bring it about. The American sociologist Robert K. Merton gave the idea its name in 1948, with the example of a sound bank that fails because a false rumor that it will fail sends every depositor to withdraw their money at once. The oldest example on our route is the myth of Oedipus. Chapter 17 traced its chain: Laius abandoned his son to escape the prophecy, and Oedipus fled Corinth to escape it, and each escape was a link in the chain that fulfilled it. Would it have come true if no one had heard it? In the myth, no.

The opposite also happens. A self-defeating prophecy is one that fails because it was made: a forecast of a traffic jam on the road to Delphi at 9 AM sends drivers out early, and the jam never forms. Both kinds matter for predictive models, because a model's prediction is not only a statement about the world; when people act on it, it becomes part of the world. The more a prediction is used, the more it changes the data from which the next prediction will be learned.

A Prediction Is Also an Action

Notice that a weather forecast cannot change the weather, but a forecast about people can change the people. Once a prediction is used to decide where police patrol or which class a child joins, it stops being a neutral report and starts pushing on the outcome. Ask of every prediction about people: what will we do because of it, and how will that change what happens next?

docs.title: Student Risk Prediction
docs.text:
Student risk prediction is the use of a predictive model to estimate which students are likely to fail a course, fall behind, or drop out, so that schools can help them early. Many school systems use such early-warning systems, built from attendance, grades, behavior records, and sometimes family and neighborhood data. The goal is good, since help that comes early works better, and a simple, transparent warning, such as "three weeks of missed classes," can be valuable.

The risk is a self-fulfilling loop. If a "high-risk" label leads to lower expectations or a less demanding class, the student may learn less, which raises the risk score, which confirms the label. Research on teachers' expectations, beginning with a famous and much-debated 1968 study known as Pygmalion in the Classroom, suggests that expectations can affect students' results, though how strongly is still argued. There is also the question of fairness: AI-Native Schools reports a 2023 investigation finding that Wisconsin's dropout early-warning system gave false alarms more often for Black and Hispanic students than for white students (Student Privacy and Data Governance). The test of a risk prediction is what the school does with it: a flag that brings a tutor helps; a flag that lowers the ceiling harms.

docs.title: Predictive Policing
docs.text:
Predictive policing is the use of predictive models, trained on past crime records, to forecast where crimes are likely to happen or who is likely to be involved, so that police can send patrols in advance. Its weakness is a feedback loop built from measurement bias. Crime records are not a measure of crime; they are a measure of crime that was reported or discovered. If patrols are sent where the model predicts crime, officers there will discover more of it, which adds more records from that area, which raises the next prediction for that area, while crime in unpatrolled areas goes unrecorded. In 2016 the statisticians Kristian Lum and William Isaac used police records from Oakland, California, to show how such a loop could send officers again and again to the same neighborhoods, even though health surveys suggested that drug use was spread widely across the city. Several American cities that tried predictive policing have since stopped using it, citing doubts about both its effectiveness and its fairness. The general point is the one Oedipus teaches: when a prediction guides the action that produces the next data, the model can end up predicting its own behavior.

The MicroSim below lets us trace three loops like these and tell which kind each one is.

docs.title: Diagram: When a Prediction Feeds Itself
docs.text:
When a Prediction Feeds Itself

Type: causal-loop sim-id: prediction-feedback-loops Library: vis-network Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate reinforcing loops, in which a prediction helps bring itself about, from balancing loops, in which a prediction helps prevent itself, by labeling the direction of every link in three prediction loops and classifying each loop, with at least 9 of 10 links and all 3 loops correct.

Prerequisites: predictive model, data bias (measurement bias), self-fulfilling prophecy, self-defeating prophecy, student risk prediction, predictive policing (defined in Parts One and Four above).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner labels each of the 10 links as "same direction" (+) or "opposite direction" (−), then classifies each of the 3 loops as reinforcing or balancing, then answers one question per loop. A label, classification or answer is correct when it matches the Content tables. Mastery is at least 9 of 10 links, 3 of 3 loops and 2 of 3 loop questions correct on the first attempt. Opening a node's explanation is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A loop with a minus sign in it must be balancing (Loop 2 has two minus signs and is reinforcing). (2) A prediction that comes true proves the model was accurate (Loop 1). (3) A forecast that "failed" was a bad forecast (Loop 3). (4) Taking more data from the same source fixes a feedback loop (Loop 1 question).

Instructional Rationale: Analyze-level work means taking a loop apart into its links and finding the structure that decides its behavior. Labeling each link before classifying the loop makes the learner derive the loop type from the parts, using the counting rule, rather than guessing from the story's moral.

Content:

Definitions shown to the learner:

  • Same direction (+): if the first factor rises, the second rises; if the first falls, the second falls.
  • Opposite direction (−): if the first factor rises, the second falls; if the first falls, the second rises.
  • Reinforcing loop: a change travels around the loop and comes back larger, in the same direction. A self-fulfilling prediction is a reinforcing loop.
  • Balancing loop: a change travels around the loop and comes back opposed. A self-defeating prediction is a balancing loop.
  • Counting rule: a loop with an even number of opposite (−) links, including zero, is reinforcing; a loop with an odd number is balancing.

Nodes, links and correct labels (loops are named Loop 1, Loop 2 and Loop 3 so that no name gives the answer away):

Link Loop From To Correct label Why (shown as feedback) L1 1 Predicted crime in a district Patrols sent to that district + Police send more patrols where the model predicts more crime. L2 1 Patrols sent to that district Crimes recorded in that district + More officers on the street discover and record more of the crime that is there. L3 1 Crimes recorded in that district Predicted crime in a district + The model is retrained on the records, so more records raise the next prediction. L4 2 Student's risk score Placement in a lower-level course + A higher score makes a lower-level placement more likely. L5 2 Placement in a lower-level course Access to challenging coursework − The lower-level course offers less challenging work. L6 2 Access to challenging coursework Grades and test scores + Students who are taught more challenging material tend to score higher on it. L7 2 Grades and test scores Student's risk score − Higher grades lower the risk score. L8 3 Predicted traffic at 9 AM on the Athens–Delphi road Drivers who leave earlier or take another road + A forecast of heavy traffic sends more drivers out early or onto other roads. L9 3 Drivers who leave earlier or take another road Traffic at 9 AM − The more drivers avoid 9 AM, the lighter the 9 AM traffic. L10 3 Traffic at 9 AM Predicted traffic at 9 AM on the Athens–Delphi road + Next week's forecast is learned from this week's traffic.

Loops and correct classifications:

Loop Links Opposite links Correct classification Why (shown as feedback) 1 L1, L2, L3 0 Reinforcing No opposite links: a higher prediction brings more patrols, more records, and a still higher prediction, whatever the true crime rate. 2 L4, L5, L6, L7 2 Reinforcing Two opposite links cancel: a higher risk score leads, through less challenging work and lower grades, to a still higher risk score. 3 L8, L9, L10 1 Balancing One opposite link: a forecast of heavy traffic leads to lighter traffic and a lower forecast next week, so the prediction defeats itself.

Outside factor shown in Loop 1 but not part of the loop: "True crime in the district," with a + link to "Crimes recorded in that district." Its note reads: "Records rise with true crime and with patrols; the model cannot tell which."

Loop questions (one per loop, three choices each):

# Question Choices Correct Why (shown as feedback) Q1 Which change would weaken Loop 1? Train the model on crimes reported by victims and residents rather than on crimes discovered by patrols; send more patrols to every district; retrain the model every week instead of every month Train on reported crimes Records that do not depend on where the patrols went no longer carry L2's effect into L3; more patrols or more frequent retraining only feed the same loop. Q2 Which use of the risk score would turn Loop 2 from harm to help? Keep the student in the challenging course and add tutoring when the score is high; hide the score from the student; recompute the score every month Keep the course and add tutoring Adding support instead of lowering the placement replaces link L5's loss of challenging work with more help, so a high score leads to higher grades. Q3 Next Sunday the 9 AM forecast said "heavy traffic," and the road was light. What is the best explanation? Drivers acted on the forecast, so the jam it predicted did not form; the model was badly trained; traffic is purely random Drivers acted on the forecast In a balancing loop a useful forecast can look wrong, because people change their behavior to avoid what it predicts.

Provenance: The loops are simplified from the chapter sections "Self-Fulfilling Prophecy," "Student Risk Prediction," and "Predictive Policing." The link directions are the chapter's qualitative claims, not measured effects; the sim labels the diagram "Simplified causal model: directions only, no sizes."

Rules:

  • Links are labeled one at a time in the order L1 to L10 (fixed). Each link has one scored attempt; after it, the correct label and Why text are shown and the link displays its correct sign.
  • A loop can be classified only after all of its links are labeled. Each loop has one scored attempt.
