docs.title: Wheels Up from Athens
docs.text:
Tuesday, November 24, is the day after Day 13, and the guide's last reading. The plane climbs out of Athens International Airport, the coast drops away behind us, and somewhere in the overhead bin are the saffron and the Turkish delight from the Spice Bazaar. Thirteen days ago we landed in Istanbul, and since then we have read eighteen chapters, one or two a day. Now the reading is done and the stories are ours, and there is time, for once, to put them side by side. It happens to be a good day for it: November 24 is Teachers' Day in Turkey, the anniversary of the day in 1928 when Mustafa Kemal was named Head Teacher of the Nation's Schools, as Chapter 7 told.

Every daily chapter ended with a Learning for All note, one story about who got to learn and who was shut out. This short chapter gathers those notes and weighs them together, adds a few ideas about doing good things with people rather than to them, and leaves the last page for us to write.

One Last Look Out the Window

For two weeks we read one story a day; on the way home we finally get to read them all at once, like a mosaic seen from across the nave instead of one tile at a time. The pattern that shows up is simple, a little uncomfortable, and useful for anyone who wants to bring good news about learning to someone else. By the time the drinks cart comes around, we'll have written some of our own. Look closer.

Part One looks back at what we found behind the tourist scripts, and at two lessons that kept recurring: the cost of waiting for a new knowledge technology, and the resistance of those whose living depended on the old one. Part Two weighs good news against its shadow, from top-down reform to evangelism imposed. Part Three argues for learning with communities, in their own languages, with AI translation as a new tool. The closing section asks us to write our own good news.

docs.title: Part One: What We Found Behind the Scripts
Seeing Past the Tourist Script
docs.text:
Chapter 2 defined the tourist script as the standard story told to visitors in the standard order: the shortest story that sells. Seeing past the tourist script is the habit of asking, at every stop, what the standard story leaves out, and in this guide the question was most often "who got to learn here, and who did not?" The script of the Library of Celsus is a beautiful facade and a number of scrolls; behind it was a son's endowment of 25,000 denarii and a reading room that most Ephesians probably could not use, because they could not read. The script of the Grand Bazaar is carpets; right beside it was a book market where copyists sold handmade books for almost three centuries after Gutenberg.

The table gathers the Learning for All stories in the order we met them. The last column is the lesson each chapter drew for AI in education.

Chapter Stop The story The lesson we carried away 2 Before we go The Greek alphabet, learnable in a season Lower the price of the first step 3 Istanbul Theodosius II's 31 paid teachers in 425; Bessarion's manuscripts given to Venice in 1468 Copies outlast walls; check who actually walks through the door 4 Istanbul Justinian's law of 529; the copyists' bottleneck Deciding what gets copied decides who gets to learn 5 Istanbul Endowed medreses with a room, meals, and a stipend Funding that outlasts enthusiasm, and a way to keep changing 6 Istanbul Scribes, Müteferrika, and a press about 275 years late Copies are not readers 7 Istanbul The 1928 alphabet and the Nation's Schools A fast reform can leave a generation cut off from its past 8 Troy Homer written down A tool that composes for us can take away the practice 10 Ephesus The Library of Celsus A gift reaches only as far as the means to use it 12 Rhodes Cicero sails to his teacher; the list of 1944 Learning for all means protecting the learners 13 Crete Linear B lost; Kober and Ventris read it again Elite knowledge is fragile; credit the groundwork 14 Crete Cretan editors and Aldus's pocket classics Cheap is not the same as open; someone must check the text 15 Athens Herodotus' historia Show the inquiry 16 Athens Socrates free in the Agora; who democracy left out Count the people a system does not reach 18 Delphi Freedom carved in the polygonal wall A learner's record should be trusted and the learner's own 20 Athens Aristotle tutoring Alexander; the Phaedrus A tutor for every child, if it leaves them better at thinking

Read down the third column and Chapter 2's four-step pattern appears in almost every row: learning locked up, opened by a new technology or institution, resisted, and widened but never all the way. Two of its steps recur so often that they deserve their own names.

docs.title: Cost of Delaying Technology
docs.text:
The cost of delaying technology is what a society loses in the years between the arrival of a better way to store or spread knowledge and its adoption: the books not printed, the readers not made, the ideas that traveled more slowly than they could have. The clearest case on our route is Chapter 6's gap of about 275 years between Gutenberg's Bible and İbrahim Müteferrika's first book in the Arabic script, in 1729. Istanbul had Jewish, Armenian, and Greek presses long before that, so the delay was not ignorance; Chapter 6 found several reasons working together, from reverence for the handwritten Quran to the copyists' livelihoods and the authorities' wish to control what was written.

Chapter 6 also warned against the easy moral: even after the press came, most people could not read the script, so printing made copies cheap but did not make readers. And waiting has an opposite cost. AI-Native Schools opens its chapter Implementing the AI-Native Model Responsibly with the risk of rushed procurement, a school buying AI faster than it can judge it. The lesson of the delayed press is not "adopt everything at once," but "count what waiting costs, and who pays it."

docs.title: Scribal Resistance
docs.text:
Scribal resistance is the opposition to a new knowledge technology from the people whose skill, income, or prestige depended on the old one. Our route was full of it, and four cases stand out.

  • Homer's reciters, the rhapsodes, kept their prestige for centuries after the poems were written down (Chapter 8).
  • Demetrius the silversmith called together his fellow craftsmen at Ephesus against a message that threatened their trade in silver shrines, and the riot filled the Great Theater (Chapters 10 and 11).
  • Ottoman copyists and calligraphers lived by handwriting, and the craft's prestige and jobs were at stake when printing came (Chapter 6).
  • The abbot Trithemius wrote In Praise of Scribes in 1492, urging monks to keep copying by hand, and had it printed (Chapter 20).

Chapter 11 drew the lesson that matters most: these people were not irrational. Demetrius was right about his market, and the copyists were right that the press would end their way of life. Chapter 4 added that scribes were also gatekeepers, choosing in the 9th century which books to copy into the new script. Resistance is information about who stands to lose, and the scribes' successors today, teachers, aides, tutoring companies, and textbook publishers, are owed what Chapter 11 called a hearing.

docs.title: Part Two: Good News and Its Shadow
Costs of Top-Down Reform
docs.text:
The costs of top-down reform are the losses that come with a change decided by a ruler or government and imposed on the people it affects, without their choice or consent: the knowledge, trust, and ways of life that a faster, more uniform change sweeps away. Top-down reform can work, and quickly. It can also leave people feeling that the new learning belongs to someone else, the difference Chapter 2 drew between doing something with a community and doing it to one.

Our route held several examples of different sizes. In 529, Justinian decided by law who could teach, and the school that had taught philosophy in Athens for centuries came to an end soon afterward, though historians debate how directly the law caused it (Chapter 4). In 161 BCE the Roman Senate expelled Greek philosophers and teachers of rhetoric from Rome (Chapter 12). And in 1923, two governments agreed on the compulsory exchange of about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians and about 400,000 Muslims, none of whom could return (Chapter 7). That convention sorted people by religion, not by the language they spoke, so Turkish-speaking Christians from Cappadocia went to Greece and Greek-speaking Muslims from Crete went to Turkey. A rule drawn far away decided where millions would live, and it did not ask what language they spoke at home. The largest education reform we met, the alphabet of 1928, is the hardest to judge, because it worked.

Worked example: a ledger for the 1928 alphabet. Let's set the reform's gains and costs side by side, using only what Chapter 7 reported, and then ask which costs came from the new letters and which from the way the change was made.

Gains Costs A script whose first step takes weeks, not years Within one generation, most Turks could not read their grandparents' letters or the inscriptions on fountains and gravestones Free evening classes for adults across the country from January 1, 1929, and, by the government's own count, more than a million certificates in the first years The classes reached towns faster than villages and men faster than women, and many adults lost the skill without books to practice on Literacy from about one person in ten (1927) to one in five (1935), and well over 95 percent today Imposed by a one-party government without a vote; the Arabic script banned from public use From 1940, Village Institutes trained teachers from village families to go home and teach A campaign from 1932 to replace Arabic and Persian words widened the gap with the past

Now sort the costs. Some came with any change of script: once schools teach new letters, children stop learning the old ones unless someone teaches both. Others came from the method. The ban, the absence of a vote, and the speed set by a one-party state were choices, and they are why the reform is still argued over, now that Ottoman Turkish has returned as a subject in some Turkish schools. Notice, too, that even this reform held a piece built closer to communities: the Village Institutes, which trained teachers from village families and sent them home to teach. A ledger like this does not say whether the reform was right. It says that speed bought by command is paid for later, often by the grandchildren.

The AI parallel is close. AI-Native Schools describes, in Sustaining Change: Systems Thinking and National Adoption, a national rollout of AI textbooks that, as reported, met such strong objections from teachers and parents that within months they were reclassified as supplementary materials. A mandate can move a country fast. It cannot make people trust what it brings.

docs.title: Education Evangelism
docs.text:
Chapter 9 traced the word euangelion, "good news," from Homer's reward for a messenger, through a calendar inscription at Priene in honor of Augustus, to Paul's letters, and the word evangelist, a bearer of good news, to Apple's "software evangelists" in the 1980s. Education evangelism is the work of persuading schools, families, and governments to adopt a new way of teaching that the evangelist believes will help learners, today most often AI tutoring and intelligent textbooks. Dan, as Chapter 9 said, would describe himself as an evangelist for AI in education. Chapter 9 also offered a test for any evangelist, that news is only good news if the hearer finds it good, and read Paul's Ephesian years for method alone, setting his message aside.

Worked example: running Paul's method on a school pitch. Let's take a pitch an evangelist might give a rural school district, "AI tutors will give every child a personal tutor," and ask of it the questions that each of Paul's practices suggests.

Paul's practice (Chapter 9) The question for an AI evangelist What a good answer sounds like Went to a hub Where will others see it working? One pilot school that nearby schools can visit Worked alongside people in their trade Who in the district does this with us? Two veteran teachers who help design it and can say no Spoke their language Does the tutor speak the children's language? Yes, checked by teachers who speak it Stayed long enough Who keeps it going after the launch? A local team and a budget for year four Built a team that led without him Who leads it if the evangelist leaves? A teacher named in the plan Answered actual questions What do families here worry about? We asked them first, and the plan answers privacy and screen time Met opposition Who stands to lose? Aides and tutors, given new roles in writing

The pitch itself does not change. What changes is that every answer in the last column involves someone from the district. That is the difference between announcing good news and spreading it, and it leads straight to the shadow.

docs.title: Evangelism's Shadow
docs.text:
Evangelism's shadow is the harm that follows when good news is imposed on people rather than chosen by them, or when the people who carry it come to treat those who decline it with contempt. Chapter 11 named it as a limit of the Paul parallel: Paul's hearers chose to join and could leave, but good news has too often been imposed, "in the history of missions and of school reform alike."

The darkest form of the shadow on our route was the one Chapter 11 told with care. Paul wrote of his own people with "great sorrow," and pictured Gentile believers as branches grafted onto Israel's olive tree, warned not to boast. Later Christians quoted his harshest lines and forgot the olive tree, and what the historian Jules Isaac called "the teaching of contempt" ran from John Chrysostom's sermons in Antioch, through Luther's tract of 1543, to the Nazis who reprinted it, and to Rhodes, whose Jewish children were deported in 1944 (Chapter 12). After the Holocaust, churches began to repudiate that teaching, as Nostra Aetate did in 1965. Chapter 11 showed that Paul's own words point in more than one direction; the shadow grew when later carriers of the message chose the harshest lines and came to see the other as an error to be corrected rather than a people to be heard.

Schooling has its own version. Missions have often printed the first books in a people's language, and mission and state schools have also, too often, punished children for speaking it. In Canada, for example, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015 that many Indigenous children in the church-run residential schools were punished for speaking their own languages. The intention was to bring education. The method taught children that their language, and so their families, stood in the way of it.

The Evangelist's Blind Spot

A common trap for anyone sure their news is good is to hear every objection as misunderstanding. When someone resists, before explaining again, write down what they would lose and what they know about their own place that we don't; then answer that list, or change the plan.

Worked example: the shadow test. Let's take three questions that would have caught each shadow on our route, and put them to the same AI pitch from the section above.

  1. Who chose? The alphabet of 1928 was chosen for Turks, not by them. For the AI pitch: did the district ask for it, or was it offered as a gift that cannot be refused?
  2. What is treated as the obstacle? The residential schools treated a child's language as the obstacle to learning. For the AI pitch: does the plan treat the community's language, teachers, or ways of teaching as something to work through, or something to get around?
  3. What happens to those who say no? Paul's later readers turned his words against those who declined the message. For the AI pitch: can a teacher or family opt out without being labeled backward, and will the plan still serve their children?

A pitch that passes all three can still fail, but it will not fail in the shadow's way.

docs.title: Mother-Tongue Learning
docs.text:
Mother-tongue learning is teaching and learning in the language a child speaks at home, especially in the early years of school, so that learning to read and learning new ideas do not both have to wait until the child has learned a second language. Chapter 9 showed the opposite approach: Koine carried Paul's letters because many peoples had learned one common language, and over centuries it crowded out the older languages of Anatolia. Our route showed a smaller version of the same divide: the Erotokritos, a Cretan poem printed only in 1713, lived for centuries in villagers' memories and songs, while the printed classics of Chapter 14 spoke Latin and Greek to men who had been to school.

UNESCO's position has been consistent for a long time. In 1953 a UNESCO report on vernacular languages in education called it axiomatic that "the best medium for teaching is the mother tongue of the pupil." UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report returned to the point in a 2016 policy paper whose title asks, "If you don't understand, how can you learn?", and estimated that as much as 40 percent of the world's people do not have access to education in a language they speak or understand. The research behind this position generally finds that children learn to read more easily in a language they already speak, and that a strong start in the first language supports learning a second, rather than holding it back. It also finds that mother-tongue programs succeed only with trained teachers and books in that language, which is exactly where the copyists' bottleneck of Chapter 4 reappears: most of the world's languages have little written material, in print or online.

docs.title: AI Translation
docs.text:
AI translation is the use of machine-learning systems, now mostly large language models and related translation models, to translate speech and writing between languages, and to read text aloud or transcribe it. Chapter 9 named its promise: instead of everyone learning one common language, as Paul's world learned Koine, each learner can keep their own language and still reach ideas written in any other. For mother-tongue learning that changes the arithmetic. A story, a science lesson, or a page of this guide could be put into a small language for a tiny fraction of the cost of a human translation, and read aloud to a child who cannot yet read it.

The risk is the copyists' filter of Chapter 4. AI systems learn from digitized text, most of it in a handful of large languages, so they translate those well and smaller languages poorly, often fluently and wrongly. The remedy is to involve the speakers. Masakhane 🔊 Pronounce mah-sah-KAH-neh, a grassroots research community whose name is isiZulu for "we build together," brings speakers of African languages together to build translation tools for their own languages, rather than waiting for distant companies to do it. Chapter 7 offered a hopeful twist in the same spirit: researchers are now training text-recognition systems on the Ottoman script, so the tools of our time may reopen archives that the reform of 1928 closed.

Fluent Is Not the Same as Right

Watch out for machine translation into a language you can't read: it will sound smooth whether or not it is correct, especially in languages with little text online. Before any translated lesson reaches a child, have a fluent speaker from that community read or listen to a sample, as AI-Native Schools advises in Measuring AI Capability: The METR Task-Horizon Studies, and fix what they find.

docs.title: Education With Communities
docs.text:
Education with communities is the practice of designing, running, and judging an effort to widen learning together with the people it is meant to serve, in their language, with their consent, and with their hands on how it continues, rather than delivering it to them from outside. It is the positive half of Chapter 2's distinction between with and to, and the trip offered both halves. The Greeks borrowed Phoenician letters for their own purposes; as Chapter 2 put it, the alphabet spread because people chose it, not because it was imposed. The ibn Nahmias brothers, refugees from Spain, printed a code of Jewish law for their own community, in its own script, in 1493 or perhaps a decade later (Chapter 6). Andrew Carnegie paid for library buildings only if the town provided the land and promised to pay for books, staff, and upkeep every year, so that each town was invested in its library (Chapter 10). And Turkey's Village Institutes trained village teachers to go home and teach.

AI-Native Schools reaches the same conclusion from modern cases. Its chapter AI-First Case Studies II: Lessons for Practice finds, looking across a run of failed school-technology projects, that the technology mostly worked as designed: what failed was planning, trust, and listening, as when students walked out of school and told a district, loudly, what a program had missed.

The Last Step Is Decided at the Second

Notice where the fourth step of the pattern, "never all the way," usually comes from. The people left out of the circle are most often the people who were not in the room when the opening was designed. Inviting them in at step two is the cheapest way to shrink step four.

The sorter below lets us test our judgment on route stories and two imagined AI projects.

docs.title: Diagram: With or To?
docs.text:
With or To?

Type: microsim sim-id: with-or-to-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of eight efforts to widen or control learning, six from the trip and two imagined AI projects, was done with the people it affected or done to them, sorting at least 6 of 8 correctly on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: costs of top-down reform, evangelism's shadow, education with communities, mother-tongue learning, and Chapter 2's with-versus-to distinction (defined in the sections above); the route stories in the table in "Seeing Past the Tourist Script" and in the sections "Costs of Top-Down Reform" and "Education With Communities".

Evidence of Mastery: The learner places each of 8 cards in one of two bins, "Done with people" or "Done to people". A placement is correct when it matches the Correct bin column in Content. Only the first placement of each card counts toward mastery. Mastery is 6 of 8 correct on the first attempt. Reading the four judging questions and opening a card's chapter link are exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A reform that widened literacy must have been done with people. (2) Anything paid for by a donor is done to the community. (3) Using AI in a school is itself top-down, whoever chose it. (4) If an effort is in the learners' language, it was done with them.

Instructional Rationale: Judging requires applying criteria to cases and committing to a verdict, so each card asks for a verdict against four stated questions rather than a recall of facts. Mixing a reform that succeeded (the 1928 alphabet) with a donor's gift that was shared (Carnegie) forces the learner to judge how a change was made, separately from whether it helped, and the two AI cards transfer the judgment to the learner's own time.

Content:

The four judging questions, always visible: (1) Who chose it? (2) Whose language is it in? (3) Who was consulted? (4) Who keeps it going?

The two bins: "Done with people" and "Done to people".

# Card shown to the learner Correct bin Why (shown as feedback) 1 Greek traders adopt the Phoenician letters and add vowels to write their own language, about 800 BCE. Done with people The people who used the script chose it for their own purposes; no one imposed it. 2 The Roman Senate expels Greek philosophers and teachers of rhetoric from Rome, 161 BCE. Done to people The Senate decided for Roman learners which teachers they could have. 3 Justinian issues a law forbidding pagans to teach, 529 CE. Done to people An emperor decided by law who could teach, and a school with centuries of teaching ended soon after. 4 The ibn Nahmias brothers, Sephardic refugees, print a code of Jewish law in Istanbul in their community's script, dated 1493. Done with people Members of the community printed a book for it, in its own script. 5 Andrew Carnegie pays for a library building only if the town provides the land and promises to pay for books, staff, and upkeep every year, 1883–1929. Done with people The town had to choose the library and keep paying for it, so the community shared the decision and the cost. 6 Turkey replaces the Arabic script with a Latin-based alphabet by law within months, and bans the old script from public use, 1928. Done to people It widened literacy, but it was imposed by a one-party government without a vote. 7 A national ministry signs one contract and installs the same English-language AI tutor in every primary school by next term, without asking teachers or families. Done to people It was chosen far away, in a language many children may not speak, with no one consulted. 8 Village teachers and parents choose the stories their AI reading tutor uses, have it read them aloud in the children's own language, and check its translations before each term. Done with people The community chooses the content and the language and keeps checking the tool.

Provenance: Cards 1–6 come from this chapter's sections "Costs of Top-Down Reform" and "Education With Communities", which draw on Chapter 2 ("Learning for All: Two Dozen Letters"), Chapter 4 ("Learning for All: The Bottleneck of the Copyists"), Chapter 6 ("The Hebrew Press of 1493"), Chapter 7 ("The Alphabet Reform of 1928"), Chapter 10 ("Learning for All: A Son's Gift of Books"), and Chapter 12 ("Traveling to the Teacher"). Cards 7 and 8 are illustrative scenarios written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "Imagined AI project".

Rules: Eight cards, shown one at a time in the fixed order 1 to 8. A card may be moved to either bin. The first placement of each card is recorded for the score; after feedback the learner may move a wrongly placed card to the correct bin, which does not change the score. A card cannot be skipped. The score counts first placements matching the Correct bin column. Mastery is score >= 6.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the four judging questions and the first card.
  2. The learner places the card in a bin. Feedback appears at once, and the card stays in the bin the learner chose until the learner moves it.
  3. The learner continues through the remaining cards in order.
  4. After card 8, the sim shows the score and both bins with all eight cards.
  5. The learner should notice that card 6 is in "Done to people" even though the reform worked, and that card 5 is in "Done with people" even though a rich donor paid.

Feedback: Correct: "Yes." followed by the card's Why text. Incorrect: "Look again at the four questions." followed by the card's Why text, with an extra line for the likely misconception on three cards: card 5 adds "A donor paid, but the town chose the library and kept it running."; card 6 adds "Whether a reform helped and how it was made are separate questions."; card 8 adds "Using AI is not top-down in itself; it depends on who chose it and who keeps checking it." The final screen shows "First-try score: n of 8." At 6 or more: "You can judge how a change was made, not only whether it worked." Below 6: "Go back to the four questions and try the cards you missed."

Starting State: Two empty bins, the four judging questions, card 1 face up, and the prompt "Was this done with the people it affected, or done to them?"

Chapter Anchors: the 161 BCE expulsion; Justinian's law of 529; the Hebrew press of 1493 "or perhaps a decade later"; Carnegie's condition that the town provide the land and pay for books, staff, and upkeep every year; the 1928 alphabet imposed by a one-party government without a vote, with the old script banned from public use; "route stories and two imagined AI projects"; eight cards, four in each bin; mastery 6 of 8.

docs.title: AI-Native Schools Companion
docs.text:
The AI-Native Schools companion is AI-Native Schools, the companion textbook this guide has linked to since Chapter 2, which works out in detail how a school might use AI tutoring and intelligent textbooks well. This guide's Learning for All notes pointed to it whenever a story from the route raised a question that book answers. For the flight home, three of its chapters belong together, because they are about how a change is made rather than what it is.

  • Implementing the AI-Native Model Responsibly: buying carefully, piloting before scaling, and measuring group by group whether a change closes gaps or widens them.
  • AI-First Case Studies I: Promise and Peril: a framework for reading every story for both its benefit and its risk, including the Turkish high school study that Chapter 20 described.
  • AI-First Case Studies II: Lessons for Practice: why school reforms fail, and how two-sided stories teach.

Our Learning for All notes were two-sided stories of the same kind, told in stone and parchment instead of contracts and test scores.

docs.title: Good News Message
docs.text:
A good news message is a short statement, in our own words, of why something about learning is good news, drawn from one real story and written so that the people it concerns would find it good. Chapter 11 promised that on the flight home we would write our own, and the travel journal of Chapter 2 has been practice for it: one thing we noticed, written the same day, in our own words. A good news message adds three tests from this chapter: it comes from a story we actually saw, it is honest about the cost, and it names who the good news is with. Chapter 9 supplies a fourth: the people it concerns must hear it as good.

Worked example: the fountain we could not read. Let's write one from Day 3. Just outside the Imperial Gate of Topkapı stands the Fountain of Ahmed III, carved with a poem that most Istanbulites today cannot read (Chapter 7). Here is a first draft, under a hundred words.

Outside the gate of Topkapı Palace is a fountain carved with a poem that most people in Istanbul can no longer read, because in 1928 their country changed its letters. The change taught a nation to read, and it cost them their grandparents' handwriting. Researchers are now teaching machines to read the old script. The good news is not that a machine can read the fountain. It is that a Turkish student, with her teacher beside her and the tool speaking her language, might choose to read it herself.

Now test it. A story we saw: yes, the fountain, on Day 3. Honest about the cost: yes, it names what the reform took as well as what it gave. With whom: a student and her teacher, in Turkish, by her own choice. Heard as good: here the draft is careful on purpose. How much Ottoman Turkish every Turk should learn is part of today's politics, so a visitor's message should not take a side; it says "might choose," and leaves the choice with the people whose history it is.

Write It for One Reader

Here's a way to get the draft right on the first try: before writing, name one real person the story concerns, a teacher, a grandmother, a student, and write the message as if they will read it over your shoulder. Then cut every sentence they would not find good.

docs.title: Lessons Across the Route
docs.text:
Lessons across the route are the conclusions we draw by reading all of the trip's stories together rather than one at a time, and the questions they leave for our own work. Chapter 11 ended with three leadership questions and Chapter 19 with seven Delphi questions; these are the last ones in the guide. Each takes a sentence or two in the travel journal, and the flight is long enough for all of them.

  1. Which story will I retell first, and what will I say behind its tourist script?
  2. Where did a delay cost the most, in the trip's stories or in my own work, and who paid for the waiting?
  3. Who is my scribe? Whose skill or living depends on the way things are done now, and what would a fair hearing look like?
  4. Where have I been tempted to move fast by command, and what would the ledger of that change look like in a generation?
  5. In whose language would my good news have to be told, and who would I ask to check the translation?
  6. For Dan, the evangelist's question: in the next school I talk to about AI, what will I ask before I explain, and how will I know whether the people there hear it as good news?
  7. My own good news message: from one story I actually saw on this trip, write it in under a hundred words, and test it the way the worked example did.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Seeing past the tourist script meant asking at every stop who got to learn and who was left out; gathered in one table, the Learning for All stories follow Chapter 2's four-step pattern almost everywhere.
  • The cost of delaying technology is real, as Chapter 6's press about 275 years late shows, but printing made copies, not readers, and rushing has costs too.
  • Scribal resistance, from Homer's reciters to Demetrius and Trithemius, is information about who stands to lose, and they are owed a hearing.
  • The costs of top-down reform show in the 1928 alphabet's ledger: fast gains, and a generation cut off from its past, partly by choices of method.
  • Education evangelism persuades people to adopt a better way of learning; Paul's method turns a pitch into questions that involve the people it concerns.
  • Evangelism's shadow falls when good news is imposed or its hearers despised. Ask who chose, what is treated as the obstacle, and what happens to those who say no.
  • Mother-tongue learning has long been UNESCO's position, and AI translation could make it affordable in small languages, if fluent speakers check its work.
  • Education with communities designs, runs, and judges a change with the people it serves; those left out at the end are usually those absent at the start. The AI-Native Schools companion works this out for schools.
  • A good news message comes from a story we saw, is honest about the cost, and names who it is with; the lessons across the route end the guide with questions for our own work.

Home, With a Notebook Full of Good News

You can now line up fifteen Learning for All stories on one four-step pattern, weigh what waiting cost against what rushing cost, and draw up an honest ledger for a reform that worked. You can also tell good news done with people from good news done to them, and you have written a message of your own from a story you saw with your own eyes. That's the whole route handled: for the next trip, start again at the beginning and Chapter 1's long timeline, and for the next school, open AI-Native Schools.

docs.title: Character Sheet: Glaux the Little Owl
docs.text: The canonical identity document for Glaux, the mascot for the Mediterranean Travels travel notebook. Every pose prompt and every piece of AI-generated content involving this character must re-anchor to the description below. It is the source of truth for visual and voice consistency.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
• Name: Glaux (pronounced "glowks", the ancient Greek word for owl)
  • Species: Little Owl (Athene noctua)
  • Subject: the history, culture, food and people of Turkey and Greece
  • Catchphrase: "Look closer."

docs.title: Visual Description
docs.text:
• Body color: warm earth brown with cream spots — hex #7a5a3a
  • Accent color: Aegean blue — hex #1f6f8b
  • Clothing / accessories: a small Aegean-blue scarf; a tan canvas satchel worn across the body with a small leather-bound travel notebook peeking out; a sprig of three olive leaves tucked into the satchel strap (the owl and olive sprig of the ancient Athenian silver coin)
  • Features true to the species: small, round and compact, with a flat rounded head and no ear tufts; bright lemon-yellow eyes under pale cream "eyebrows"; a cream-white throat patch; a short pale greenish-yellow beak; cream-spotted brown wings
  • Expression: alert, curious and warm, with the slight frown-browed look that is natural to little owls softened into friendliness
  • Size proportion: small and compact, readable at icon size (about 90px tall)
  • Art style: hand-drawn travel-sketchbook style: clean dark ink outlines with flat, softly shaded color fills, like an illustration in a traveler's journal

docs.title: Personality
docs.text:
• Curious: notices the detail most visitors walk past
  • Observant and patient: happy to stand still and look a while longer
  • Warm toward people: as interested in who lives here now as in who built the ruins
  • Gently witty: dry humor, never silly

docs.title: Voice
docs.text:
• Speaks to Ann and Dan as a fellow traveler, using "we", not as a teacher addressing students
  • Short, concrete sentences that point at something specific to see, taste or ask about
  • Adult tone: no baby talk, no exclamation-mark pile-ups, owl puns at most once in a long while
  • Signature phrases: "Look closer.", "Who lived here?", "Ask someone who lives here."

docs.title: Pronouns
docs.text: Glaux has no gender. Always write "Glaux" or they/them.

docs.text:

docs.title: Why This Mascot
docs.text: The little owl was the emblem of Athena and of Athens, stamped on the city's silver coins with an olive sprig, and it still lives across both Greece and Turkey, so it belongs to every stop on the route. Owls are proverbially watchful, which fits the guide's purpose: to slow down, look closer and notice more. The travel satchel and notebook make Glaux a traveler alongside us rather than a lecturer.

docs.title: Learning Graph for Mediterranean Travels
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement View the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 16 entry points
  • 598 concepts and 942 dependency edges in a single connected graph
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with 15 categories that follow the eras of the route and the guide's three threads
  • Category organization - foundations and travel skills first, the Learning for All synthesis last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 9.4% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
Every concept in the learning graph belongs to exactly one of these fifteen categories. The categories follow the shape of the trip: a foundation layer, the historical eras from the Bronze Age to today, the food along the route, and the three threads that run through the guide (leadership and change, prediction and AI, and learning for all). The TaxonomyID is the short code used in learning-graph.csv.

Category TaxonomyID Concepts that belong here Foundations and Timeline FOUND Geography of the region, the long timeline of periods, the big faiths and empires we assume the reader has heard of, and the skills of reading a ruin: classical orders, mosaics, frescoes, inscriptions, spolia, and stratigraphy Thoughtful Travel and Etiquette TRAV The cruise and itinerary, off-season timing and weather, useful Turkish and Greek phrases, hospitality customs, etiquette, and what tourism means to the people who host us Bronze Age Troy and Crete BRONZ Minoan Knossos, Linear A and B and their decipherment, Troy and its excavators, Homer and the Iliad, the Bronze Age collapse, and the alphabets that followed Classical Greece and Athens CLASS The Acropolis and its buildings, the Agora, Athenian democracy, the Persian Wars, theater, and the philosophers from Socrates to Aristotle Hellenistic and Roman World HELRO Alexander and Koine Greek, Hellenistic Rhodes and its Colossus, the Roman province of Asia, and the streets, theater, library, and houses of Ephesus Paul and Early Christianity PAUL Paul's life, journeys, and letters; his years in Ephesus; his core ideas; his legacy, including the harmful parts; and the Christian sites around Ephesus Byzantium and Constantinople BYZ Constantine, Justinian, Hagia Sophia, the cistern and walls, Orthodox icons, the schism, and the fall of Constantinople Knights and Venetians MEDV The Crusades, the Knights Hospitaller in Rhodes, Venetian Crete and its fortresses, and the Cretan scholars and Venetian printers who spread Greek texts Ottoman Empire and Islam OTTO Sultans and Sinan, Topkapı, the great mosques and their endowed complexes, the bazaars, the multi-faith empire, printing in Istanbul, and Islam in daily practice Modern Turkey and Greece MODRN Greek independence, Gallipoli, Atatürk and the Republic, the 1923 population exchange, the Jews of Rhodes, World War II, and daily life in each place today Food and Drink FOOD Turkish, Greek, and Cretan dishes and drinks, and the history carried in each one Delphi and the Oracle DELPH The sanctuary and its monuments, how a consultation worked, the famous answers, the oracle's flaws and decline, and the inscriptions "Know thyself" and "Nothing in excess" Prediction and AI PRED Machine learning and prediction, and the parallels between Delphi and modern models: data, ambiguity, bias, trust, calibration, horizons, and consent Leadership and Change LEAD Paul as a case study in change leadership and its lessons for moving schools from direct instruction to AI-native learning Learning for All LFA The stories along the route of who got to learn and who was left out, and their lessons for bringing AI-powered education to every child

See the Taxonomy Distribution Report for how many concepts fall into each category.

docs.title: Course Description Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the Trip Description for Mediterranean Travels as the seed document for the learning graph. It was generated by the learning-graph-generator skill (v1.07) on 2026-11-24.

Overall quality score: 97 / 100

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text: Element Points Score Notes Title 5 5 "Mediterranean Travels" — clear and descriptive Target Audience 5 5 Curious adult travelers, with an explicit note on their professional interest in AI and school change Prerequisites 5 5 Stated as "None", with the general knowledge assumed spelled out Main Topics Covered 10 10 24 numbered topics spanning Bronze Age to modern Turkey and Greece, plus two deep dives and a thread Topics Excluded 5 2 Implied ("This is not a textbook", no professional archaeology or theology) but no explicit out-of-scope list Learning Outcomes Header 5 5 "By the end of the trip, we will be able to:" Remember Level 10 10 Three outcomes: civilizations in order, Paul's journeys and letters, how a Delphi consultation worked Understand Level 10 10 Four outcomes across the trip, Paul, Delphi, and Learning for All Apply Level 10 10 Three outcomes: plan days around hours and prayer times, apply Paul's lessons, apply Delphi questions to AI Analyze Level 10 10 Four outcomes, including comparing builders' layers and who gained or lost from each reform Evaluate Level 10 10 Four outcomes, including weighing contested histories and where each parallel breaks down Create Level 10 10 Four outcomes with a natural capstone: the daily travel journal, plus leadership and Delphi reflections Descriptive Context 5 5 Strong "why this chapter exists" sections for each deep dive and the Learning for All thread Total 100 97

docs.title: Content Found
docs.text:
• A 13-day itinerary with dates, ports, and port times
  • One chapter per day, plus orientation, two deep-dive chapters, and a closing chapter
  • An eight-part template for every daily chapter (sights, history, things to notice, food, people, etiquette, practical notes, Learning for All)
  • Paul at Ephesus: seven content areas and a 13-row table of leadership lessons mapped to AI-Native Schools chapters
  • The Oracle and the Algorithm: eight content areas and a 10-row table of parallels between Delphi and machine prediction
  • Learning for All: 17 stop-by-stop stories, each with an AI-and-education parallel and a chapter link
  • Honest "where the parallel breaks down" sections for both deep dives

docs.title: Estimated Concept Count
docs.text:
The description supports roughly 450–600 distinct concepts. Each of the nine stops contributes 25–50 concepts (sites, people, events, objects, dishes, customs), and the three cross-cutting threads (leadership and change, prediction and AI, learning for all) add another 100+ concepts that connect places to ideas.

Compared with a typical general-education travel or history course, which yields 250–350 concepts, this description is unusually rich because of its cross-cutting threads and its explicit tables.

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Specificity. Named people, objects, scripture references, and dates give the generator concrete labels rather than vague topics.
  • Built-in dependencies. The tables already pair a historical story with a modern concept, which maps directly onto learning-graph edges.
  • Source awareness. The description repeatedly asks the guide to say which source a claim comes from (Acts vs. Paul's letters, Herodotus, Plato), which supports concepts like Primary Source and Myth Versus History.
  • Empathy and honesty. The "where the parallel breaks down" and "caution" sections add evaluative concepts that most travel guides lack.

docs.title: Gaps and Under-Represented Areas
docs.text:
• No explicit exclusions. A short "What this guide does not cover" list (for example detailed military history, Byzantine theology, or sites off the route such as Pergamon) would earn the remaining points and keep chapters focused.
  • Rhodes' Italian period (1912–1947) and modern Crete are only hinted at; they matter for understanding the 1944 deportation and the island's present.
  • Daily life today is a single topic; it could name specific themes (economy, migration, family, faith) per country.
  • Istanbul's day-by-day split across Days 1–5 is left open; naming a focus per day would sharpen chapter boundaries.

docs.title: Bloom's Taxonomy Suggestions
docs.text:
The outcomes already cover all six levels of the 2001 revised taxonomy. Two small improvements:

  • Remember in the general outcomes has a single bullet. Adding "recall a few Turkish and Greek courtesy phrases" and "name the signature dish of each stop" would round it out.
  • Create outcomes could name a final artifact for the closing chapter, such as a one-page "lessons from the route" summary that combines the journal, the leadership reflection, and the Delphi reflection.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text: With a score of 97, the description is well above the 70-point threshold and ready for learning-graph generation.

docs.title: Intelligent Textbook Feature Checklist
docs.text:
This checklist helps authors and product managers understand what features are available in the MkDocs Material intelligent textbook ecosystem. For each feature, you'll see whether it's implemented in this book and how much effort it takes to add.

Note

A level 2+ textbook is one that has rich interactivity but does not store any personal student data. A level 2+ textbook can be converted to a level 3 textbook by sending event data to a learning record store (LRS) to create a hyper-personalized learning experience for each student. The five levels of intelligent textbooks are described in the Intelligent Textbooks course.

An intelligent textbook goes beyond static text to include interactive simulations, personalized learning paths, auto-graded quizzes, and AI-generated content. This checklist tracks which of these capabilities are present in this textbook.

Legend:

  • Feature is not yet implemented
  • Feature is partially implemented

docs.title: List of Posters
docs.text:
Interactive infographics for the trip. Each poster is an illustration with an overlay: hover over a region for its name, click it for details, and switch to Quiz mode to test yourself.

Poster What it compares The Three Classical Orders Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian columns

docs.title: The Three Classical Orders
docs.text: Run the Three Classical Orders MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Greek architects worked in three related systems of design, called the classical orders: the Doric, the Ionic, and the Corinthian. Each order fixes the shape of a column's base, shaft, and capital, the parts of the beam it carries, and its proportions. This infographic shows one column of each order side by side, drawn to the same height, so their differences are easy to compare. Each column also carries a short piece of its own entablature.

The capital is the quickest clue. A plain cushion means Doric, a pair of spiral scrolls means Ionic, and a bell of acanthus leaves means Corinthian. The base, the flutes, and the proportions then confirm the answer.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  1. Hover over a column to see a short tooltip with its name and key feature.
  2. Click a column to open an infobox below the image with its base, shaft, capital, frieze, proportions, origins, and where we see it on our route. On a tablet or phone, tap a column instead.

Quiz mode: press Quiz Mode at the bottom. The name pills disappear, and a question appears below the image. Click the column that answers it. A correct answer shows a short explanation; a wrong one shakes the column so you can try again. The score counts your correct answers, and Try Again starts a new round with the questions in a new order.

Edit mode: add ?edit=true to the address of main.html to drag the corners of each column's zone, then press Copy JSON and paste the zones into data.json.

docs.title: The Three Columns
docs.text:
1. Doric: no base, about 20 sharp-edged flutes, a cushion capital under a square slab, and a frieze of triglyphs and metopes. Sturdy, about 4 to 6 diameters tall. The Parthenon.
  2. Ionic: a molded base, about 24 flutes separated by flat strips, and a capital with two spiral volutes. Slender, about 8 to 9 diameters tall. The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus and the Erechtheion.
  3. Corinthian: an Ionic-like base and shaft with a tall bell-shaped capital wrapped in acanthus leaves. The most slender, about 9 to 10 diameters tall. Roman Ephesus and the Temple of Olympian Zeus in Athens.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: The learner will identify the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders from their capitals, bases, flutes, and proportions, and name a building on our route built in each order.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Adult travelers on the trip (Mediterranean Travels).

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10–15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: The parts of a column and its entablature (base, shaft, flutes, capital, architrave, frieze, cornice), introduced in Chapter 10: Ephesus.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Hover over all three columns, then click each one and read its infobox. Name the single feature that best separates each order from the other two.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Compare the Ionic and Corinthian infoboxes. Which features do they share, and which one feature tells them apart?
  3. Assessment (5 min): Switch to Quiz mode and answer all nine questions.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: The learner answers at least 8 of the 9 quiz questions correctly on the first try and can explain, in one sentence, why a fluted drum alone cannot separate Ionic from Corinthian.

MicroSims are small interactive tools, such as maps and timelines, that help us see where we are going and how the places fit together. Each one can also be embedded in a daily chapter.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).

  • Viking Cruise Map - an interactive map of the Istanbul-to-Athens cruise and our Delphi day trip, with times, key sights, and the route.
  • Eras of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline - the nine periods from the Bronze Age to today drawn to scale, with six questions about how long each era lasted.
  • Events of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline - the same nine periods with 29 events on our route, each linked to the chapter that covers it.

  • Learning Graph Viewer - an interactive map of the 598 concepts in this guide and how they depend on each other, with search and category filters.

  • Antikythera Gears - a simplified p5.js gear model for Sun, Moon, and Mars cycles, with time and speed controls.

docs.title: Antikythera Gears
docs.text: Run the Antikythera Gears MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A gear train turns tooth counts into a calculation. Here, three expanded trains share the same time input: every tan gear on the left turns once per model year. The colored output gears represent simplified Sun, Moon, and Mars cycles. Numbers inside the gears are tooth counts; the dark spokes show rotation. The counters show total output turns since the starting position, ignoring direction.

For two meshing gears, the output speed is the input speed multiplied by the number of driver teeth divided by the number of driven teeth. The direction reverses at each mesh. A larger gear driving a smaller gear increases speed.

Output Tooth-count calculation Turns per model year Sun 48 / 48 1 Moon (48 / 12) × (39 / 12) 13 Mars 24 / 48 0.5

The Moon's 12-tooth intermediate gear and 39-tooth driver share a rigid axle, so they turn together. They are drawn apart and joined by a dashed line to make both stages visible. The dashed line represents that shared axle, not another pair of meshing gears. Likewise, the three left input gears are separated for readability; their common drive is omitted.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Leave the model paused and drag Year to compare any time from zero to two years. The slider also works backward.
  2. Use +1 month to advance by one twelfth of a model year. Each step pauses playback.
  3. Press Start to watch the meshing gears. Adjust Speed to change playback speed without changing any ratios.
  4. Press Pause to inspect a position, or Reset to restore time zero and the default speed. Playback stops at two years; Start then begins again at zero.

At one year, the output counters read 1, 13, and 0.5. At two years, they read 2, 26, and 1. The small Moon gear moves quickly because both stages multiply its speed.

docs.title: What We Simplified
docs.text:
This is an Antikythera-inspired teaching model, not a reconstruction of the ancient gear arrangement. Its tooth counts were chosen for easy arithmetic. The annual Sun cycle, 13 lunar circuits per year, and two-year Mars orbital cycle are rounded teaching values. The lunar circuit is a circuit relative to the stars, not a new-moon-to-new-moon phase cycle. Mars's orbital cycle is not its apparent geocentric motion or its interval between oppositions.

The model omits lunar phases, variable orbital speed, retrograde motion, eclipse prediction, calendar spirals, and the other planets. Gear rotation direction is a mechanical consequence of meshing, not a prediction of which way a body moves across the sky. The triangular teeth are a schematic drawing, not a manufacturing template.

Read the Antikythera mechanism appendix for the historical setting and the more complex functions of the original.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: Audience: adult travelers and introductory science learners. Duration: 10–15 minutes. Prerequisites: fractions, multiplication, and the idea of a rotating axle. Learning objective (Bloom: Apply): Calculate output turns from gear tooth counts and test the calculation by changing the model's time input.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict: Before moving the time slider, calculate the three output counts after half a year.
  2. Test: Set Year to 0.500. Compare the counters with your prediction: Sun 0.50, Moon 6.50, Mars 0.25.
  3. Trace: Follow the Moon train. Explain why the dashed axle connection preserves speed while each meshing pair changes it.
  4. Compare: Advance to one year, then two years. Identify which output completes a turn last.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: If the Mars driver had 48 teeth instead of 24, how many turns would its 48-tooth output make in one year? Explain using the ratio before answering: 48 / 48 gives one turn. This is a paper calculation; the model's tooth counts remain fixed.

        title="Simplified Antikythera gear model"></iframe>

To experiment with the code, copy antikythera-gears.js into the p5.js Editor using p5.js 2.3.4.

docs.title: Eras of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline
docs.text: Run the Eras of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
More than five thousand years separate the first Bronze Age villages from our trip, and that span is hard to feel. This timeline draws the nine periods of Eastern Mediterranean history to scale, from the Bronze Age (c. 3200 BCE) to the modern era (2026 CE), so their lengths can be compared by eye. The Bronze Age fills almost half the line. The Classical period, the age of the Parthenon and Socrates, is a thin sliver, and the Byzantine period is longer than most travelers expect.

The timeline shows periods only. Events are left out on purpose, so the band lengths are the one thing to look at. Clicking a band names one or two sites on our route from that period. The full version, with 29 events and the chapter that covers each, is the Events of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline in the appendix.

The timeline is also a short quiz. It asks six questions about proportion, one at a time. Each answer is committed before the relevant bands are highlighted and their lengths shown, so the display checks the learner's mental picture instead of handing over the answer.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Answer question 1. The nine bands are visible at full scale. Choose an answer by judging the band lengths.
  2. Read the feedback. The bands named in the question are highlighted, their lengths in years appear on the bands, and the timeline zooms to them. The feedback explains the answer either way.
  3. Press Next. The view returns to the full span and the next question appears.
  4. After question 6 the right-hand panel shows the final score. Press Full span to see all nine periods, then click any band to read its dates, length, and the sites on our route from that period.
  5. Restart clears the score and returns to question 1.

Drag the timeline sideways to pan. The mouse wheel scrolls the page, not the timeline.

docs.title: Reading the Dates
docs.text: Years BCE are counted down and years CE are counted up, and there is no year zero. The axis marks the line between them as BCE | CE. The quiz uses the chapter's rule for spans that cross that line: add the two numbers and subtract one. From 31 BCE to 330 CE is 31 + 330 − 1 = 360 years. Dates marked "c." (circa) are approximate. Period boundaries are rounded and vary from place to place, so each band's infobox says so.

        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: The travelers on this trip: curious adults who love the history of civilization, culture, and food.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Compare the order and length of the nine periods of Eastern Mediterranean history by answering six proportion questions before the answers are revealed, scoring at least 5 of 6 (Bloom: Understand, verb: compare).

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: The sections "The Historical Timeline" and "BCE and CE Dating" in Chapter 1: historical timeline, period (era), BCE and CE dating, no year zero, and the names of the nine periods.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (5 min): Answer the six questions in order by eye, without working out the numbers first. Note which answers surprised you.
  2. Explore (3 min): After question 6, click each band and find the period of the site you most want to see.
  3. Reflect (2 min): Using the 24-hour clock from the chapter, say in one sentence why the Classical period feels long but is not.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Exploring the timeline and clicking bands are practice, not evidence. Each question targets a misconception:

Question Misconception it tests 1. Bronze Age or Classical? The Classical period was long because it is famous. 2. How much of the timeline is the Bronze Age? Prehistory is a short prelude to "real" history. 3. Byzantine or Ottoman? The Byzantine period was a short epilogue to Rome. 4. Classical + Hellenistic + Roman, or Byzantine? The Byzantine period was a short epilogue to Rome. 5. Length of the Roman period, 31 BCE to 330 CE? Spans across the BCE/CE line are found by subtracting. 6. When was writing almost unknown? Writing in Greece was continuous from the Bronze Age on.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Bronze Age - Wikipedia - Overview of the period, its metallurgy, and the regional chronologies behind its rounded dates.
  2. Late Bronze Age collapse - Wikipedia - The destruction of palace societies around 1200–1150 BCE and the loss of Linear B.
  3. Byzantine Empire - Wikipedia - The eastern Roman Empire from the founding of Constantinople to 1453.
  4. Year zero - Wikipedia - Why the BC/AD and BCE/CE systems have no year zero, and how astronomers number years.
  5. vis-timeline documentation - vis.js - The JavaScript library used to draw this timeline.

docs.title: Events of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline
docs.text: Run the Events of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This is the full version of the Eras of the Eastern Mediterranean Timeline from Chapter 1. That version shows only the nine periods, so a first-time reader can see their lengths without distraction. This version adds 29 events on our route, from the first palace at Knossos (c. 1900 BCE) to the founding of the Republic of Turkey (1923 CE), on the same to-scale line. Each event names the chapter of this book that covers it in depth, so the timeline doubles as a map of the book in time. It is the timeline in the Timeline of Events appendix.

The timeline is also a short quiz. It asks six questions, one at a time, about the lengths of periods and the gaps between events. Each answer is committed before the relevant bands and events are highlighted, so the display checks the learner's mental picture instead of handing over the answer.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Answer question 1. The nine bands are visible at full scale; the events are hidden. Choose an answer by judging the band lengths.
  2. Read the feedback. The bands and events named in the question are highlighted, their lengths in years appear on the bands, and the timeline zooms to them. The feedback explains the answer either way.
  3. Press Next. The view returns to the full span and the next question appears. Events from earlier questions stay on the timeline.
  4. After question 6 all 29 events appear and the right-hand panel shows the final score. Press Full span to see everything, then click any band or event to read its dates, description, and the chapter that goes deeper.
  5. Restart clears the score and hides the events again.

Use ◀ ▶ to pan, + − to zoom (down to a 200-year window), or drag the timeline sideways. The mouse wheel scrolls the page, not the timeline.

When events are crowded, some are drawn as a dot without a label. Hover over a dot to see its name, or zoom in to make room for the labels.

docs.title: Reading the Dates
docs.text: Years BCE are counted down and years CE are counted up, and there is no year zero. The axis marks the line between them as BCE | CE. The quiz uses Chapter 1's rule for spans that cross that line: add the two numbers and subtract one. From 480 BCE to 330 CE is 480 + 330 − 1 = 809 years. Dates marked "c." (circa) are approximate.

docs.title: Regions of the Eastern Mediterranean Map
docs.text: Run the Regions of the Eastern Mediterranean Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Chapter 1 opens with a map because almost every later chapter leans on it. This MicroSim is that map, drawn like an atlas plate from Natural Earth coastlines. Only the places named in "Part One: The Map" carry labels, along with the seas and the two countries we travel through, Greece and Turkey.

Twelve places are key regions, the ones the rest of the book keeps returning to:

Kind Key regions Seas Eastern Mediterranean, Aegean Sea Straits Bosphorus, Dardanelles Land regions Thrace (European Turkey), Anatolia, Ionia, Attica and Central Greece Islands Crete, the Cyclades, the Dodecanese, the North Aegean Islands

Nine more places are labeled as context and can also be clicked: the Black Sea, the Sea of Marmara, the Ionian Sea, the Sporades, the Saronic Islands, the Ionian Islands, Cyprus, the Levant, and Egypt.

Historic regions such as Ionia and Thrace never had fixed borders, so their inland edges are drawn as dashed lines and called approximate. Their coastlines are exact.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  • Hover over any region, sea, or strait to see an infobox: what kind of place it is, its other names, a one-line summary, and which of our stops are in it.
  • Click a key region to explore it. It turns olive green, gets a ✓ on the map and on the checklist, and a small burst of confetti marks the find. The detail panel below the map gives the fuller story.
  • Explore all 12 and a confetti cannon fires.
  • Can't find one? Click its name on the Checklist and the map zooms to it and makes it flash. That gives no credit: the region still has to be clicked on the map.
  • Drag to pan, and use + and − to zoom in on the islands. The mouse wheel scrolls the page as usual, not the map.

Find the Region mode hides the names of the 12 key regions and asks for them one at a time, in random order:

  • A correct click turns the region green and moves on.
  • A wrong click names the place that was clicked and gives a hint about where to look.
  • After two misses, or after pressing Show me, the answer flashes yellow and must be clicked to continue. It then counts as found, but not on the first try.
  • The score is the number found on the first try. Finishing fires the confetti cannon.

Keyboard users can Tab to each region and press Enter to click it.

docs.title: Learning Events (xAPI)
docs.text:
This MicroSim records what a student does as xAPI statements, the standard format a Learning Record Store reads. It does not send them anywhere yet.

Students never see the statements. To watch them arrive, add ?show-events=true to the URL, either the sim's own URL or the URL of a page that embeds it, such as this page. An Event stream tab then appears under the map, already open. Copy JSON copies every statement.

Verb When it is emitted What it carries initialized The map loads, or a Find challenge starts — experienced A hover of at least 0.6 seconds in Explore mode how long the hover lasted interacted A click on a region in Explore mode, or a mode change first visit or revisit, count explored asked Show me, or a click on a checklist name which region answered A click in Find mode correct or not, what was clicked, attempt number completed All 12 explored, or the Find challenge finished first-try score out of 12

Shorter hovers are treated as the mouse passing over, not as evidence, and are not recorded. The actor is always anonymous. Each statement is also announced to the page in three ways a future connection can use: a microsim:xapi window event, a postMessage to the page that embeds the iframe, and window.MicroSimEvents.statements().

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Locate the 12 key regions, island groups, seas, and straits of the Eastern Mediterranean on an unlabeled map (Bloom's level: Remember; verb: locate).

docs.title: Audience and Duration
docs.text: Travelers preparing for the trip, or any adult or high-school learner meeting this geography for the first time. 10–15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read "Part One: The Map" in Chapter 1, or at least its first section, "The Eastern Mediterranean".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 minutes). Hover across the map from Istanbul to Crete, reading each infobox. Then click all 12 key regions until the cannon fires. For each one, say aloud which continent it is on.
  2. Notice the straits (2 minutes). Zoom in on the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles. Explain to a travel partner why whoever held these two narrow waters could "tax, feed, or starve" the cities of the Black Sea.
  3. Find the Region (5 minutes). Switch modes and find all 12 with the names hidden. Aim for at least 9 on the first try.
  4. Retry the misses. Any region marked red on the list needed a hint. Explore it once more, then play the challenge again.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 9 or more of 12 found on the first try in Find the Region mode. The completed statement records that score, so an instructor connected to a Learning Record Store can see it without asking.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Eastern Mediterranean - Wikipedia - The region this map covers and the countries usually counted in it.
  2. Anatolia - Wikipedia - Name, extent, and geography of the Asian part of Turkey.
  3. Ionia - Wikipedia - The ancient Greek region on Anatolia's Aegean coast.
  4. Aegean Sea - Wikipedia - Area, boundaries, and island groups of the Aegean.
  5. Bosporus and Dardanelles - Wikipedia - The Turkish Straits.
  6. Natural Earth - public-domain map data - Source of the 1:10m country outlines, loaded through the world-atlas package.
  7. D3.js - Observable - The JavaScript library that draws the map.
  8. xAPI Overview - Rustici Software - What xAPI statements and Learning Record Stores are.

docs.title: Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text: This interactive viewer lets you explore the 598 concepts in the Mediterranean Travels learning graph, from the Bronze Age to the eggplant on our dinner plates. The 15 colored categories follow the eras of the route and the guide's three threads. Larger boxes are concepts that more of the guide builds on.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Search: Type in the search box to find specific concepts
  • Category Filtering: Use checkboxes to show/hide concept categories
  • Interactive Navigation: Click and drag to explore, scroll to zoom
  • Statistics: View real-time counts of visible nodes and edges

docs.title: Using the Viewer
docs.text:
1. Search for Concepts: Start typing in the search box to find concepts. Click on a result to focus on that node.

  2. Filter by Category: Use the category checkboxes in the sidebar to show or hide groups of related concepts. Use "Check All" or "Uncheck All" for bulk operations.

  3. Navigate the Graph:

  4. Drag to pan around the graph
  5. Scroll to zoom in and out

  6. Click on a node to select it and highlight its connections

  7. View Statistics: The sidebar shows counts of visible nodes, edges, and foundational concepts.

docs.title: Graph Structure
docs.text:
• Foundational Concepts (left side): Prerequisites with no dependencies
  • Advanced Concepts (right side): Topics that build on multiple prerequisites
  • Edges: Arrows point from a concept to its prerequisites
